RING, BELLS, RING. Written in honor of the marriage of the Duke of Albany to the Frinc Sc Helen of Waldeck, April 27th, 1882, Ring, bel!s, ring! Ring out the note; of a great prean ! Ring loudly, let your ring ng be an Euphony to ro.alty. Ring with symphonious power, From each moss-discoinred tower, (Hid amongst its ivy-dower), pa•an 01 ioyaltr. • Ring, bells. ring ! Ring, bells, ring! Ring from your balfries o'd and crumbling, Though time-born dust around be humbling, Around in merry company! Ring ft om Minster's dashing fires From their crested Gothic spires, Ring as he who never tires: Long live the Duke of Albany. Ring, bells, ring! Ring, bells, ring ! Ring fr in even/ spire and steeple, This message from the British people To; he Princess Helen; Welcome as a bride whose graces Fit thee for life's higher placss ; May the smile of royal faces Ever greet the, Helen ! Ring, bells, ring ! Warrington, April 27th, 1352.
BENJAMIN SAWDON.

ELOPIS G. (A monologue, by the Lady.) "It is coming, it is coming, Such a wealth of joy for me! Hark! the birds are sweetly humming • Happiness is nigh to thee!' Yes. I feel it; yes, I know it. For my lover's word is true; He has written—wll I show ii? No, my friend, not e'en to you!" "How my heart is growing lighter— Once I feared impending gloom; And the sun is shining brighter. Yea, the flowers more richly bloom. Oh! the easta.cy of hoping, Yet the time is strangely slow. I shall almost dread eloping It it does not quicker go! "NOW's the hour, and yet how horrid! Arthur, this, this is too bad; I had thought the prospect florid, Now I find it only sad Possibly the boy is teasing. Or perhaps he's seen a face- More than mine his fauey pleasing For its purer, fresher grace. " Still no Arthur ! It is awful ! Os ! my fate is quite intense. Is his conduct is it lawful? Can I get no recompense? Now, upon my word! 'tis raining ! No! well, well, it's very dark; And, without unjust complaining, This is such a (Leary park! " See, the sun is scarcely shining, And the flowers ab not my feet Seem to languish; are they pining For the summer's absent heat? Arthur, Arthur, how unkindly You are treating* me to-day! Yet, I trow, that loving blindly, I for you have gone astray. " So I'll leave this spot in sadness, To return, alas! not home; But, perchance, to strive with madness, I a fugitive will roam. And among the world's grim shailows I will blue my a• hing head, Till the Angel of the Flades. Calls me to the peaceful dead. "It is coming, it is coming— Life with rain and tears for me. Mark! I hear a doleful humming: Misery is nigh to thee.' Nought but crying, nought but moping, Nought but ever-flowing tears; This resultant from eloping Ere the mazy pathway c!ears. "It is coming; he is truly; ' There, I see him, walking fast! Heart, be stiil you are u ruly, And, and Arthur may go past! No, he's coming, nearer, nearer; Oh ! I'm fainting frcni delight. And the atmosphere is clearer, And the sun shines very bright. "All the trees look so resplendent, Nature vernal, fresh and sweet, Fragrant perfumes are ascendant, And this is a rare retreat. Fie to shadows, fie to Hades, Fie to sorrowful designs! I shall envied be of ladies Ere this golden day declines." Warrington, April 17, 1882.
BENJ. SAWDON.

"Though thou art false, I love time still !" said the old maid, as she saw her false teeth drop overboard. Sam: "What is bigot-id ?" "Why," said Pete," bigoted Is knowing too much for one, and not enough for two. Dryden' s translation of Virgil being commended by a right reverend Bishop, a witty Earl said, "The original is indeed excellent, but everything suffers by translation—ex- cept a Bishop." Doctor: t! Well, mariner, which tooth do you want ex- tracted ? Is it the molar or the incisor ?" Jack: "Itis in the upper tier, on the larboard side." Speak in language your hearer understands. A. gentleman relating an accident he had met with at Greenwich front a fall, was asked by a sergeant if it was near the vertebra that he had been hurt. "No, sir," was the reply, "it was Lear the observatory." Mr. Charles Mathews, in pro?osing the toast of the Army and Navy at his farewell banquet, said, "I have never been in the army, though I have been in many a mess; and the only chance I ever had of joining the navy was once when I had a narrow escape of getting into the Fleet !" Judge Burke, of South Carolina, died an old bachelor, and in his will left a maiden lady in Charleston six hundred pounds sterling, and gave as a relson for leaving this legacy, that he had courted the lady ten years, and, " be- fore Josbua, he believed that if he had persevered she would have had him."—Harper's Monthly. It never pays to fret and growl When fortune seems our foe, The better bred will push ahead, And strike the braver blow. For luck is work. And those who shirk Should not lament their doom, But yield the play, .Aucl clear the way,
That better men have room.

Sin WALTEit RALEIGH'S GALLANTRY EMULATED,—It IS related in a French memeir that when the Queen was leav- ing Eu a heavy shower of rain fell, and the ground was very damp. There was a space to be traversed between the can!. age and the royal yacht. All the French courtiers took off their cloaks and overcoats, and speedily spread a carpet for her Maj estseto walk on dryehod. A precisely similar occurrence Is related in the life of Dr. Wbewell, of some noblemen and gentlemen doing the same thing when the Queen visited the chapel of Trinity College. It is curious that Sir Walter Raleigh's famous episode of gallantry should thus be re- peated both in England and 'France.— London Society. "OPEN-MINDEDNESS."—The following is the prefatory dedication to Robert Bowring of a recently published work, the Graphic Arts, by Philid Gilbert Hamerton :—"I wish to dedicate this book to you as the representative of a class that ought to be more numerous—the class of large-minded persons who can take a lively interest in arts which are not specially their own. No one who has not carefully observed the narrowing of men's minds by specialities could believe to what a degree it goes. Instead of being open, as yours has always been, to the influences of literature in the largest sense, as well as to the influences of the graphic arts and music, the specialised mind shuts itself up in its own pur- suit so exclusively that it does not even know what is nearest to its own closed doors. We meet with scholars who take no more account of the graphic arts than if they did not exist, and with painters who never read; but what is still more surprising is the complete indifference with which an art can be regarded by men who know and practice another not widely removed from it. One may be a painter, and yet know nothing whatever about any kind of engraving: one may be a skilled engraver, and yet work in lifelong misun- derstanding of the rapid arts. If the specialists who devote themselves to a single study had more of your interest in the work of others, they might find, as you have done, that the quality which may be called open-mindedness is far from being an impediment to success, even in the highest and most arduous of artistic and intellectual pursuits. How LONG ?—A Chicago correspondent sends us the following : —During a recent trial before Justice Dougherty It was thought important by counsel to determine the length of time that certain "2 quarters of beef and 1 sheep" re- mained in an express waggon in front of plaintiff's store be- fore they were taken away by the defendant. The witness under examination was a German, whose knowledge of the English language was limited; but he testified in a very , plain, straightforward way to having weighed the meat, and to having afterward carried it oat and put it into the afore- mid waggon. Then the following ensued: —Counsellor Enos : "State to the jury how long it was after you too': the meat from the store and put it into the waggon before it was taken away."—Witness : "Now I sheen cand dell dat. I dinks 'bout dwelve feet. I not say nearer as dat."— Counsel: "You don't understand me. How long was it from the time the meat left the store, and was put into the waggon, before it was taken away by the defendant?"— Witness : "Now I know not what you ax dat for. Der mit der siile-valk, anti dat's shoost so vaggon h. l.vas bYacckvuudpell me how long der sideevalk long as it as. VAS. Den feet? D welve feet? Den I dells you how long it vas." —Counsel: "I Oon't want to find out how wide the side- walk was, but I want to know" (speaking very slowly) "how —long —this—meat—was—in—the waggon—before—it was—taken—away ?"_Witness: "Oh ! dat! Veil, now, I not sold any meat so. I all time weigh him; never mea- sured meat, not yet. But I dinks 'bout dree feet." (Here the spectators and his Honour end the jury smiled audibly.) "I know nr:, ntlemens, how is die. I dell you all I can, CO good as I know."—Counsel: "Look here, I want to know how long it was before the meat was taken away after it was put into the waggon ?"—Witness (looking very knowingly at counsel): "Now you try and get me in a scrape. Dat yncat ass shoost so long in der voggon as he vas in der shop. Dat'm all I told you. Dat meat was dead meat. He don't go no longer in den donsan' year, not mooch."—Counsel: That will do."—Harper's Monthly.

This two children. A leading feature of her successful manage. is provable by comparative weighing.—Gentleman's Maya- ment was "soiling the poultry," especially in winter. zin-e. "She kept the'south windows of her house full 'of trays about 18in. wide, 3ft. long, and 3in. deep. These trays were filled with earth and sown with wheat. The earth was kept well watered. As often as the spires or foliage grew to be two or three inches long she clipped it wkh her shears and fed it to the laying hens. This soiling method may be en- larged on and supplemented by a system of grazing. Few sights are more desolate than most gardens in late autumn, during the winter, and in early spring. Much of this may be changed. As late even as the sunehiny days of the last of November, and which extend often into December, the whole surface of the garden may be raked over and sown with winter wheat or winter rye. Of course it is better to be done in October. It will do often, however, as late as November or December. This winter grain comes up, and during the late fall, at open times in"the winter and in the early spring it furnishes first-class grazing for the hens, in- creasing their laying qualities to a remarkable degree. At least a bushel of seed should be sown on a quarter of an acre. This is more than double the seed used when sowing for a crop of grain. It makes the ground look even and green in- stead of rough, disorderly, and desert like. It therefore pays abundantly for the trouble and expense, simply as an element of beautifying the premises and making the home surroundings look cheerful. Last, hut not least, the heavy growth of green, when turned under in the spring, more than pays for itself by fertilising for the next season's gar- den growths. The chief gain on the whole operation, how• ever, is the grazing it supplies to the laying hens."—New York Tribune.

ILLUSTRIOUS IRISH MEN.

The harp that once through Tara's hall The soul of music shed, Now hangs as mute on Tara's walls, As if that soul were fled— 1 Bo sleeps the pride of former days, So glory's thrill is o'er' And hearts that once beat high for praise Now feel that pulse no more. No more to chiefs and ladies bright The harp of Tara swells, The chord alone that breaks at night It's tale of ruin tells. Thus freedom now so seldom- wakes, The only throb she gives Is when some heart indignant breaks To show that still she lives. It must be admitted that the Melodies are not so distinctly national as they might have been, but considered as poetry it would be difficult to improve on most of them. Other poets may have shown greater powers, greater connections, greater sublimity in their more sustained flights, but to none was ever given so fall a gift of sweetness, and no one ever possessed the. fascination of numbers equal to the author of the "Irish Melodies." Byron, the grand Napoleon of the realm of rhyme, ruled the world of poetry in his day, but Moore charmed Byron, and there exists no true worshipper of song who has not trembled to the heart's core beneath the passionate notes, conquered by the winged words of the " Bard of Erin." How much Tom Moore accomplished for Ireland we cannot tell. He has been styled the national poetry of Ireland, and so he is in the same sense as TASSO is to the Venetians, or Beranger to the French, or Burns to the Scotch, for he patri- otically consecrated his finest powers to the exposition and illustration of Ireland's peculiar feelings and associations local, personal, and traditionary. Certainly it was not his mission to evoke the lightning of the national spirit, and hurl its consuming fire at the men' who, had they possessed the power, would have rivited the fetters of the people, but he did soothe the surging paroxysms with lulling words of praise and hope, and, transforming their terribly real physical and moral griefs and ills into picturesque and senti- mental sorrows, he did awaken in the languid admiration and a passing sympathy for the nation which could boast such beautiful music, and whose woes were so agreeably, so charmingly, sung. Apart from this, his influence over Ire- land and the Irish must have been immense and for good. The power of song is proverbial, and beyond all question. "Give me," said the patriotic Fletcher, of Saltonn, strong in his knowledge of man's nature, "give me the making of the nation's songs, and I will leave to others the making of its laws." Bishop South was of.opinion that one song like the Hymn of Harmodies did more towards rousing the spirit of the Romans than the phillipics of Cicero. John Leyden, in the delirium of a mortal fever at Java, was heard repeat- ing snatches of old Border songs Verstigan mentions that a traveller in Palestine was once startled by a captive Scotch woman singing as she dandled her baby at the door of one of the Arab tents, "Oh, Bothwell banks, thou bloomest fair." Even among the hireling Swiss we know that Napo- leon, to prevent desertion from his ranks, found it necessary to prohibit the chanting of the "Rang des Vaches,'s and Campbell has finely said, and not less truly than finely, that Encamped by Indian rivers wild, The soldier, resting on his arms, In Burns's carol sweet recalls The songs that blest him when a child, And glows and gladdens,at the charms Of Scotia's woods and wfferfalls. " One touch of nature," says Shakspere, "makes all flesh kin," and what that national music and that national poetry are to the Scotch, the national poetry and music of Moore are to the Irish. Hence. like Burns, Moore has a double guarantee of immortality, for he has wedded undying lays to undying notes, and thus not only driven the nail securely to the head, bet has riveted it on the other side. He died in 1852, and the green grass is now waving over his head, but "his soul is marching on." And though he may be censured and justly criticised for some of his lifework, it is nevertheless pleasant to think that it is the best of him that lives in the love, the tenderness, the homejoys, and the chastened griefs of millions, and will so live through many a generation.

BY ILLIAM FRANCIS. No. XVII.—TOM MOORE: THE BARD OF ERIN. Oh turn awhile and though the shamrock wreathes My homely harp, yet shall the song it breathes Of Ireland's slavery and of Ireland's woes Live when the memory of her tyrant foes Shall but exist, all future knaves to mourn, Embalm'd in hate and canonised by scorn, When Castlereagh in sleep still more profound Than his own opiate tongue now deals around, Shall wait th' impeachment of that awful day, Which ev'n his practised hand can't bribe away. Torn Moore. This Illustrious Irishman was born on the 30th of May, 1780, in Dublin, where his father carried on a small and an- remunerative trade in spirits and grocery. Some men are ashamed of their pedigree, and consider it a disgrace if it should be known that their parents earned their bread and cheese in an honest but humble manner. Not so Tom Moore. He never attempted to conceal the humbleness of his origin. When introduced by the Earl of Mona to the Prince of Wales soon after the publication of his translation of Anacrcon his Royal Highness inquired of the poet whether he was not the son of Dr. Moore, the author of Zeluco? "No, sir," replied Moore, without hesitation, "my father was a grocer in Dublin." Both his parents were strict Catholics, and he, of course, was educated in the same faith —a faith which was not only at that time under the ban of penal statutes, but of influential opinion both of Great Britain and Ireland. As a child Moore was, we are told, re- markable for beauty, and might have sat, says a writer not over friendly to him, as "Cupid for a picture." This early promise was not fulfilled. Sir Walter Scott, speaking of him in 1825, says:—" He is a little MAU, less, I think, than Lewis, whom he resembles. His countenance is plain, but very animated when speaking or singing." When a lad he was sent to an excellent echool kept by a Mr. Whyte. This was the Mr. Whyte who, thirty years before, attempted to educate Richard Brindsley Sheridan,and pronounced him to be "an incorrigible dance"—a verdict in which at that time the mother of the future author of the School of Scan- dal fully coincided. But Moore was one of Mr. Weyte'e favourite pupils—his show scholar, as he himself says. It was in 1789 that the French Revolution broke out. This meteor blaze, which suddenly leaped forth and dazzled the astonished world, seemed a light from Heaven to the oppressed nations of Europe, and in Ireland especially it was hailed as the dawn of a great deliverance by many whom an unwise legislation had alienated and almost maddened. Young Moore was little more than twelve years of age when he sat upon his father's knee at a great banquet in Dublin where the toast—" May the breezes from France fan our Irish oak into verdure," was received with a frantic vehemence which, child as he was, left an impression upon him that did not pass away for many years. The "Day Star of Liberty," as it was called, set in blood and tempest, but the Government, alarmed at the ominous aspect of the ' times, relaxed the penal laws, and Catholics for the first time were eligible for admission to the Dublin University— eligible, that is, to partake of the instruction conferred at the national seat of learning, but not for its honours and re- wards. From Mr. Whyte's school, therefore, Moore was transferred to Trinity College, where he became intimate with the two Emmets, and an active member of the debating club in which the eldest and the unfortunate Robert en- deavoured to mature their oratorical powers against the time when their dreams of political regeneration should be real- ised. Towards the close of the year 1797 the paper called The Press was started by Arthur O'Connor, the Einmetts and other chiefs of the United Irishmen. eMoore first con- tributed a poetical effusion fo this paper—afterwards a fiery letter which had the questionable honour of being after- wards quoted in the House of Commons by a Minister as one of the proofs that severe repressive measures were required to put down the dangerous spirit ia Ireland. From Dublin he went to London to study law, practically ceasing to be an Irishman, except in genius and in love to the land, for after travelling on the Continent and in America, and some residence abroad (as he had obtained a Government place in Bermuda), he settled in England and there remained till his death in 1852. Moore did not apply himself diligently to law. The charms of poetry diverted him from those of jurisprudence. In 1800 he published the Anacreon. His reputation was made at once. Scholars admired his learning and critical skill, and poets hailed another master of the lyre. Erskine said with characteristic neatness : Ah mourn not for Anacreon dead Ah weep not for Anacreon fled The lyre still breathes he touched before For we have our Anacreon Moore. He did not altogether escape censure, however. Anacreon (or the writer whose works are known under his name) was, alas! a teacher after the time in which he lived, and Moore "bettered the instruction." A severe reviewer, speaking-of him as a translator, said too truly :—" His muse must only be seen in ball costume or if ever he allows her to appear in undress it must be the neglige of the Paris elegante." For, a severe critique of one of his works in the Edinburgh, in which it was justly denounced as licentious and a public nuisance, Moore challenged Jeffry, but the parties were saved from shooting at each other by the police. Then the reviewer took back the severe parts, and he and Moore be- came good friends Probably Moore was none the worse for the literary castigation, and Jeffry had sufficient reason to justify generous acknowledgment of his later excellencies. Moore tried his hand on various styles of literary work in prose and poetry, but made several failures. Some of these, including a comic opera, he did not place in his collected works. He also wrote the Sceptic and two short poems called "Corruption" and "Intolerance," in the stately Juvenalian style of satire. The vein was, however, -too serious for one of Moore's lively temperament, and they met with little snccess. The poet, therefore, seized a lighter weapon, which he handled with a skill and efficiency that left him without a rival. In 1812 he published "The In- tercepted Letter, or the Twopenny Poetbag, by Themes Brown, the Younger." This was a collection of sarcastic poems levelled at the Prince Regent and the ruling poll. ticians of the day. These poems were better adapted to the popular taste than his philosophic and semi-religious efforts, and they had a great but necessarily transient success. Such pieces lose their force and piquancy by the passing into oblivion of the ephemera against which they were directed. Wit which strikes at individuals dies with the world's re- membrance of the crimes or follies of the persons assailed, and who cares now for the brilliant butterflies of Carlton House, or the gilded gadflies, social or political, which in- fested the atmosphere of the vain Regent's Court. But in the days when Punch was not, Moore's pungent hits at reigning follies, delivered in brilliant verse, found an echo on every tongue, and did at that time what the caricatures of Mr. Punch do now. They showed forth at a glance the comic side of every event, and never failed to bring forth as vividly the ridicule appropriate to the subject. It were easy to furnish our readers with illustrations of Moore's peculiar style in this line of composition. We will content ourselves with one, and that because it is apropos of the series we have in hand. O'Connell had been invited to dine with the Viceroy, and there had been no little stir about the matter. All manner of reports were in circulation. Whereupon our "Illustrious Irishman" published "Some account of the late dinner to Dan" on this wise:— From tongue to tongue the rumour flew; All ask'd aghast Is't true? le't true? But none knew whether t'was fact or fable; And still, the unholy rumour ran From Tory woman to Tory man Though none to come at the truth was able, Till, 10, at last, the fact came out, The horrible fact beyond all doubt, That Dan had dined at the Viceroy's table Had flash'd his Popish knife and fork In the heart of the Established mutton and pork. Who can forget the deep sensation That news produced in this orthodox nation? Deans, rectors, curates all agreed, If Dan was allowed at the Castle to feed, T'was clearly all up with the Protestant creed There hadn't indeed such an apparition Been heard of in Dublin since that day When during the first grand exhibition Of Don Giovanni, that naughty play, There appeared as if raised by necromancers An extra devil among the dancers • Yes, everyone saw with fearful thrill That a devil too much had joined the quadrille And the sulphur was smelt and the lamps let fall A grim green light o'er the ghastly ball And the poor sham devils didn't like it at all For they knew from whence the intruder had come Though he left that night his tail at home. This fact we see is a parallel case To the dinner that some weeks since took place, With the difference slight of fiend and luau; It shows what a nest of Popish sinners That city must be where the Devil and Dan May thus drop in at quadrilles and dinners. But mark the end of these foul proceedings, These demon hops and Popish feedings, Some comfort 'twill be to those at least Whole studied this awful dinner question, To know that Dan on the night of that feast, • Was seized with a dreadful indigestion, That envoys were sent, post haste to his Priest, To come and absolve the suffering sinner For eating so much at a heretic's dinner. And some good people were even afraid, That Peel's old confectioner still at the trade Had poison'd the Papist with orangeade. Tom Moore had long cherished a hope of allying his poetry with the expressive music of Ireland—of giving ap• propriate vocal utterance to the strains which had, broken fitfully from out the tumults and tramplings of centuries of noblest rule. This was a noble task, which demanded great powers and deserved high praise for even partial success. The execution of this long-cherished design now com- menced, and the "Melodies," as they appeared, obtained immense and well•deserved popularity. It is upon these his fame as a poet will mainly rest. While "Lalah Rooke" has been much printed and read, and really represents much learning as well as much imagination, it appeals to a narrower circle than the Melodies. The softness, the rhythm the tenderne.s, the naturalness of the Melodies have se- cured for them a permanent place among lyric productions. No one can deny that as a whole they exhibit great felicity of expression and much graceful tenderness of thought and feeling, frequently relieved by flashes of gay and genial wit and humour. Some of them, like "The Last Rose of Summer," or "Love's Young Dream," or "The Harp that once through Tara's Hall," will awaken, and thrill, and melt the hearts of multitudes wherever the English tongue is spoken. The Editor will kindly allow us to give his readers one of them

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The dispute at the Glynrhonwy slate quarry, Llanberis, has been settled, and the men resumed work on Monday. A meeting of coal-owners and workmen was held at New- castle on Saturday, on the question of an advance of wages claimed by workmen in the Durham coal trade. After a lengthy discussion it was agreed,to adjourn the matter for a week.

The drivers and tramcar conductors of Portsmouth struck work on Saturday owing to a refusal of the manager of the company to accord extra time for meals and holidays. The strikers and their friends subsequently paraded th. 3 streets and interfered with the car traffic.

Delegates from South Wales and Monmouthshire collieries met on Monday, at Pontypridd, 30,000 men being repre- sented. It was decided that should the house coal men ter- minate the sliding scale, the steam coal representative should be empowered to draw up a scale. _

At a mass meeting of the Fite and Cliackmannon miners, at Dunfermline, on Monday, a letter Trom the employers was read, stating that they could not withdraw the recent reduction of 121 per cent. Resolutions were passed res- tricting labour to five days per week. A movement is on foot among the Festiniog quarrymen to shorten the hours of labour. Some time ago circulars were sent to the employers on the subject, aud as they did not produce the desired result, a mass meeting has been held, and a resolution passed to carry on the movement. A strike, which threatens seriously to affect the Liverpool building, trade, broke out on Tuestlay morning among the " wheelers " who are employed in the making of bricks. The men demand an advance of threepence per thousand, and have for the present ceased work, thus bringing the brickmaking trade to a standstill, and throwing some 3,000 or 4,000 men out of work. On Monday a large meeting of colliers was held on Wrex- ham racecourse. About 2,000 were present, representing 14 collieries in North Wales, It was resolved that no deputa- tion should be sent to the masters' meeting, but that negotia- tions should be conducted by correspondence. The masters have replied that the reduction of five per cent. in wages is an absolute necessity. The correspondence leaves matters exactly in the same position as last week. The strike of spindle makers, which has been in existence for seven weeks, has at length terminated. The men have agreed to the proposal of the masters to give an advance of 5 per cent. in two months, and work will, therefore, be resumed. The dispute affected some 300 men employed in Manchester, Bolton, Bury, Dukinfield, Ashton, and Staley- bridge._ _

THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark-lane Express says:—"The past week has been of unsettled weather and varying temperature. Light frosts have been almost continuous, but the rainfall which occurred on Satur- day was warm and genial. Discolouration of wheats has increased rather than otherwise. Some of it has assumed a weak and spindly appearance, and red rust has attacked a considerable acreage in the eastern c4unties. Shmild the presence of red rust at this unusually early stage of the crop be found to be general, it would be idle to disregard the serious consequences which must reasonably be looked for at harvest. Another week will probably reveal the extent to which this parasitical fungus is present amongst young wheat. With the exception of night frosts, the weather has been favourable to spring corn. Fresh samples of English wheat, a good quantity in fine condition, maintain firm prices. Foreign arrivals in London dewn to Friday were 53,801 quarters. In Liverpool, trade was quiet on Friday, and values generally id. per cental lower than on Tuesday. Maize marked a similar decline. Flour sold quietly in London at Monday's improved rates. Maize was in small request. Barley continues rather against buyers. I Oats, in small supply, improved 6d. in London since ' Monday." THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES: MANCLIESTE WEDNESDAY.—The business doing in the iron trade of this district continues very limited in extent. Buyers who ha-re orders to place, only offer them at under current rates, and makers as a rule, have to give way to secure business. During the week expiring local contracts for a fairly large quantity of Lancashire forge iron have been renewed, but to meet the competition of other brands, local makers have had to take very low figures, and 465. 6d., less 21, for delivery equal to Manchester, has been about the basis upon which business has been done. For foundry iron, however, the in- quiry continues very small, but with the large sales of forge, local makers are less.inclined to push for orders. District brand of pig iron can be bought as low as 465. 6d. to 478., less 21-, delivered here, but only a very limited business is reported. Finished iron makers are showing more anxiety to secure new orders, and local bars, delivered into the Man- chester district, can be bought at prices ranging from £6 10s. to £6 15s. per ton. The engineering trades generally, both in the light and heavy branches, are kept well employed.- -The coal trade continues generally dull, with the pits throughout the district on short time. For house-fire pur- poses there is a moderate demand for the time of the year, and of the common qualities of round coal a fairly large qantity continues to be taken by consumers for iron-making and steam purposes; but the supplies in the market are so much in excess of requirements that very low prices have to be taken, and there is a good deal of underselling to secure orders. Engine classes of fuel move off tolerably well,,but the stoppage of the river Weaver navigation has thrown some of the slack usually going into the salt district upon this market, and caused supplies to be rather more plentiful. Prices, however, are steadily maintained, and even for good orders sellers are hot inclined to make any concession. The average prices at the pit mouth remain at about Bs. 6d. to 9s. for best coal, 03s. 6d. to 7s. for seconds, ss. ss. 61. for common, 4s. 6d. to ss. for burgy, 3s. 91 to 4s. 3d. fer best slack, and about 3s. for common sorts.

A man went into a druggist's shop and asked for some- thing to cure a headache. The druggist held a bottle of hartshorn to his nose, and he was nearly overpowered by its pungency. As soon as he recovered he began to rail at the druggist, and threatened to punch his head. "But didn't it help your headache?" asked the apothecary. COST OF PAUPERISM IN CIIESIIIRE, An important official return has just been issued by the Local Government Board, showing the cost of in-mainte- nance and out-door relief in England and Wales, in the half- year ended Michaelmas last. The amount expended in the 647 unions into which the country is divided was £886,071 for in-door maintenance, and £1,330,831 for out-door relief —total, £2,216,902. This, compared with the expenditure in the corresponding half of 1879, is an increase of £35,399, or 1.6 per cent.; compared with 1880 it is a decrease of £24,708, or 1.1 per cent. In the half-year the total amount paid in school fees, which are included in out-relief, was £16,784, against £16,984 in 1880 Cheshire is grouped, along with Lancashire, in the North Western Division, in which there are 42 unions, whose 952 parishes (with a population of 4,107,155) cost £192,644 last Michaelmas half-year, or £4,192 more than at the cprre.sponding period in the preced- ing year. During the Michaelmas half-year ending 1881 the sum of £14,293 was expended for in-maintenance, and £26,044 for out-door relief, making a total of £40,337. This, compared with the corresponding half of the previous year is a decrease of £759, or a difference of 1.9 per cent. The cost in the undermentioned unions was as follows: CHESTER—This union consists of 55 parishes, with a pcpulation of 48,410; and the cost of in-maintenance was £2,776, and of out-door relief (whereof £44 was given in kind, and £7 in shape of school fees) £1,894, making a total of £4,670.

NANTIVICIL—Number of pirishes 78, with a population of 61,561; cost of in-maintenance £1,142, and of out-door relief £3,790, beinv..a total of £4,932, of which £l4O was paid in kind, anti £C in school fees.

Notaiiwiell.—Number of parishes 59, embracing a popu- lation of 44,045; cost for in-door maintenance £5lO, and for out-door relief £3,650, totalling £4,160, which includes £l9B paid in kind and £9B for school fees.

RUNCORN.—Number of parishes 37, consisting of a popu- lation of 34,022; expenditure for in-door maintenance £630, and for out-door relief £1,642, making a total of £2,272, of which £34 was given in kind. . _

MR. G. W. LATHAIM AND THE FARMERS' ALLIANCE.

A meeting for the purpose of explaining the objects and principles of the Farmers' Alliance was held in the Lecture- room at the Temperance Hall, Leicester, on Saturday after- noon, when the attendance was moderate. The Mayor of Leicester presided, and among those present were Mr. James Howard, M.P., president of the Alliance, Mr. G. W. Latham, ex-president, and many others. Mr. Latham, in explaining the objects of the Alliance, said at the outset that he was not a tenant but an owner of land, and he fully:believed that unless the programme of the Alliance was carried out almost in its entirety the landlords would soon have to go without tenants, and consequently without rents, and therefore it might be for selfish reasons that he interfered in the matter. Up to the present the farmers had had no alliance or cohe- sion except the Chambers of Agriculture, where mostly land- lords' agents met, with a few farmers, who fully agreed with what they said. This Alliance had been started with twelve objects, and they would be attained ultimately. But the main object of the Alliance, in his mind, was to obtain security for capital placed upen the land. (Cheers.) If that was obtained, and there was a law that no man's rent ' should be raised in consequence of the improvements he had himself made, they would have farming in a very different position from what it was at present. ef pi tal would not be invested in the land unless the investor could see his way to save what he was going to invest. Referring to the Agricul- tural Holdings' Act of the late administration, he said it was a sham, and no one gained a benefit from it. The legal pre- sumption ef the Bill should be made imperative by law. The Bill the Alliance intended to present to Pirliameot would provide for legal compensation for unexhausted improve- ments, and that if the parties desired arbitration they should be able to get it, whereas if a sale was preferred there would be a clause authorising such sale. With such powers more money would be invested in the land. Another cardinal point in the programme of the Alliaece was to do away with the law of distress, as they believed that that law was unfair, as it was a class law, and it was said that the rents of the farms of England had been raised 15 to 20 pr cent. in con- sequence of it. He for one did not see why the landlords should have the benefit of the law any longer. (Cheers.) Another item in their programme was the desire to obtain a fair apportionment of rates between landlords and tenants. He believed it would be best for the landlords to pay all the rates and the tenants to give them a lump sum annually, but that might interfere with the rights of the tenants in the matter of the local government. They also wanted some advantage from a re-adjustment of rail way rates, and that the regulations affecting cattle disease should be more perfect and effective. They also required some relief from the Game Laws, and above all freedom of cultivation, that a man should be able to grow what he chose on the land that he paid for. (Cheers.) It was in the power of the tenant farmer to see the objects of the Alliance carried out, or if they refused to act they might remain as they were for years. What they sou.r,ht to do was to make the property of the tenants safe, and they believed that lly doing so they would enhance the value of the property oi the landlords. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: HOME SECRETARY AT DERBY.
div.p: THE HOME SECRETARY AT DERBY.

Sir William llarcourt addressed a crowded meeting of his constituents at Derby, on Tuesday evening. He referred to the attacks recently made on the Liberal party, and what he called "offences against good breeding and good feeling by those who ought to know better," observing that, as long as the Government retained the confidence of their friends they cared very little for the menaces of their foes. All decent people, he added, must have" been disgusted with the "violent injustice" with which Mr. Gladstone had been personally attacked. In his opinion this venomous malignity defeated itself, and did much more good than harm to the Govern- ment it was intended to destroy. Mr. Gladstone assailed the late, Administration most vi_;orously, but he never descended to personal imputations against the motives and character of his great antagonist. The Home Secretary called attention to this matter not because he believed the Prime Minister or his Government suffered from such language, but because he was convinced that this "marked deterioration in the tone of public manners was a national misfortune." He sup- posed that in all parties there were "coarse and brutal minds" who were unable to distinguish between political antagonism and personal hatred, who could not discriminate between strong invective and vile calumny, between severe censure and vulgar insult. Turning to the subject of Ireland, he replied to Lord Salis- bury's charge that the Land Act of 1870 was hostile to the rights of property. He said it was an unstatesmanlike argu- ment to sty that this legislation was yielded to agitators, for many great reforms had been yielded to agitations. The only way to meet agitation was first to take away all just cause of complaint, and then if the agitation were continued to suppress it. That had been and was the policy of the Government. Having provided a remedy for all just coin- plaints, they were prepared to encounter an agitation which was without reasonable pretext, and to put down with a clear conscience and with a firm hand combinations which aimed not at land reform but at the disintegration of the ' Empire. There were signs that the Land Act was win- fling its way, and was beginning to have a healing opera- tion, and to detach from the cause of revolution those who had only allied themselves to it on account of real grievances. Speaking of the Lords' Committee on the Land Act, he said that if it had been allowed to proceed un- challenged all hope of conciliation in Ireland would have been at an end. Other questions referred to by the Con- servative leaders at Liverpool were also dealt with, and a remarkable demonstration of feeling was evoked when Sir William justified the devotion which Liberals show to their Chief, the "grand old man," as, he said, Sir Stafford North- cote had been pleased to call him.

AGGRAVATING.—" Stop that tram," cried old Mr. Nosen• gale, chasing a flying tramcar up the street, the car fresh as a daisy, and Mr. Nosengale badly._ blown. "stop that tram! he shouted to a distant but fleet-limbed boy. "Cer- tainly," shrieked back the obliging boy; "what shall I stop it with ?" "Tell it to hold on !" shouted the abandoned passenger. "Hold on to what ?" yelled the boy. "Make it wait for me !" puffed Mr. Nosengale. "You've got too much weight now," said the boy, "that's what's the trouble with you!" "Call the driver !" gasped the perspiring citizen, and, as the tramcar rounded the corner and passed out of sight, the mocking echoes of the obliging answer came floating cheerily back," All right! What shall I call him?"

THE ART OF DRESSlNG.—Trimming for trimming's sake is a fault which cannot be too carefully avoided. The em- broidering of a border—provided the colours and designs be well chosen—or even the sewing on of braids in the form of a border, on the hem of petticoats, skirts, or jackets, is a quite admissibler, because a reasonable, form of decoration; so is a border of fur, or a hanging frill of lace or of fringe; but the unconsidered use of these things in inappropriate positions is a flagrant error. Lace, instead of being used at the edge, or apparent edge, of a garment, is too often sewn tight upon its surface, to "show the pattern ;":whereas all such trimmings, being presumably the working or fraying of the border of the stuff, must necessarily be placed at its limit. Thus, too, insertions are applied upon a material in- stead of being sewn in between its edges ; and frills are. placed anywhere but as a pendant edging, their only legiti- mate use. Nor in adopting suggestions from the rich cos- tumes of past days are drevmakers wont to be a whit more reasonable. For instance, slashed sleeves and bodices have been in vogue among us lately; and it may sometimes have been noticed that the "slash," instead of being a material, presumably that of an undergarment, pulled through holes cut in the ton wear, haa been a piece of stuff palpably sewn on outside the dress or sleeve, in the guise of a puff. So, again, with velvet collars and cuffs put on to trim a stuff dress; they should suggest an underdress turning back at the throat and wrists, but they are often separate, and re- I moved from the edges, thus effectually dispelling the SiDP..—Tho, Magazine of Art for April,
