div.p: THE Coniturr PRACTICES BILL.—The discussion on thq motion for the second reading of the Corrupt Practices PAU was resumed by Mr. BALFOUR, and some SuggestionS were made in the debate which followed. Mr. Sergeant StmoN welcomed the bill as an endeavour to secure as members men of moderate means, and hoped to see the time when, instead of one or two, there would be at least a dozen working men in the House. He thought the bill in some respects was too severe in its penalties. Lord GEORGE HAMILTON contended for a distinction being drawn between boroughs and counties. Mr. DIXON-HARTLAND regarded the bill as a measure of coercion against candidates, while Mr. STANTON, who had gone through the experience of five contested elections in thirteen months, desired that future petitions should not be exactly "trials," but "inquiries." Mr. SCHREIBER followed with a Tory speech of the olden type. He knew nothing but what was good of his own constituency, and wondered how a candidate would be able to make himself agreeable if his expenses were to be brought down to the starvation point. As to the admission of poor men into the house, had not the liberties of the country been won by men of independent means? He held that they had, and he thought the House ought to continue to be composed of men who could snap their fingers at the 'threat of dissolution made by any Minister.—Mr.O'DoNNELL thought the Bill a good one as far as it went, but regretted that it did not touch the wealthy men who practiced " nursing " constituencies. He believed a large dose of cor- ruption was a very necessary part of party government.— Mr. LEWIS thought that if the bill passed as many Liberals as Conservatives would find themselves in gaol, and he pro- pounded the idea that the measure should be called "a bill for the purpose of frightening persons from becoming can- didates, and for imposing penalties on those who do."—Sir W. HART DYKE gave a general supporeto the bill as one who had been for some time the exponent of a system which had existed in both parties in the State for many years.—Ulti- mately the bill was "talked out" by Mr. Callan, and tte sitting was suspended at 7 o'clock.—At the evening sitting there was a discussion upon the proper method of dealing with lunatics. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

--- THE IRISH LAND ACT: THE GOVERNMENT AND ARREARS OF BENT.-Mr. EDMOND, in moving the second reading of the Land Law Ireland Act 1881 Amendment Bill, asserted that the Act had proved a melancholy and disastrous failure. The main proposal of the bill was to get rid of all arrears up to the 31st of August last, and to apply the funds of the Irish Church to the payment of the 'residue. He urged that the question of arrears formed an impassable barrier between the tenants and the protection of the Land Act, and he added that so long as the work of eviction was allowed to continue in Ireland, peace was impossible, and discontent, outrage, and bloodshed were an absolute necessity of the situation. Mr. GLADSTONE said it was not in the power of the Government to support the second reading. They were not prepared to depart from the ground on which they urged objections to a Parliamentary inquiry into the work- ing of the Act; but there were matters outside the main sub- ject of the tenure clauses with respect to which the objec- tions did not apply. They certainly did not apply to the question of the purchase clauses and in the judgment of the Government they did not apply to the question of arrears. These might be dealt with without the slightest degree dis- turbing the general structure of the tenure clauses. He ad- mitted that the arrears clause in the Land Act had been proved to fall very far short of the necessities of the case, and the Government looked with con- fidence to legislating on the subject on some early day in the present session. They desired to approach the question in a spirit of impartiality, and to move in accordance with a wide concurrence of Irish opinion. The Bill before the House contained a compulsory clause, and on this point the choice of the Government would be materially influenced by the state of Irish opinion. The hon. member proposed that the sum which might be advanced in respect of this clause should be a gift, and nc..• a loan. He (the Premier) entirely agreed with him, if they were to proceed on the basis be had described, that that wan a proper course to fol- low, and be thought the bon. member was right in drawing the sums required from the Irish Church surplus funds. He should not make it a fundamental objection that something might be required from the public exchequer to work that clause. The right hon. gentleman con- cluded by expressing his desire that the important legislation of last year should be completed in a most essential point for the benefit and happiness of Ireland.— A debate, moderate and hopeful in spirit, followed, the Irish members cordially acknowledg;ng the manner in which the arrears difficulty had been met by the Government.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE said that if the arrears settlement were not made compulsory, the question had better be left alone. He also stated that he did not see the slightest reason for objecting to something being done in regard to leases.—Mr. SHAW said he would support Mr. Redmond's bill, at the same time declaring that the question of arrears was at the foundation of the settlement of the land problem.—Mr. Gummi complained that the Premier's statements were in- definite and vague. Seeing that the question of arrears was admitted to be of vast importance, they had a right to ex- pect something in the shape of a definite plan which the House might criticise, instead of being asked to give the Prime Minister something which he might criticise.—Mr. ISITARTHY moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. FORSTER did not oppose the motion, but he hoped it did not mean an adjournment of the consideration of the very im- portant and urgent practical question of arrears. He did not think the House would blame the Government for trying to ascertain in the course of the debate how this question was viewed from different sections of the House. He thought it had been shown that the question could be approached without any strong party feeling, and that the whole tone of the debate was hopeful for the future govern- ment of Ireland. The Government would take up the 4uestion of arrears as soon as they could, and would submit their views to the House. The debate was adjourned, and the House shortly afterwards rose.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.

The Army Bill was read a third time.—A Bill brought in by Lord Denman for allowing soldiers who have committed offences the option of receiving so many lashes instead of suffering imprisonment or carrying heavy weights was op- posed by Lord MORLEY on the part of the Government, and rejected. HOUSE OF COMMONS—THURSDAY. _ .

THE OLT-T-R—A—G-E—S ON JEN-VS.-Sir CHARLES MUM, in reply to a question from Varon Henry de Worms, stated that the British Nice-Consul at Odessa had visited Balta since the recent outbreak against the Jews, and had reported that one Jew had been killed and many were badly injured. There were three cases of gross outrage upon women, while the v.lue of the property destroyed was estimated at 1,000,000 roubles. Sir Charles promised to lay the full report on the table when it should be received. _

_ TILE CONVEYANCE OF DISTINGUISHED PERSONS.—Lord FREDERICK CAVENDISH, in reply to a question from Mr. Arthur Arnold with regard to the cost of conveying distin- guished persons across the English Channel, said the system now in force was adopted -some years ago as a more conve- nient one than that of providing a ship of the Royal Navy, and, as far as he was aware, no complaint had arisen with respect to it until the mishap to the Albert Edward. ZULULAND.—RepIying to a question from Mr. Alderman Fowler regarding the state of aff,irs in Zululand, Mr. COURTNEY said a telegrhm had bcen received from Sir H. Bulwer, dated Wednesday, which referred to a large demon- stration there, but as Sir Henry had promised to communi- cate the facts by letter, it was inferred that he did not con- sider the matter of the came importance as a correspondent of the Daily _Yews. _ _ _ _

THE GLOUCESTER WRIT.—Mr. C. LEWIS moved for the issue of a new writ for Gloucester, but the motion was evidently not made with a serious intention, as after some criticism upon the delay of the Government in the matter, which was answered by the Attorney-General, the motion was withdrawn. THE CORRIIIIC PRACTICES BILL.—The debate on the Par- liamentary Elections Corrupt end Illegal Practices Preven- tion Bill was resumed by Mr. CALLAN, who described the measure as" crotchets, ill considered, and ill advised."—Mr. T...COLLINS suggested that instead of disqualifying a can- didate for life from sitting for the same borough on account of blibery practised by his agent, the period should be lim- ited to seven years. He objected to the bill going into Com- mittee before the measure dealing with past corruption bad been disiNsed of.—Mr. RYLANDS thought if the measure passed in its present form it might give rise to new evils possibly as objectionable from a public point of view as those now complained of. It might make an opening for political adventurers. He suggested that one of the best means of stopping corruption would be to get rid of small and moderate sized constituencies.—The debate was con- tinued by Mr.Onslow, Mr. M. Lloyd, Mr. Shiel, Mr. Greg- gory, Mr. Dawson, Sir G. Goldney, Sir W. Barttelot, Mr. Gorst, Mr. Bulwer, and Mr. Jesse Collings. The second reading was agreed to, and the House ad- journed at one o!clock.

div.head: POLITICAL IT En.
div.p: POLITICAL IT En.

Two Liberal candidates will be run for South Lincolnshire at the next general election. It is stated that the Scotch Education Bill will take prior- ity of the Welsh Bill this year. At a Liberal meeting held in Oxford on 6aturday, Mr. Thereld Rogers, MY., presiding, resolutions were passed expressing unabated confidence in the Government, and sup- porting the extension of the franchise and reform of the rules of procedure. Mr. Edward James Stanley,Conservative, was on Tuesday returned unopposed for West Somerset. The election does not affect the balance of parties. The Government, it is stated, remain unshaken in their determination to proceed with the first resolution :on pro- cedure. They will not listen to any proposal to give pre- tedonce to the second or any other of the rules; nor are they prepared to accept any of the amendments to the first rule now standing on the paper. The Standard says the relinquishment of the County Government Bill will, it is believed, be followed by the abandonment of the Bill dealing with the municipal Government of London. It is now expected that the latter part of the session will b 3 chiefly occupied with Irish legis- lation. A special meeting of the Richmond Conservative Associa- tion was held on Tuesday evening, to take into consideration the representation of the borough in view of Mr. Dundas having announced his determination not again to offer him- self as a candidate. Mr. Roper, mayor of Richmond, was unanimously selected as the future candidate. At a meeting of the political council of the City of Lon- don Liberal Club, held on Wednesday, it was resolved to congratulate the Government upon the defeat of Mr. Mar- riott's amendment on the question of procedure in the House of Commons, and to express tin; hope that every Liberal member would heartily support the Government in passing the romigder pf their resolutions.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 29, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 29, 1882.
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

On Tuesday the King and Queen of Holland left the Hague for England, via El hing. The Sultan has appointed a commission to study the " question " of reforms in Asia Minor. By a cyclone at Monticello, Mississippi, 21 persons were killed and many more injured, some of them fatally. Lieutenant Danenhaner and his crew of the Jeannette have arrived safely at Orenburg. They are in excellent health. Latest advices represent that intelligence from Catalonia tends to show that perfect tranquillity now prevails in the provinces. Nechid Pasha has been appointed governor of the Archipelago in place of Said Pasha, who remains in Con- stantinople. The Emperor of Russia has ordered that all the trials for outrages on Jews shall be proceeded with as urgent, without regard to their order on the lists. A despatch from Eauclare. Wisconsin, reports a fire at that place, by which over 60 buildings were destroyed, causing an estimated loss of $250,000. The French Minister of Justice has under consideration the question of reorganising the judicial system in Tunis and the creation of a French tribunal in the Regency.

General Ignatieff, the Minister of the Interior in the Russian Government, has, according to one account, re- signed his post. Another asserts that he has been dismissed. A semi-official contradiction is given in Vienna to the report that arrangements have been entered into between Austria, Germany, and Russia for the extradition of political offenders. _

It is announced that although Prince Bismarks' bill for creating a tobacco monopoly was carried by a majority in the Federal Council, the minority included Bavaria, Saxony, Hesse, and the Hanseatic Towns. Mr. Evans, the Ragusa correspondent of the Manchester Guardian, has been liberated by the Austrian authorities, the Public Prosecutor having withdrawn the charges Upon which he was arrested. Luigi Daquila, the man who recently attacked and robbed Captain Bosanquet, of Her Majesty's ship Northumberland, at Cagliari, has been sentenced by the Assize Court of Cagliari to 15 years' hard labour, followed by five years' police supervision. A case of high treason is being investigated in'Munich. A French officer, a Bavarian officer on half-pay, and a Munich merchant have been arrested. It is stated that plans of the fortresses were obtained under false pretences and delivered to the French. It is stated that on the re-assembling of the French Parliament several motions will be placed on the table directed towards a resumption of commercial negotiations with England. One of these will be introduced by M. Rouvier, the late Minister of Commerce. Arrangements are being made at Brady for sending to the United States over 2,000 Jewish emigrants every week. It is stated that thousands of Jews settled in Moscow have been expelled, and the Governor General asserts that he is powerless to give aid, as he has " direct orders which he must obey." The United States House of Representatives has, by resolution, requested President Arthur to lay before it any further correspondence which may have passed between the American and English Governments in reference to the im- prisonment of American citizens in Ireland, and to continue his efforts for the release of such persons. The Pope. a correspondent at Rome says' is so indisposed as to cause disquietude to those around him. There is nothing in his condition' the writer adds, immediately alarming, but his prolonged confinement to the Vatican is telling seriously on his health and causing great pro- stration.

A committee has been formed in Southern Russia to aid the movement for the emigration of the Jews. The authori- ties, however, seem to have raised some difficulty as to the granting of the necessary passports, and many of the in- tended emigrants are detained pending the decision of the magistrates. The Chamber of Deputies at Madrid has approved of the commercial treaty with France by 273 votes against 59. In the course of the debate Senor Canovas, the ex-Premier, de- clared the protection to native industry was an article of belief with his party, and he predicted that Spain would never become a free-trading nation. The Rome correspondent of the Standard states that the question put to the British Government in the House of Commons with regard to Mr. Errington's "mission" to Rome has caused some disquietude at the Vatican, where it is considered that the publication of papers on the sub- ject would tend to destroy the hope still entertained of the establishment of diplomatic relations. In the Dominion House of Commons, the other day, Mr. Costigan, a Conservative, moved an address to the Queen praying that some form of self-government may be granted to Ireland similar to that enjoyed by Canada, and that clemency may be extended to the political prisoners in Ire- land. The resolution was supported by Sir John Mac- donald, the Premier, and carried unanimously. The address will be sent to the genate for its concurrence. The war between the white settlers in New Mexico and the Indians has broken out afresh. The Warm Spring In- dians have taken to the "war path," and are committing terrible outrages. The Indian method of warfare i., as the frontiersmen know too well, to torture, mutilate,and murder all the white people who fall into their power, without dis- tinction of age or sex. Several families have been destroyed in this new raid, and troops are gathering with the intention of taking vengeance on the savages.

MIDHAT PASHA'S CAPTIVITY.—Midhat Pasha and the other prisoners condemned with him for having taken part in the assassination of the ex-Sultan Abdul Aziz are reported by an Arab, who lately visited Taif, a town near Mecca where the prisoners are confined, to he in a wretched con- dition. They are said to be fettered, and so strictly guarded that they cannot communicate with their friends in Con- stantinople. Midhat Pasha's wife and family are also represented to be in a state bearing upon destitutioon at Smyrna, JUMBO'S Thum—Jumbo started on his tour of the Ameri- can continent on Saturday night, his first stopping place being Philadelphia. He has grown in popularity since his arrival in New York, and the streets on the line of match were filled by thousands of people. The behaviour of Jumbo has been excellent. In the procession he led the advance, and in a kind of patronising way encouraged the other elephants ; but he became somewhat alarmed at the sight of the ferry-boat, probably because it reminded him of his sea voyage, and awoke disagreeable impressions. His keepers, however, succeeded in chaining him on the deck of the vessel. For Jumbo's transportation across the country a special car has been constructed, 40 feet long by 13i- feet high. It is a work of the utmost solidity, and weighs 12)1 tons.

RUSSIAN AFFAIRS.—" A well-informed man" supplies the Paris correspondent of the Times with an explanation of the recent changes in Russia. The retirement of Prince Gort- chakoff, which has been regarded as a defeat for the Pan- slavists, was, according to this authority, a pure formality, for the Prince had really been removed from the direction of Russian policy since the death of Alexander H. "It is a positive fact" that Gortchakoff "has always been Ignatieff's adversary." The report that the General would be sent to France as Ambassador was started at Berlin and denied at St. Petersburg. The Paris correspondent of the Times says that General Scobeleff's experiment is not calculated to recommend the production of another scare much more dangerous than that of the Panslavist General whose utter- ance' proved so startling. "General Ignatieff's presence in Paris would have had such an effect that it can safely be affirmed that, even if he were proposed, which he will not be, he would not be accepted by the French Government." THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.

Osman Pasha, former Minister of War, who first arrested the colonels who took part in the military inotte of a few months since, and was afterwards himself placed under arrest, is accused of complicity in the plot to assassinate Onrabi Pasha.

According to a Paris telegram, the French Government has expressed a determined opposition to any acknowledg- ment of the Sultan's right to any control in Egypt, and refuses to permit his intervention under any circumstances. This opposition, it is added, is not favoured by the English Government, and is retarding the issue of a manifesto by the Powers against the encroachments of the Egyptian nobles upon the control of Egyptian finances.
M ISCELLANEOUS.-
The Duke of Teck on Saturday opened the public baths at Richmond.
The Congrezational Union Jubilee Fund has now reached the sum of £125,000. _ _
Two sons of Sir Salar Jung are about to come to England to complete their education. _ _

- Nothing is known by the Glasgow police of a reported threat to blow up the municipal buildings. All the bodies have now been recovered from the Tudhoe Colliery, the last two having been brought to bank on Saturday. Mr. George Grant Francis, F.S.A., the savant and anti- quary, died suddenly on Saturday, at Swansea, from paralysis, at the age of 68. The O'Donoghue, M.P. has passed his public examination in binkruptcy. The debts secured and unsecured amounted to £7,000, and the assets were nil.' The convictions for Sunday drunkenness in England and Wales from September, 1879, to September, 1851, numbered 26,523. Liverpool figures in the list for 2,915. At Belgrave, near Leicester, on Saturday evening, a man named Arthur Smith and his son, Herbert, a youth, quar- relled over a game of draughts, and the lad stabbed his father twice with a knife. A deputation from the Wiltshire Society 6f London waited on the Duke of Albany at Windsor Castle on Satur- day and presented him with a piece of plate and an address 'congratulating him on his approaching marriage. The gift was suitably acknowledged. An application was made on Saturday, in the Queen's Bench Division, to have a day fixed for the hearing of the case Gurney v. Bradlaugh, which raises the question whether Mr. Bradlaugh properly took the oath when he administered it to himself at the table. Lord Coleridge said at present a day could not be fixed. The Board of customs have issued an order that tobacco will no longer be allcwed to be remeved from bonded ware- houses in London when shipped on board any vessel leavirg the port after she has departed from her place of lading. The permission formerly given has been much abased. A reward of £l6O has been offered and a free pardon to any accomplice for information which shall lead to the con- viction of the murderer of Icy Sands, whose body was found concealed under a stone heap at Workington, on the Ist of March last, and who was missing since December. An " infant " of the name of Robertson was sued in the Queen's Bench division for a sum of over £6OO for goods supplied within a period of 18 about months. Among the articles sold were 15 head-stalls,l7 whips,and nine walking- sticks. Acting on the advice of the judge an arrangement was come to. A sculling match for £lOO, over the Thames champion- ship course, was decided on Monday afternoon, the competi- tors being Charles Brightwtll, of Putney, and George Per- kins, of Rotherhithe. Perkins led until just belew Barnes' Bridge, when Brightwell went to the front, and won a splendidly contested race by three lengths. A heartless case of desertion by a father came before Mr. Raffles, stipendiary magistrate of Liverpool, on Saturday, when a man named John Murphy was proved to have endeavoured to get rid of his infant child by representing to the parish authorities that a strange woman had left it with him, and who afterwards deserted it in St. Nicholas's Roman Catholic Church. He was sent to jail for six weeks.

At Birmingham, on Monday, George Frederick Horsefall, aged 23, clerk, was sent for six months' imprisonment for stealing £lOO, belonging to Hyman Hyman, jeweller, Bir- mingham. Last Wednesday, the prisoner was sent to cash a £lOO note, but, instead of returning, absconded. He was arrested in London when about to leave for Sydney, hav- ing paid £42 for a second-class passage and bought a good outfit. At the Chester Assizes, on Tuesday, a man named Thomblin, of Manchester, was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude for having, along with another man now under- going penal servitude, committed a burglary in November, 1880, on the premises of Mr. Mitchell, pawnproker, Maccles- field ; and John Hill, who at that time kept a public-house at Macclesfield, was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for being accessory after the fact. The Heme Secretary on Monday informed a deputation which waited on hitn in reference to the licensing laws that he had become an abstainer on the ground of health. The right hon. gentleman was asked to support Mr. Lewis Fry's bill, which proposes to give to licensing authorities the same discretionary power with regard to grocers and other " off " licenses as they now possess in regard to publicans The Home Secretary promised to give a favourable consider- ation to the measure. A MISLEADING MEDICAL CERTIFICATE.--An inquest was held at Balham, on Saturday, on Mr. George Jennings, a well known sanitary engineer. The evidence showed that five days before his death he broke his collar bone. One of the surgeons who attended him gave a certificate that death resulted from bronchitis and congestion of the lungs, aided by senile degeneration, but admitted in evidence that but for the accident he would not have died when he did. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and the coroner severely censured the surgeon for giving such a certificate. One of Prince Leopold's gifts to his bride is a fan of most delicate workmanship and design. The sticks are of goldfish pearl, inlaid with gold, which grows paler in tint as the tapering points are approached. The material of the fan itself is lace leaf, on which the designs of the garlands on the sticks are repeated, the blossoms chosen being marguerites, flowers which, with the daffodil and pink, are immensely in favour. Between each daisy wreath are roses, the petals of which are detached and form a fluttering shower with the slightest movement of the fan. DOUBLE MURDER BY A. FATHER: SENTENCE OF DEATH. —At the Manchester Assizes, on Tuesday, Benjamin Bouch was indicted for the murder of his two children. About a month ago he took them along the canal bank and returned without them, and on being asked where they were he said he had drowned them, and that he had been driven to it be- cause they were poor; and he preferred to drown them than that they should starve. For the defence Mr. Byrne con- tended that the prisoner was not accountable for his actions, and that trouble had rendered him insane. The jury, how- ever, rejected that theory, and, returning a verdict of " Wilful murder," the prisoner was sentenced to death in the usual manner. EXTRAORDINARY SCENE IN A CHURCH.—As the Rev. Father Bailey was conducting divine service in St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, Newport, Mon., on Sunday morn- ing, a middle-aged man, named John Murphy, pushed past the verger and walked excitedly up the aisle brandishing a large knife, with which he threatened to commit murder. There was a large congregation present. The man was not in liquor, but his eyes were blackened and his face bruised. A panic ensued, the service was stopped, and the congrega- tion left their seats and rushed to the doors. Mr. Woollett, a borough magistrate, ran to the Town Hall to procure police, and two officers eventually captured the fellow in 1 the building.

DOUBLE MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.—A corres- pondent at Skipton reports that a shocking tragedy was enacted there on Tuesday afternoon. Matthew J. Hunter, a rate collector, murdered his wife and child, and then attempted to commit suicide. For about a month past Hunter has suffered from severe mental depression, and on Tuesday morning be asked his wife to accompany him for a walk. They took the child with them, and about noon pro- ceeded by an unfrequented route to a field overlooking the town. After remaining there about an hour the father, with a shoemaker's knife, cut his wife's throat and then his child's, death in each case being, it is thought, instan- taneous. Afterwards the man cut his own throat, severing the windpipe, but not inflicting fatal injuries. He now lies in the workhouse hospital. DEATH OF DR. GERVASE SMITII—The Wesleyan Con- nexion has sustained another great loss by the decease of the Rev. Gervase Smith, D.D., on Saturday alorning last, at his residence, 13, Leigh-road, Ilighbury-park. Dr. Smith entered the ministry in 1844, and laboured in some of the most important circuits of the Connexion—Queen-street, Huddersfield; King-street, Bristol; Great Bridgewater-street, Manchester; Highbory, City-road, and Hammersmith being among them. He was a most able administrator' and one of the most popular preachers and lecturers in Methodism, being frequently associated in this work with his most in- timate ministerial friend, the late Dr. Punshon. In 1873 he was elected secretary of the Conference, and in 1875 fol- lowed his friend Dr. Punshon as president. In 1870 he was appointed secretary of the Metropolitan Chapel Building Fund; and to his great ability and the zeal and generosity of the late Sir Francis Lycett the success of that movement is largely due. Called in 1880 to succeed the late Rev. John Rattenbury as treasurer of the auxiliary fund, shortly after- wards his health failed, and he retired from active work. His death will be mourned by multitudes to whom he was endeared by his geniality, kindness, and faithfulness. THE REV. Da. GARRET AND HIS DOG.—At Lancaster Castle, on Saturday, the Rev. John Garret, D.D., of Moss Side, Manchester, was charged with keeping a dog without a license. Dr. Garrett said his son had a house at Morecambe, and for the last seven or eight months his mother had been living there and minding his children whilst he was in Sweden. She had her (Fog with her, and was entirely in doubt as to whether a license should be bought in Manches- ter or at Morecambe, and whilst she was expecting some in- formation a policeman dropped in and found that there was no license in force for the doe..—:Superintendent Moss said two dogs were found there, and no time was lost in taking out a license after the policeman's visit.—Dr. Garrett said a license bad been taken out in Manchester the year pre- viously.—Mr. H. Garnett, a magistrate, told Dr. Garrett that he should have known a license was necessary this year. —Dr. Garrett believed it was usual to allow parties to make some arrangement with the Excise in a case of this kind. —The Chairman said Dr. Garrett was under a mistake in that respect. A fine of 255. and lls, costs was ordered to be paid.

TRAGIC AFFAIR IN WESTMORELANI).-OTI Saturday after- noon, at Burrells, a village hear Appleby, a farmer named Waistall shot his housekieper, killing-her immediately. He afterwards blew out his brains. No cause is assigned for the act. The family consisted of two brothers, John and Thos. Waistall, and an elder half-brother, Mr. Matthew Bunn, a considerablo farm bolder. The brothers were all bachelors, and employed a domestic servant named Ann Wilson. Be- tween two and three o'clock in the afternbon, whilst Mr. Bunn was at market, a quarrel occurred in the kitchen be- tween the housekeeper and Thomas Waistall. • The other brother, John, who is afflicted with rheumatism, was present. Thomas Waistall, who bad a double-barrelled gun in his hands, worked himself into a frenzy and fired the gnn. The shot did not take effect. The woman fled towards the back door, pursued by Waistall, who fired again, this time with fatal effect, the charge striking her in the waist. Waistall then ran down the field about four hundred yards, and, recharging the gun, shot himself.

I The Prince's Theatre at Portsmouth was destroyed by fire: I on Tuesday. It is officially announced that Mr. Spencer Walpole has succeeded Sir Hem y Loch as Governor of the Isle of Man. Edward Haworth, iron merchant, Stockton, was sentenced to five years penal servitude at Durham on Wednesday for forgery. The Skye crofters imprisoned at Inverness were committed for trial on Wednesday on a charge of assault in connection Avith the recent evictions in Skye. At the meeting of the Liverpool City Council, on Wed- nesday, a recommendation to expend £10,336 upon the ex- tension of the Walker Art Gallery was passed. While the judge was passing sentence, on Wednesday, at Chester, upon a youth named Edward Murray, for a feloni- ous assault, the prisoner fell back, apparently unconscious, and did not recover while he remained in court. On Wednesday morning an express goods train on the Great Northern line ran off the line at Peterboro, and the engine embedded itself into the masonry of a tall chimney attached to a pumping station. The chimney was reduced to ruins, and much damage was otherwise done. At Overton sessions, Hants, on Wednesday, the captain and three other members of the Salvation Army were com- mitted to gaol for one month with bard labour, for obstruct- ing the police ley. forming processions after the issue of a prohibitory notice. In several towns in the black country smallpox has broken , out, and has resulted in several deaths. At Wednesbury 33 persons have been attacked with the disease, and three who ' had not been vaccinated have died. The authorities are doing their best t,o starAp it out, and are urging the people to be re-vaccinated. Professor Blackie, of Edinburgh, seems to entertain a very poor opinion of the Revised New Testament. He is reported to have told the Royal Society the other day that it "is in , the highest degree undesirable that a version so marked by ' minute scrupulosity about trifles, servile verbalism want of taste, and disregard of English idiom should take the place " ' of the Authorised Version. ENGLISH PIANO FOR THE KING OF PORTUGAL.—Messrs. John Brinsmead and Sons, of London, have specially manu- factured for the Palace of the King of Portugal, in accordance with his Majesty's commands, an oblique pianoforte, in a handsome dull-black case, decorated with cupids and gar- lands of flowers in the Adam's style.—Daily Chronzele. The remains of Charles Darwin were interred on Wednes- day in Westminster Abbey, the grave selected being at the eastern end of the north aisle, not far from the spot where 1 Sir John Herschel and Sir Isaac Newton lie buried. An immense number of persons attended the funeral, including deputations from the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge, and eminent representatives of art, literature, and science. There was on Tuesday night another shameful interrup- tion of the services of the Salvation Army at Oldham. The police had to be called in to expel a body of roughs. Another disorderly scene was witnessed on Wednesday night. A correspondent remarks that these disturbances are becom- ing a disgrace to the toitin, and hints that those who take part in them are encouraged to do so by the lenient view of their heathenish behaviour taken by the magistrates. A new Liberal Club was opened on Tuesday afternoon at Upper Wortley, Leeds, by Mr. J. Barran, M.P., in the ab- sence of the Solicitor General (Mr. Farrar Herschel') who I was expected to perform the ceremony. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., was present and delivered a short address. ! He referred to the subject of the caucus and denied that it had any existence in the Liberal party. A great Liberal mee- ting was held in the evening. An influential deputation of landowners and members of Parliament waited upon Mr. Dodson, President of the Local Government Board, to protest against the rating of uplands I proposed by the Rivers Conservancy Bill. It was suggested, that the matter should be sent to a committee ot inquiry. , Mr. Dodson, in reply, said the measure was the outcome of I exhaustive enquiries, and there would be no use in opgning another. The right honourable gentleman held out no hope to the deputation. An official inquiry is being held in Glasgow into the affairs of the Scottish Legal Life Assurance Society. This being the first investigation of the kind under the Friendly Societies Act, considerable interest attaches to the proceed- ings, which are, however, being conducted in private. The official report will be published in due course, and will be awaited with some anxiety, the society having a very large membership throughout the kingdom. Serious charges are made of mismanagement and squandering of the funds. I The people of Flintshire have thoroughly reprobated the I spiteful and petty conduct of those magistrates who, on the ; suggestion of a political filibusterer from London, objected the other day to pay for Mr. Gladstone's protection out of the county rates. The ratepayers of Bagillt, Rhyl, and Mold have all held indignation meetings, at which the con- duct of the justices has been severely condemned. On Wednesday a small deputation from the Association of Trade Protection Societies of the United Kingdom had an interview with the President of the Board of Trade, and requested him to oppose Mr. George Anderson's bill for the abolition of imprisonment for debt, on the ground that the measure would cause debts to be more recklessly incurred, and recovered with greater difficulty. Mr. Chamberlain asked for facts and detailed information, and promised to give such representations careful consideration. The Mayor of Gloucester has received at autograph letter from the Premier, acknowledging the receipt of a petition , against the propcsed disfranchisement ef that city. Mr. Gladstone begs the Mayor to accept the assurance of the great regret with which the Government arrived at their decision, and added that that decision was adepted in a judicial spirit. Full time will be allowed for Parliament to consider the case before the enactment now proposed can take effect. A Conference of Parliamentary Debating Societies was held in Liverpool, on Tuesday, for the purpose of comparing notes as to the best rules, modes of procedure, conduct of I debate, and all the various details of management. A large I number of delegates from various parts of the country were present. Mr. Thomas Cope, of Liverpool, presided, and I delivered the inaugural address, dwelling on the important I educational influence exerted by these societies—which now number 105, and had about 34,000 members—in- political and national affairs. • PROPOSED VErERINARY COLLEGE.—An important depu- tation waited upon Earl Spencer and Mr. Mundella on Wed-I nesday, at the Privy Council Office, to urge the prayer of a inetnorial in favour of Government assistance for the erection of a national veterinary college. Among the gentlemen I present were Earl Fortescue, Viscount Down, Sir T. D. , Acland, M.P., and Colonel Kingscote, M.P. Earl Spencer, while recograising the great importance of veterinary science, said there were so many competitors for Government aid that he could not promise success. He would, however, I certainly lay the memorial before his colleagues, and do ; what he could to support its prayer. Effectual ptecautions have been taken to prevent a repeti- tion of the disturbances which arose at Camborne through, an attack by Irish labourers upon an Englishman. Rein- , forcements of police have been sent to the town, and on Tues- day two companies of infantry were sent thither from Devonport. One of the alleged ringleaders was brought I before the magistrates on Tuesday, but was discharged. The; disturbances were regrettable enough, but they scarcely s justify the' simulated wrath of some Dublin journals, which ! abuse England and the English press in unmeasured terms on account of the "atrocities" at Camborne. We have not I seen the Freeman so excited over any one of the Land League murders and outrages in Ireland as it is over the riot in Cornwall.-211-anchester'Guardian. The Archdeacon of Manchester (the Ven. G. H. Anson) i commenced his annual visitation on Wednesday. In the I course of an address to the gathering of churchwardens and ' sidesmen in the Cathedral he alluded to the various Incas- ' ures affecting the Church of England which are now before Parliament, and in explaining the provisions of Mr. Stan- hope's bill said that everyone must feel the time had come i for removing the great scandal which has arisen from the way in which livings have been bought and sold. It was I notorious that the first principle of patronage. had been ' thrown to the winds and that the exercise of a sacred trust s had been degraded into a dishonourable traffic. Referring to the Parish Church Bill, he said it should ever be re- membered that churches were built to contain a certain number of parishioners, but that number was not often ob- tained under the plan of appropriation. Complete and full s occupation of the seats should be the object of all who had! any office or charge in connection with the Church of ' England. THE ATTEMPT TO POISON A HUSBAND AT MANCHESTER. —Mr. Justice Matthew had before him in the Crown Court at Manchester Assizes, on Saturday, the case of Annie Goulthorpe, who was charged with having, at Manchester, on the 31st ult.' administered poison to her husband with , the intention of murdering him, or of causing him grievous ' bodily harm. It appeared from the evidence that on the day in question the husband of the prisoner was ill, and as medical man prescribed for him containing a quantity of I hydrate of chloral, which is a poison. The woman, instead of giving him a dose containing between 20 and 30 grains of the chloral, administered one that con- tained over 100 grains. Had not prompt medical assistance been at hand the result would have been a fatal one. It was stated by the prosecution that there had been many disagreements between the prisoner and her husband, and it was suggested that these furnished a sufficient motive for the prisoner's act. The Judge pointed out that the prisoner I was under the influence of drink when she committed the alleged offence, and under his direction the jury returned a verdict of not guilty. FREE LIBRARIES. Several statntes have been passed since 1850 with regard to the establishment of free libraries. These Mr. Hopwood, M.P.; proposes to amend and at the same time consolidate. The objects of his bill are the es- tablishment and maintenance not only of free libraries and museums, but of schools of science or art and galleries of art. Of these the libraries and museums are to be free; but a charge is permitted for admission to lectures, special exhibitions, or school instruction. The maximum amount to be expended on these matters, which may either be paid out of the eeneral rate or be raised be a special one, to be called the "library rate," is increased to twopence in the pound. Town councils and local boards are empowered to adopt the Act. Another mode of bringing the measure into operation is for ten or more ratepayers to require the local authority to call a meeting of ratepayers to determine the question for the borough or the urban sanitary district, sub- ject to a poll being demanded. Moreover, any "rural parish "within three miles of a borough or local board dis- trict is authorised to agree with the town council or the board to combine with it in adopting the Act. Such an agreement on the part of the rural parish is to be resolved on by a majority of ratepayers present at a meeting, subject to an appeal to a poll. The authority for executing the Act is time town council or the local board, three or fewer persons being added for each "rural parish" that co-operates. With regard to the metropolis and ,Oxford the bill contains some special provisions.

1 An estimate of the number of copies of the revised edition of the New Testament Abows that at most not more than 500 copies have been sold at Oldham. Foot-and-mouth disease has appeared in a virul.mt form a tnong some cattle recently purchased by Mr. Hale, Ridley Cheshire. The chief constable has declared the place an infected district.

A grand bazaar was opened at St. Paul's Schools, Royton on Thursday morning, the object of which is to liquidate a debt of about £l,OOO which has been incurred in the enlarge- ment of the schools. Mr. Robert Whittaker, J.P., opened the bazaar. _ _

At the Hanley police court, on Thursday, a shocking case of cruelty to a horse was heard. John Pickering, a wag- goner in the Top Pits, Great Fenton, was charged with striking a horse with a bar of iron about three feet long, and inflicting a wound four inches deep. He was sent to prison for one month with hard labour. On Thursday afternoon a melancholy boat accident oc- curred opposite Ullapool, on the Scotch west coast. James Macgregor, aged 67, and his son Duncan, aged 19, were re- turning home in a boat heavily laden with seaware, when the craft was swamped, and both father and son were drowned in sight of eye-witnesses on the shore, who were powerless to render help. _ _

On Thursday morning, at Chester, an inquest was held on the body of Elizabeth Lloyd, domestic servant, employed by Messrs. Jones. The deceased was engaged on the cellar stairs when she slipped and fell to the bottom. A brush handle came in contact with her side, causing such terrible injuries that she died almost immediately. A v3rdict of accidental death was returned.

George Cartwright, of Walsall, who has been taking part in a 9ix days' "go-as-you-please" contest now in progress at Sheffield, was apprehended as he left the track on Thurs- day. A warrant charged him with deserting his wife and five children, and leaving them chargeable to the Lichfield Guardians. Cartwright wanted to pay the money, but the officer who apprehended him said he had no authority to receive it.

On Wednesday, two men named William Marsden and Samuel Preston were engaged emptying aslapits at Long- worth Mill, near Bolton. Preston had occasion to leave the place for a few minutes, and on his return he discovered Marsden headforemcst in the rubbish. The unfortunate man was pulled out as soon af possible, but he was quite dead. Marsthn was subject to fits, and he must have been seized with one in Preston's absence.

At Accrington, on Wednesday afternoon, William Clegg, a labourer, was charged with attempting to strangle his wife. The prisoner attacked his wife at midnight and almost strangled her, leaving fearful marks on her neck through his violence. The prisoner was drunk, and he said he was sorry for it. He was committed to prison for two months with hard labour, and was ordered to find sureties at the expira- tion of that term, or, in default, go to prison for another month.

THE YILDING MIIRDER.—The trial of Esther Pay on a charge of having murdered Georgina Moore, who was missed from her home at Pimlico last December. and whose body was found in the river Medway on the 30th January last, was opened at Sussex Assizes Court, Lewes, on Wednesday. Mr. Poland prosecuted; Mr. Edward Clarke defended. The prisoner exhibited great confidence in the dock, and pleaded not guilty in a firm voice. The trial is expected to last several days. On Wednesday night an inquest was held at the Preston Police Station on the body of George Holland, 43, railway constable, in the employ of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company. The deceased, on Tuesday night, was on duty at the goods station, Preston, and at midnight was crossing the line near the Vicar's Bridge, right in front of a train of waggons.that were being shunted. Sumner, a goods inspector, called out to him, but the decnsed could not avoid the danger. The first waggon knocked him down, and six passed over him, cutting one arm off. He was taken up dead. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

The Daily Ilrews published the following telegram in a second edition on Thursday :—Pietermaritzburg, April 25. A serious cris!s exists in Zulu affairs. A Zulu deputation, numbering nearly 1,000 persons, chiefs and followers, is now waiting a few miles from here for an audience with the Governor. The deputation essentially represents the ex- king's party. Three of Cetewayo's brothers are present in pbrson. It also includes several chiefs living under John Dunn, who come to protest against his authority. The de- putation come without a pass from the President, which makes matters more critical. Great care is necessary to prevent civil war and terrible bloodshed in Zululand. ELOPBMENT IN HIGH LlFE.—Teddington, a correspondent informs us, was in a state of considerable excitement on Tuesday, in consequence of an elopement which is alleged to have taken place from that neighbourhood on Sunday night. The story is that the wife of a prominent resident has gone away with an officer "who is believed to be con- nected with one of Her Majesty's crack regiments stationed in the vicinity." It is stated that the lady retired somewhat abruptly from the dinner table on Sunday night, and almost immediately afterwards made her way to a secluded part of the village, where a carriage was in waiting. Thence she drove to a station of the London and South-Western Rail- way, where she was met by the gentleman in question, who had previously taken tickets for a southern watering-place. They were seen to enter the last up train in company.—St. James's Gizette.

THE FRENCH RAILWAY MYSTERY. Mr. Willoughby, father of Assistant-Paymaster Willoughby, arrived at Ply- mouth on Monday night from France, where he has been during the past week investigating the circumstances of the supposed murder of his son. On reaching Calais, M. Wil- loughby, who was accompanied by his wife, was joined by Inspector Moser, of Scotland-yard, and together they vis:ted the cemetery of Pishau, where the deceased had been in- terred. It was at first supposed that death was due to acci- dent, but an investigation of the facts led to the English Government requesting the exhumation of the body. This was done, and judicial investigations followed. These were attended by Mr. and Mrs. Willoughby, who identified the deceased as their son by means of his clothing. They were, however, desired on their honour to reveal nothing of the judicial proceedings, and Mr. Willoughby feels bound by this pledge. No reason existed for the deceased leaving his ship at Malta, and his parents believed that he remained ashore until after his ship had sailed, and finding himself a leave-breaker determined to hurry home overland, report himself as a deserter, and get his friends to use their influence in his behalf. An interview with the captain of the Tamar has proved these mis2ivings to be without foundation. FATAL COLLIERY EXPLOSION AT WHITEFIAVEN : Form LIVES LOST.—A terrible eplosion occurred in the William Pit, belonging to the Earl of Lonsdale, at Whitehaven, about midnight on Tuesday, by which four men lost their lives. At the time, the overman, Williamson, who was in the pit, heard the explosion in what is known as the Countess Dis- trict, where a new seam of main coal has been lately opened about three miles underneath the sea. This seam has been making a good deal of gas lately, and " Geordie " lamps have been used instead of Dary lamps. The overman, with other colliers, went in the direction of the explosion, and found Edward Martin alive, but badly burnt. He was quickly removed to the lock shop. In the meantime an alarm was raised, and the manager of the pit, Mr. Harper, eccompluied by Dr. M'Loughlin, descended the shaft. By this time another man had been found in the workings alive, but much burnt. He expired as soon as Dr. M‘Loughlin saw him, and and before he could be removed to the surface. Efforts were then made to restore the ventilation. There were known to be three more men in the working, who were engaged at pumpine... It was not, however, until about eleven o'clock on Wednesday morning that they were reached, and they were then found to be quite dead. The names of the killed are Henry Finch, Thomas Colvin, and James Geddes, who are married men with families, and John M`Guinness, a young man about 22._

EXTRAORDINARY SCENE IN A POLICE COl:MT.—Great consternation was caused among the prisoners at the Bir- mingham Police Court on Wednesday by the sudden ap- pearance of a bear in their midst. Bruin made his entrance from the cells below, and as he thrust his head above the stairs one of the occupants of the dock made a desperate effort to leap over the front, in his fright. For the moment the whole court was surprised at the unusual visitant, hut the astonishment gave place to roars of laughter when Bruin's presence was explained. It appeared that some zealous constable found the animal in the morning, perform- ing, under the direction of two Frenchmen, and at once took all three into custody. The dockkeeper, being ignorant of the remarkable capture, stood dumbfounded as the ungainly brute made its startling entry into the court, and while its owners retreated to the back of the court the animal reared itself above the railings of the dock, exhibiting a formidable front to the magistrates, and causing a general scramble from its vicinity. The policemen charged the Frenchmen with causing an obstruction in the streets, but the magistrates , laughed at the complaint, and discharged the remarkable I " trio "on the men promising to leave the town. As they left the court, the bear was made to descend the staircase on its bind legs, amid the roars of laughter from the spectators.

THE BISHOP OF SALFORD ON INFIDELITY, RATIONALISM, AND RITUALISM—The Bishop of Salford preached the annual school sermons at St. Mary's, Burnley, on Sunday. He dwelt at length on the subjects of faith and unbelief, laying it dawn as a principle that faith was the foundation of every Christian virtue. We lived in an age in which faith was attacked and divine revelation abrogated alto- gether. This class of unbelievers was largely on the in- crease. The opposite of faith was unbelief, infidelity, and Rationalism ; and Catholics frequently found themselves un- able to answer objections without being prepared. The most profound student of theology, whether Pope, bishop, or pro- fessor, believed in the doctrines of the Catholic Church upon the same principle and for the same reason as the poorest and least enlightened. It sometimes happened that persons who went over from Protestantism went back again in a few years, because they exercised the principle of private judg- ment. Their new faith rested on a wrong basis. If they simply believed because they thought that seven sacrament, were more serviceable than two, that daily sacrifice was more in accordance with the needs of man, that the supremacy of ' the Pope gave greater strength and unity, and that they were entitled to exercise their private judgment instead of ' bowing to divine authority—such people entered upon false principles and returned to rank infidity. Large nurnb?r aof the present day went by the name of Ritualists, teaching nearly all the doctrines of the Catholic Church, adopqng , her ritual and ceremony. for which they were sometittr4 persecuted, as they considered it, yet they persisted. in i':e face of legal processes. As they simply exercised ti !r reason and private judgment, and were not snbject to t'4, obedience required by the Catholic Church, thy were 0,4 Catholics. Faith and revelation were of God. Dr. VaugbAn cautioned the Congregation not to allow their steadfOst- ness of faith to be shaken by the attioits of Ritualists or unbelievers..e \thlljaB : , -

THE CHARGE OF SHOOTING A WIFZ
AT ALTkINCHAW

At the Chest.r assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justic Chitty, George Barker Cooper, a merchant, of Altrincham, was indicted for having feloniously shot his wife, Edith, with intent to murder her. The evidence was of a painful character. The prisoner is the son of a Manchester mer- chant, in a good position. Mrs. Cooper, who was much affected, said she married the prisoner three years ago. Lately her husband had absented himself from home a goad deal. On the sth of October she went to No. 5, Osmond- terrace, Manchester—a house occupied by Ellea Ditchfield --and there saw her husband's photograph on the mantel- piece. She took it away, and when her husband returne& he accused her of stealing the photograph, and of threaten- ing Ditchfield 's life, and said the best thing she could de was to get a divorce. Witness went to put on her jacket, and, on opening the drawing-room door, found Ditchfield there. She requested her to leave the house. Ditchfield would not go, and witness then struck her on the head with her fist. The prisoner's father, Mr. George Cooper, was in the house, and witness appealed to him not to allow her to suffer the indignity of having that person there. Her hus- band separated witness and Ditchfield, and a struggle then took place between the prisoner and his father, in the course of which-the prisoner drew a pistol. Mr. Cooper said, "For God's sake don't fire," but witness raised his hand and fired at witness. His father seiltd the prisoner's hand which contained the pistol, and witness ran towards the side door. As she did so, the prisoner fired a second time. The bullet struck the wall at the bottom of the stairs.—Cress-examined, witness said her husband was in the habit of carrying a revolver. She asked him on one occasion if it would not be better to obtain a divorce, as she knew what his relations with Ditchfield were. Prisoner, when intoxicated, had frequently beaten her.—Evidence having been called in sup- port of the prosecution, the defence rased on behalf of the prisoner was that he did not fire the revolver with intent Le harm his wife, but discharged it accidentally doring a struggle which took place between himself and his father. —The jury, after a prolonged deliberation, took this view of the case, and the prisoner was discharged. The prisoner was liberated from Chester Castle about an hour after the verdict of the jury. An immense crowd, composed chiefly of military men, roughs, and women, was outside the prison entrance awaiting his appearance. Immediately the doors were opened and the prisoner came out the military men and ronghs gave a loud cheer, tut the women hissed Cooper and endeavoured to get at him. He quickly bolted through the Castle yard, the cheering, yell- ing mob following closely at his heels. In Lower Bridge- street he espied the cabstand. Rushing up to an unoccupied cab, he jumped in, banged the door to, and was rapidly driven away from his pursuers, who gave him a parting groan. If the women could have got at him he would un- doubtedly have been severely mauled.

div.head: RISING IN AUSTRIA.
div.p: THE RISING IN AUSTRIA.

Through "Slavonic sources" we continue to receive accounts of skirmishes between the Austrian troops and the Crivoscians. From Vienna it is announced that the Hun- garian Delegation has struck two million florins from the eum demanded by the Cabinet for the "pacification " of the revolted districts.

An official dispatch from Vienna announces that on the rd inst., at Jelovids, an Austrian detachment while fetch- ing water was fired upon by a party of insurgents in ambush, and four men were severaly wounded. The insurgent band was subsequently driven back. Between the 15th and 24th inst., six companies of Austrian troops scoured the country between Trebinje, Ljubinje, Nevesinje, and Gecko, dispers- ing several smaller insurgent bands, who lost several killed and wounded, besides a quantity of ammunition and pro- visioT. Several of the insurgeants were taken prisoners. THE RELATIONS BETWEEN ENGLAND

div.head: AND THE POPE.
div.p: AND THE POPE.

Lord Denbigh, previous to leaving Rome for England (says the Rome correspondent of the Times), was received in Private audience by the Pope, and very naturally the con- versation turned on the question of the re-opening of diplo- matic relations between the Vatican and England. "His Holiness e;zpressed some surprise that doubts should exist in any quarter regarding his earnest wish for the re-estab- lishment of some cuannel, whether of an official or officious character, for direct communication and interchange of ideas between the Holy See and the British Government. He said that it was his especial desire that the Catholic clergy should everywhere give their assistance towards the maintenance of order and good gevernment ; and to that end it was necessary that he should be in such amicable rela- tions with all powers as would enable him to obtain the sore and exact information requisite to carry out his intention. He warmly expressed his admiration of the Constitution and Gbvernment of England, under which the Roman Catholic religion was able to enjoy such ample and exceptional liberty. He was desirous of possessing means for obtaining such in form ition on matters of fact, and regarding the views of Her Itlajestv's advisers, as would prevent his_acting at any time tinder a mistaken impression on "points connected with the government of an Empire embracing interests so diverse as these, for instance, represented in Ireland and in India. In brief, he expressed his desire to be of use in the interests of civilisation and his belief that he on be of use. But to enable him to be so it was obvious that he must alwap Jl3Ve 00 means of oppiymiptution at hand,"

div.head: ST. HELENS BOROUGH BENCH.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS BOROUGH BENCH.

Although no official list of magistrates appointed to sit on tile newly formed Borough Bench has been received, still eeveral gentlemen whose names were amongst those sent to the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster have been com- municated with, and asked if they would allow their names to be placed on the Commission of the Peacefor the borough of St. Helens. In all probability the gentlemen communi. cated with will accept the honour, so that we are in a posi- tion to give the names of the first borough magistrates appointed for St. Helens. It will be observed from the list appended that out of the 18 gentlemen selected, half of that number previously held Her Majesty's Commission as county magistrates; so that there are only eight new magi- strates appointed out of the list of 25 sent up for selection. It rill be remembered that through the inconvenience and other causes operating in the Police Court against justice being done to suitors, the agitation for a Borough Bench commenced. We reported in these columns the discussions that took place from time to time on this question, and the opposition which the proposed bench met with from several eminent gentlemen, most of whom were county magistrates. The question at the time was the principal topic of conversation amongst the townspeople. When the resolution in favour of a Borough Bench in the first in- stance was broaght forward it was dropped on the under- standing that the county magistrates would take steps for the appointment of additional magistrates. A considerable time elapsed without any movement in this direction being taken, and the question again came on for settlement. There was a majority of one in its favour, and the Home Secretary was acquainted with the resolution of the Council. In the in- terval between the date of that decision and the reply of the Home Secretary, the county magistrates,who had been commu- nicated with from the office of the Home department drew I up a list of objections ta the proposed new commission, and the Home Secretary forwarded a reply pointing out that the resolution had been carried by one vote only, and that several gentlemen were absent who were presumably an- tagonistic to the proposed new bench. The advocates for it were highly incensed at this interference on the part of the county magistrates, and another vote was taken, when it was found that the resolution for the Borough Bench was carried by the respectable majority of five votes. In due course a reply was received that a new commission had been ordered to be issued, and the commission now consists of the following gentlemen:—

Colon-el-Gamble J.P. ' Alderman Harrison. H. S. Hall, J.P. Alderman Jos. Cook. W. W. Pilkington, J.P. Alderman J. Mcßryde. R. Pilkington, J.P. Alderman J. Radley. J. C. Gamble, J.P. I Dr. Gaskell. Dr. Twyford,J.P. Mr. A. Sinclair. W. Blinkhorn, J.P. Mr. A. Walmsley. W. Pilkington, J.P. Mr. H. Baxter. T. Pilkington, J.P. Mr. J. C. Bishop. The appointment has not given general satisfaction, ant it will te seen that some gentlemen nominated by the To wa Council, well qualified to act as justices, have been left out of the list. The following gentlemen were in that list : Alderman E. Johnson. Mr. J. Birchall. Mr. James Marsh. I Mr. U. Bramwell.
Mr. Thomas Cook. Mr. D. McKeehnie. Messrs. Cook, McKechnie, an,
Mr. Robert Belsher.
Belsher are town councillors..

LIVERPOOL. PROVISIONS, TitußsrAY.—No change to report beef and pork, whit•li continue firm. Bacm is steady at yesterday's rater. Hams and shoulders remain unchAnged in value. Lard meets but a small demand. Cheese and butter show a better feeling. Tallnw continues strong. CLYDE CRUSHED SUG iR, THURSDAY —Demand active for all kinds at fully yesterday's prices; a large business done. The official report states. Active market; good business done at firm prices.
GLASGOW PIG IRON, TIIITESDAT.—First report: The market is firm, witia good business done at 475 Old to 475 2id cast. Closing sellers at 47s 3d cash and 47s 5d one month. Buyers near.

MANCHESTER Co, THITRFRAT.—The trade has been less motive since last market day, and prices have inclined slightly 'ln favo ir of buyers. This has been more marked with respect ' to maize, whieli has suffered considerable reaction from the high prices previously quoted. The weather has been cold and stormy. Imports into Liverpool have been large of wheat and flour, liberal of barley, and very small of maize and other pro- duce. T:iere was an average attendanfe at this morning's market, and a moderate consumptive inqt iry. Wheat was a ld to 24 per cents) lower, except low qualities of Indian, which brought full Prises Flour was steady in price and demand. Oats and oatmeal were taken by needy buyers at the full rates of last market day. Beans and peas were dull. Maize sold in retail at a reduction of 2d to 3d per c€mtal. From a correspondence received in Manchester it appears that the Home Office will not interfere in ny way in the prosecution for the alleged next-of-kin frauds. A correspondent of the Freeman's Journal says that as Americal Consul has waited upon Daniel MiSwenney, one of the imprisoned Irish-American suspects in Dundalk Gaol, and offered him .£lO of the amount required to defray hie expenses to America, provided he would consent to leave. M'Swenney, who has a large quantity of land in county Donegal, unhesitatingly rejected the offer. Arrangements are being made among the North Wales colliers to hold a great mass meeting at Wrexham, on Monii day next, when the masters will meet the delegates appointed' by the men to discuss tl:e subject. It is generally believed that concessions willike made, both oil the part of the coal owners and the miners themselves, as the results of the strike are now making themselves seriously felt. Some of the largest brickworks have been compelled to cease work, being unable to obtain coal, and hundreds of hands have thus been thrown out of work. There is also much suffer. ing among the miners, many of whom are begging bread. Most of the steady colliers have left North Wales in search of employment elsewhere. The inhabitants are a/so-sutfer- ing considerably for want of coal, house coal being ;Ow brought into the district from the Lancashire and Stafford- shire coalfields. On Wednesday morning, as Chief Constable Sheaeby, of Macclesfield, was leaving his house in Ureat King-street, he was met by a man named Joseph Potts, a shoemaker, Who has several times been b fore the magtArates, and was a fort- night ago discharged from the lunatic asylum. Ore ofThis delusions is that the chief constable has injured him.: He was armed with a shoemaker's knife, and suddenly attacking the chief constable, inflicted three wounds about theilleck and face, and then ran away with the knife still in his hVarl.
