div.head: TEE EXAMINER,
div.p: TEE EXAMINER,

of that interesting Tory acquisition, Cyprus. Truly, the Anglo-Turkish convention has not only been a most troublesome one, but a most expensive one to boot. As has already been shown, the surplus at the end of the financial year will amount to £305,000 if it is not trenched upon. It does not leave any margin for the remission of taxation, and but for a promise made some twelve months ago to Colonel Harcourt, it would not have been necessary to in- crease taxation at the present time. That promise, it may be remembered, related to the relief of local taxation especially in respect of the highway rates, and therefore it is proposed to raise £250,000 in order to relieve the farmers of the maintenanceof the high- ways, which has long been a standing grievance. That is to be done by a very equitable arrangement increasing the two guinea duty upon four-wheeled carriages to three guineas; and the fifteen shilling duty on two-wheeled carriages to 215. This placing of the burden upon the right shoulders will, it is esti- mated, realise £247,000, a sum sufficient for the pur- pose intended. It must be borne in mind this is only a temporary arrangement in redemption of the promise made by the Government last year; any per- manent arrangement is to be embraced in the com- prehensive scheme for the reform of local government which was promised in the Queen's speech, but is not now likely to be introduced this session. On the whole the budget, as we have said, is a tame one, especially for a financier of Mr. Gladstone's calibre. It is said it is the last he will introduce, but we hope not. With increased prosperity and increased revenue we trust it may yet be reserved for him to carry through those great fiscal changes which he has declared to be practicable.

LIB latest development of the temperance move- ment—the Gospel Temperance Mission Blue Ribbon Army—appears to be a great success. The movement which was originated in America by Mr. F. Murphy, was introduced in 1878 into London, where it has its head-quarters, by Mr. William Noble, and it is dis- tinguished from other temperance organisations inso- much as its meetings—as its title implies—partake of a missionary character, and a further special feature is the insignia of the members—blue ribbon. Recently the Army has extended its operations to Lancashire, and through the advocacy of Mr. Edward Murphy, son of the originator, great good is said to have re- sulted. It is stated on good authority that publicans have had to close their doors for want of customers, and several towns in North-East Lancashire have been completely transformed through the inhabitants having joined the Army in thousands. A fortnight ago the movement spread to Warrington, where en- thusiastic meetings have since been held nightly, and its success here has been no less remarkable than in the towns previously visited by Mr. Murphy. Every night during last week the Public Hall, the largest public building in the borough, was packed to its utmost capacity with eager listeners, and this week not only has the hall been crowded nightly, but overflow meetings have been held in an adjoining school-room. The vast audiences which have assembled demonstrate conclusively the change public opinion has undergone on the temperance question since the total abstinence movement was commenced in Lancashire half a century ago by that veteran teetotaller, Mr. Joseph Livesey, of Preston. Total abstinence is no longer scouted as a foolish notion, nor are its advocates sub- jected to all kinds of ridicule as in former days. Their views have been proved to be right, and are upheld by gentlemen holding high positions in the medical world ; and temperance reformers are now respected as men who are endeavouring to raise their fellows to a higher social states, and to rid their country of a national disgrace. To the evils of drunkenness it is unnecessary for us to allude. They are apparent on every hand, and our columns bear weekly testimony to the viciousness of an odious liquor traffic. The teetotallers of Warrington have our heartiest sym- pathy in their efforts to induce their fellow townsmen to free themselves from the shackles of this enslaving vice, and thus do their part in making England a sober nation. It is often said that "What Lanca- shire thinks to-day England thinks to-morrow," and it is to be hoped that the maxim will hold good in regard to the new thoughts which have been awakened in the -minds of Lancashire men through the agency of the Blue Ribbon Army. The nation needs to be thoroughly alive to the importance of the subject with which it will doubtless shortly have to deal. We believe the people of England will soon have put into their hands the power contained in I the measure so ably championed by Sir Wilfred DlRson. Parliament has already twice decided in favour of the principle 01 Local Option, and there is little doubt that when the legislative machinery is again in working order, the measure will speedily became law. It therefore behoves everyone who is anxious to see the country happy and prosperous to give the matter most serious consideration, and we are glad to see that the temperance people of War- rington are doing what they can to bring the towns- people to a sense of their responsibility on the grave question of temperance reform.
With each copy of to-day's Examiner is presented two beautiful portraits of the Duke of Albany and Princess Helen of Waldeck Pyrmont, the lithographers being Messrs. Maclure and Macdonald, of London.

THE CASE OF SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES. —On Saturday an inquest was held by Mr. C. E. Driffield, at the Angel Hotel, Mersey-road, Widnes, on the body of Wm. Roberts, furnaceman, of Irwell-street, who died very suddenly on the previous Wednesday, as reported in last Saturday's Examiner.—Edward Knowles, insurance agent, of Irwell- street, said deceased had lodged with him during the past fortnight, and was employed as a furnaceman for the Wid- nes Metal Co. On Wednesday afternoon he went to his work, at a quarter to five; and two hours later he heard that he was dead. At about half vast 8 deceased was brought home. On going to his work, deceased did not complain ef feeling unwell; but he appeared in good health, and had eaten a good tea.—Michael Carr, copper furnace mixer, said he, deceased, and others went to work on the nightshift on the night in question. Deceased fell down dead at the time when he was removing slag with a pair of irbn tongs. He fell upon the back of his head, and the noise of his fall was heard by some of the men who were working forty yards away.—Abraham Davies, coal miner, brother-in-law to Roberts, who was 32 years of age, said he had com- plained of heart disease for about twelve months. He was a very steady industrious man.—The Coroner briefly sum- med up, after which the jury returned a verdict of "Natural causes."

WESLEYA.N BAND OF HOPE MEETING AT WIDNES. On Monday evening a meeting under the auspices of the Lacey-street Wesleyan Methodist Band of Hope was held in the same school-room. The gathering had not been adver- tised except by placard, and at the commencement of the proceedings the audience consisted of about 30 people. Mr. R. A. Naylor, of Warrington, presided, and delivered an address on temperance. He urged those who were believers in the principles of total abstinence to stand firm, as he believed their influence was gradually taking a capital posi- tion in the country. Let them not forget the saying of the Book of Books, to the effect that he who went forth weep- ing and bearing precious seed should doubtless come again rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him. (Applause.)— Mr. Joseph B. Leach, secretary of the St. Helens Band of Hope Union, gave a brief sketch of the day of small things in connection with the rise of the temperance movement in Widnes.—The Rev. George Hack, of Runcorn, spoke at some length, but the speech was one which has previouslv been reported in The Examiner.—The Rev. T. Peters (Con- gregationalist) asked what were the elements of national greatness and prosperity. In the first place they must have industry and they must have religion He believed in the power of family life, in the importance of family union, and in the importance of bringing up children in the way they should go. He had known something of temperance work for a great many years. He know something of its history from the time when it was ft called ' teetotal" by the stuttering man— Livesey. Tie first form of temperance was moderation ; but that did not do. (Hear, hear.) They all claimed to be moderate (hear, hear, and applause) just as they clartnedto be i-noderate to-day between a glass and a gallon. On the platform were a large number of children who had given themselves to the temperance cause, and in them, and such as they, lay the germs of England's greatness in the future. —During the evening the proceedings were very pleasantly varied by the singing of melodies by a children's choir. Votes of thanks were passed to the speakers and the chair- man, after which the procee4ings terminated.

RUNCORN CAMDEN SENDAT SCHOOL. -On Sunday, the anniversary sermons of this school were preached by the Rev. Henry Valentine, formerly of Runcorn circuit. In the afternoon, a service was held at Camden school, when the Rev. George Hack was the preacher. The total collections were £43 6s. 6d.

RUNCORN CAMDEN NUnmul, IMPROVEMENT CLMM,- On Friday evening week, Mr. Alfred Harrison delivered a lecture on Vivisection, under the auspices of this society. The lecturer, whilst not opposing vivisection, advocated the use of drugs in order to allay suffering. An interesting discussion followed. _ _

RUNCORN HOLY TRINITY YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.—On Friday night week, Mr. John Findlow, of Liverpool, read a paper on " The life and writings of Frances L HaTergal." The Rev. D. Llewellyn presided, and there was a good attendance. _

ACCIDENT AT A RUNCORN CHEMICAL WORKS.—OII Mon- day, a furnaceman named William Garry, had his right arm severly burned whilst supplying a furnace with coal, at Messrs. Wigg, Bros., and Steele's works. RUNCORN AND THE ROYAL MARRIAGE.-011 Thursday, the vessels in Runcorn docks were gay with flags, in honour of the marriage of Prince Leopold. Similar marks of joyous sympathy floated from most of the public buildings. RUNCORN BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY —The weekly meeting was beld on Wednesday evening. The delivery-of a lecture. which had been announced on the programme, was postponed, and on the motion of the Rev. George Hack, seconded by Mr. Coventry, a vote of con- dolence with Mr. Timothy Sinister, thc president, on the death of his life partner, was passed.

LECTURE ON ANATOMY BY Du. O'KEEFFE, OF WID IfES.—On Monday evening, Dr. O'Keeffe delivered a lecture on anatomy under the auspices of St. Mary's Catholic Im- provement Class. The Rev. James Clarke presided. The lecturer, who is considered one of the chief scholars of which Widnes can boast, was very happy in his treatment of a subject which bristles with technicalities. THE PROPERTY OF THE RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS.—It is stated that the Properties Committee will, at the monthly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners, on Monday, recommend that all the properties of the Board, with the exception of the market and slaughter- houses shall be offered for sale. It is to be hoped that no such course will be approved by the Board at a time when property is realising such poor prices. We hear that the proposal is likely to raise a lively discussion. DEATH OF JOHN HARRISON, THE RUNCORN FERRYMAN. On Wednesday, John Harrison, who for about 40 years had the management of the Runcorn ferry, was interred at the Parish Church, in the presence of a goodly number of those who had always admired th a able and courteous manner in which he always discharged his duties. The service was read by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, and the funeral arrsngements were conducted by Mr. James Dutton. Some time ago Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst and several other friends raised a subscrip- tion for Harrison, which realised about £4O, and enabled him to pass his declining days in freedom from that fear which haunts many of the poor like a spectre—having to end his days in the workhouse.

THE COUNTY COURT QUESTION !AT WIDNES.—The following (copy) letter has been received from the late Home Secretary, by Mr. W. T. Husband, solicitor, of Wid- nes, in regard to this question :—" Red Scar, Preston Lan- cashire, 15, April, 1882. My Dear Sir,—l have again written to the Lord Chancellor. Please let me know if you get no reply.—Faithfully yours, RICHARD ASSHETON CROSS.—W. I'. Husband, Esq."—The following letters have also been received on this subject :—" Treasury' S.W., 22nd April, 182. Sir,—l am directed by the Lord Chancellor to return to you Mr. Husband's letter, respecting a County Court for Widnes, and to inform you that his Lordship has com- municated to the clerk of the Privy Council that he sees at present no sufficient reason to justify him in recommending the establishment of a County Court at Widnes.—l have , the honour to be, your obedient servant, HENRY NICOL.— The Right Hon. Sir Richard Cress, K.C.B."—" 22nd April, 1882.—Dear Sir,—l am very sorry to have nothing better to send than the enclosed.—Faithfully yours, 'RICHARD ASSHETON CROSS."—Mr. Husban4 has forwarded the follow- ing communication to Sir R. A. Cross :—" Widnes, 25th April, 1882 —The Right Hon. Sir Richard Assheton Cross, R.C.B.—Sir,—County Court for Widnes.-1 beg to acknow- ledge receipt of your letter with enclosure, and note with regret the result of your petition. I trust you will, however, accept from me the thanks of the petitioners for the trouble you have had in the matter.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, W. T. HUSBAND."

CHURCH MISSIONARY SOCIETY.—MEETING AT FARN - WORTH. A meeting in connection with the Church Missionary Society, was held at Farnworth, in the girl's schoolroom, on Monday evening. The Rev. Joseph Holden presided, and there were also on the platform the Revs. Geo. Bond, N. Vickers (the deputation), and S. Allen Spooner. Mr. Vickers gave a lecture on religious work in China, and the great obstacles with which missionaries had to contend. Heathenism caused trade in that densely popu- lated country to be crippled, industry was at a standstill, and the people were wallowing in misery. As an instance of this he referred to the fact that working in coalmines had been practically suspended because one of the chief ministers of China said that if it were persisted in the earth demon would be released, and innumerable evils follow! He also spoke of the opium traffic, and its frightful effccta, and remarked that we could not escape our share of responsi- bility in this matter. It was generally supposed that one of , the greatest difficulties with which missionaries ha to battle in the Celestial Empire, was that the Chinese language was so difficult to learn. However, there was this consolation, that when it was once learned it was a great auxiliary to their efforts, as anything relating to Christianity, if published in Chinese, was always kept by the inhabitants of that country owing to the great veneration which they had for their own literature.—The Rev. Joseph Holden referred to the report, which he said had not been completed, but he thought it would show the Earn worth branch was in a rather better position than last year.—The Rev. Geo. Bond moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Vickers, which was seconded by Mr. liold-m.—The Rev. A. Spooner also made a few remarks ; after which the proceedings were closed in the customary manner.
CONFIRMATION SERVICE AT FARNWORTIL —The usual

quiet of the village of Farn worth was disturbed on Wed- nesday afternoon, when large numbers of the gentler sex assembled in the quaint old church to witness the ceremony of the "laying on of hands upon those that are baptised, and come to years of discretion," in the parishes of Farn- worth, Ditton, and Sankey, in accordance with the ritual of the Church of England. Before proceeding with the cere- mony, the Bishop of Liverpool explained what the candi- dates for confirmation were called upon to confess, and in what spirit they ought to make the confession. After im- pressinw' upon them the solemnity of the occasion, and statisghe wished everything to be done fervently with the heart, and not as a mere matter of form, the Bishop re- marked that they came to take upon them what was pro- mised for them by their godfathers and godmothers at their baptism. The time had come when the young people were called upon by the Church to confess and to promise for themselves what was confessed and promised for them at their baptism. It was a wise and right profession to make. No one ought to be ashamed or afraid to make that profes- sion. It was a privilege to be a Christian, and ought he to be ashamed to profess that he knew what Christian hope, Christian peace, Christian comfolt, and Christian grace was in this evil world in which we live? They should never be ashamed of making a profession of Christianity. Of getting drunk, of swearing and cursing, telling lies, swindling, gambling, and Sabbath breaking, they should be ashamed, but of making a profession of religion they should never be ashamed. The time had come when they were called upon to make the profession, and he thanked God he saw so many present ready and willing to make it. The laying on of hands was then proceedld with, the number of candidates being as follows: Farnworth, 98 males, 94 females; Dit- ton, 13 males and 28 females; and Sankey, 6 males, 6 females; total 245. At the conclusion of the ceremony

Bishop Ryle gave them a few words by way of advice and encouragement. He desired that the day of confirmation should be a day of blessing to everyone, and that the young men and young women should have reason long after he was dead and gone to remember with thankfulness what had taken place that day. He hoped they would not go away that day with the thoughtless and careless, but would take thought about that which they had done. He coun- selled them to remember the enemies they had to contend with, and to watch and pray, but above all to remember the : last great day. He urged them never to forget to use the , means of grace which had been appointed, to mind their time, to beware of idleness, and to take care about their com- pany and chose those who would help them forward and not draw them back from the way of eternal life. In conclusion the Bishop called upon the congregation to look with deep interest upon those young persons who had been confirmed to help and assist them, to try and keep them right, and to try and keep them up to the mark, and remind them of what they had professed.

Wn)NEs Fern. This saturnalia commenced on Thursday, and was continued yesterday. The proceedings were of a very tame description.

It may interest some of our readers to kriow that 'in the Leavenworth (Kansas) Daily StaZdard of March 12th is a lengthy description of the extensive locomotive works in that town, which are superintended by Mr. George Hackney (formerly of the BeWsey Forge, Warrington) and his son. EBENEZER PARTICULAR BAPTIST CHAPEL; WAR - RINGTON.—On Sunday, two sermons were preached in the above chapel by Mr. W. Schofield, of Rochdale, in aid of the Sunday school. Mr. R. Millington presided at the harmonium, and suitable hymns were arranged and sung for the occasion. Collections were made at each service in behalf of the school fund, and they amcunted to £8 Is., for which the officials return their best thanks to their contributors.

KNITT:FORD MAY DAY FESTIVITIES.—The advent of the merry month of May will be celebrated as usual at Knutsford, on Monday, by the coronation of the May Queen on Knutsford Heath. The ancient and interesting ceremony will be observed with all the pageantry of former years, and, as will be seen from our advertising columns, several troupes of neorris dancers will take part in the festivities. SANKEY BRIDGES.—On Sunday afternoon a largo number of persons assembled at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges, to follow the remains of John Ruffel to their last resting place. He was much respected by all around, and his loss is mourned by a large circle of friends, who gathered together to show their last tribute of respect to the deceased gentleman. He was a.member of the Druid's order, and also a resident of Sankey-bridges for many years. The funeral ceremony was performed by the Rev. M. Jackson, who read the funeral service in a very affecting manner.

The public, and more especially those resident on the Cheshire side of the riv.er, will be glad to learn that Admiral Spratt, the acting conservator of the Mersey, is able to report very favourably with regard to the Plucking- ton Bank, which, in its present position has so long incon- venienced ferry traffic. Some progress has already been made towards the removal Of the huge obstruction, and in due course there is every probability, the admiral says of the bank being entirely dislodged from the neighbourhood of the Liverpool landing stage.

THE LONDON AND LANCASIIIRE FIRE INSVRANCE COM- PANY.—The twentieth annual meeting of this company was held at their offices in Liverpeol, on Thursday, when the accounts for the past year were unanimously passed, and a dividend was declared, free of income tax, of 23. 6cl. per share, or 5 per cent. on the capital. The net premiums for the year were reported at £424,556, and the losses at £333,912. After deducting all commissions and expenses, and including sum brought forward from 1880, there re- mained a balance of £32,179. After payment of the divi- dend, the assets of the company will consist of capital paid up £185,200, and reserve £232,919, apart from the capital at call of £1,666,800.

WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.—On Tuesday evening last, the above club held its annual supper at the White Hart, Sankey-street. A goodly number of members and friends partook of an excellent repast, which reflected great credit on Mrs. Brierley. After the supper Mr. J. Critchley occupied the chair, and on behalf of the members, presented Mr. E. J. Warren, their late captain, on his marriage, with a handsome pair of bronze figures of excellent work- manship, supplied by Mr. Eustance. Mr. Critchley eulog;sed Mr. Warren's conduct on the football field and to the mem- bers generally. Mr. Warren made a very suitable reply. A pleasant evening was spent, songs, etc., being given by several of those present.

WA.REINGTON ORANGEMEN AND THE QUEEN. The Secretary of the Earl of Beaconsfield Lodge of Loyal Orangemen, Warrington, has received from Sir W. V. Har- court the following reply. to the resolution of condolence with the Queen, passed by the lodge on the 20th ult.:— " Whitehall, 22nd April, 1882. Sir,—l have had the honour to lay before the Queen the resolution which has been adopted at a meeting of the members of the Disraeli and Earl of Beaconsfield Lodges of Loyal Orangemen, War- rington District, held on the 20th ultimo, on the subject of the recent attempt upon the life of Her Majesty. And I have it in command to assure you that Her Majesty is deeply sensible of the loyalty and affection of her faithful subjects." CURIOUS COUNTY COURT ACTION AT WARRINGTON. A rather curious case was heard at Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes. The plaintiff was Mr. William Fairhurst, of Bridgefoot, War- rington, represented by Mr. Thurnham (Messrs. Robert Davies and Co.), and the defendants were Messrs. C. Sayers and Co., Harrington-street, Liverpool. and Mr. Wm. Porter, timber merchant, Church-street, Warrington, garnishee. It appeared that at the February sitting of the court the plain- tiff obtained judgment against Messrs. Sayers for £9 17s. 3d. and costs. The money had not been paid, and it was alleged that Mr. Porter was indebted to Messrs. Sayers in the sum of £5. Mr. Thurnham consequently asked for the usual guarantee order. Mr. Ferrer, called, said he had tim- ber in his possession of the value of Rel 18s. 6d., which be was selling on commission for Messrs. Sayers. He was pre- pared to take the timber and hand over £4 18s. 6d. His Honour said that was no debt. Mr. Porter held certain goods in trust, and he would be responsible for the money when they were sold. But at present there was no debt, and he could not make the order. "Lux -IN TENEBRIS."—This is the title of the latest picture from the easel of Sir Noel Paton, an artist who has become deservedly famous in depicting scripture allegory. M will be aeon from an announcement in our advertisitigicolumns, the work is on view at Mr. E. Orindley's Fine Art Galleries, Liverpool. A fitting companion to "Mors Janua Vitas," "Lux in Tenebris " is, like its imme- diate predecessor, a veritable sermon upon canvas, upon which it is impossible that the spectator can look with any but the most devout feelings. The subject may be concisely described as a representation of "the struggle and triumph of faith over the last enemy," the text suggesting the theme of the picture being a verse from the Psalms: "Yea, though I wale through the valley of the shadow of death I will fear no evil; for thou art with me. Thy rod and Thy staff they comfort me." Space forbids our entering upon any criti- cism of the artist's conception, or, indeed, upon an adeqaato description of the wonderful combination of breadth and detail with which the subject is treated. Suffice it to say that the work is highly spoken of by the provincial press, and that we can bear personal testimony to its worthiness of an inspection by lovers of art. ACTION AGAINST WARRINGTON CLOTHIERS. —Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, at the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, Margaret Crank claimed for wages rom Messrs. Jesper, hitching and Co., clothiers, Sankey- street, Warrington. Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the de- fendants. The plaintiff, whose home is at Bolton, was a machinist in the employ of the defendants. On the 18th ult., she gave notice to Mr. Mawson, the foreman, of her intention to leave her situation in a week. At the expiration of that time, plaintiff alleged Mr. hitching would only pay her 10s., assigning as his reason that she had not given proper notice. Mr. Davies' on behalf of the defendants, had put in a counter claim of SI 16s. lit. He admitted the notice, but contended that the plaintiff, at the solicitation of Mr. hitching, had agreed to work another week, and take payment for the fortnight at the end of that period. She, however, did not fulfil that promise, and the defendants claim was made up of LI for breach of contract, and 16s. Id. for loss. Mr. hitching, Mr. John Mawson, the foreman, and Mr. Francis J. Dell were called to prove this agreement on the part of the plaintiff. No evidence was given of the . alleged loss. His Honour said no proof of damage had been made, and be gave judgment for the plaintiff for £l. and allowed the defendants ss. for breach of contract. Costs to follow in the ordinary way. MR. ALEX. INGLIS AT THE ASSEMBLY-ROOTI, WARRING- TON.—An interesting evening's entertainment was afforded our townsmen on Monday evening, in the visit of this gifted elocutionist, and we regret that a larger number were not present to participate in its enjoyment. The audience, though small in point of nembers, evinced, however, an amount of appreciation of Mr. Inglis's efforts to please, which goes far to confirm the favourable opinion we have formed of that gentleman's abilities and the superior char- acter of his entertainment. The nature of the pieces chosen for recital is such as to tax rather severely Mr. Inglis's histrionic and elocutionary powers. The selections from the varied branches of literature which go to make up the pro- gramme demand the utmost flexibility of style. The antithesis resulting from the juxtaposition of " King Robert of Sicily" (Longfellow) with " Horatio Sparkins" (Dickens), " The grave scene from Hamlet," with the assumption of the peculiar characteristics of the vivacious Frenchman in the piece which followed, is such as to suggest difficulties im- plying no small amount of skill in the artiste who is to adequately interpret them before the public, aided by memory alone. For two hours, however, Mr. Inglis suc- ceeded in holding the undivided attention of the audience, his wonderful command of voice, gesture, and powers of oratory enabling him to place the piece before them with much of the vividness of a stage realisation. Mr. Inglis is yet comparatively young in the profession he has chosen for himself, and we venture to predict, that remembering the degree of humour and pathos, gravity and gaiety, which his efforts now display he will mature into one of the leading " elocutionists and public recitere of the future.

div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

On Thursday afternoon, at a quarter to two, an extraor- dinary meeting of this Board was held, Mr. T. Sutton Timmis in the chair, for the purpose of filling up the vacancy caused by die resignation of the Rev. George Holloway. There were also present the Revs. James Clarke and Thos. Finegan, Messrs. Bradshaw O'Keeffe, Hartland, Shaw, Wade Deacon, Brock, Davis, and Danby (clerk). ELECTION OF A NEW MEMBER. _

The CHAIRMAN, in accordance with previous notice of motion, moved that. Mr. Henry Brunner, of Cliff House, Appleton, be elected to fill the vacancy. He pointed out how it had occurred, and said that as the Board was a nomi- nated one, and the member retiring had been a representative of the Church party, he considered it incumbent upon the members to elect a gentleman belonging to the Establish- ment. He had great pliasure iu proposing for their accep- tance the name of a gentleman who lie was sue would be acceptable to every one around the table—that of Mr. Henry Brunner. Most of them would remember him as a col- league upon the previous Board, and they would no doubt recollect the ability which he brought to bear on all ques- tions coming up for consideration. They had had great pleasure in workirg with Mr. Brunner. Mr. BRADSHAW (vice-chairman, anti one of the represen- tatives of the Catholic party) seconded the proposition. Mr. ROBERT SHAW (Nonconformist) supported the resolu- tion, and it was carried unanimously. The business of the monthly meeting was then proceeded with.

The General Purposes Committee recommended that the salary of the caretaker and cleaner to the Board's offices- be increased from £1 to £1 ss. per month. The Revs. FINEGAN and CLARKE did not see any necessity for an advance, and the recommendation was rejected by six to four votes.

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

The committee reported that during the month of March (five weeks!, the number of cases summoned before them had been 450, of which 143 were applications for payment of fees, and 307 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees had been recommended to be paid in 121 cases; 22 ap- plications had been refused; and there had been 28 prosecu- tions, and a like number of convictions by the magistrates.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.

The West Bank Managers recommended that Miss Mar- garet R. Hunter be appointed assistant mistress in the senior girls' department, rice Miss Foster, at a salary of 50 pe-r- -annum. This was agreed to, as was also a recommendation of • the School Management Committee that Mr. Henry Brunner be appointed a member of that body in the place of the Rev. George Holloway, resigned.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

er. Slum read the re-p-r;r-t-- of the Finance Committee. Accounts amounting to £548 13s. 9d. were recommended for payment. There had been paid into the bank since the last report £316 us. 2d., including £lB5 from the overseers, snd £6 15s. Bd. from the Science and Art Department at West Bank.
ST. MART'S SCHOOL AND THE EDUCATION DEPARTMENT.
The CLERK read the following communication:—

Itducation Department, sth April, 1882.—Sir,—I am directed to inform you that the managers of the Widnes St. Mary's 11.,man Catholic school have recently added to their school a boys' deptrtment, for which they now seek annual grants. Look- ing to the terms of section 98 of the Element try Education Act, 1870. my Lords request to be favoured with any remarks which your Board may wish to make upon this application before any answer is made to the managers.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, P. Cumm. 'rho CHAIRMAN said the PS h section was the one referred to in the letter, and it stated that if the managers of any school, not previously in the receipt of a Parliamentary grant, applied to the Education Department for such grant, they might, if they thought necessary, refuse it. It was, however, proviaed that the Department should cause to be laid before the Houses of Parliament every year the cases in which they had refused the grant, and also state the reasons for such refusal. Mr. SiLkw asked Father Clarke bow, if the case at St. Mary's applied to an addition, it was covered; but the reply was inaudible to the reporters. The CHAIRMAN: The Department evidently think it does apply. The CLERK: It is a new school; it has not been in exist- ence before. _

_ The CHAIRMAN: I think that all the Board have to do is to ascertain that the school is necessary. I suppose that you have the children, Father Clarke. Rev. J. CLARKE: Yes, it is pretty full. Mr. BROCK : Now that Father Clarke has removed I hope he will take care that the children at Moss Bank are pat into the school. (A laugh.) The CHAIRMAN: I don't think that this communication rcquires any reply. We have no remarks to make. If we don't wish to make any observation, there is an end to it. Mr. SHAW: I am afraid we shall be in a difficulty if we make any remarks, Mr. Chairman. What answer will you give if you are tackled on the subject of accommodation? It is a delicate matter to return the right answer. Mr. DEACON: It seems to me that all we can do is to acknowledge the receipt of the letter. The CHAIRMAN : As a matter of courtesy, we must acknowledge it, but I don't see the absolute necessity of doing so. Perhaps, however, it will be more courteous to let them have an answer. We might acknowledge the re- ceipt of the communication, and say that the Board have no remarks to make. Mr. SHAW: Would you go so far as that? I would say that the letter had been brought before the Board, and the Clerk had been instructed to acknowledge the receipt. Rev. T. FINEGAN : Might not you say that you have no remarks to make or objections to raise? The CHAIRMAN did not think it would be well to say any- thing about objections. It was ultimately agreed, without any formal motion, that the Clerk should aeknowledge the receipt of the letter, and say the Board bad no remarks to make upon it. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF PRINCE LEOPOLD.
div.p: THE MARRIAGE OF PRINCE LEOPOLD.
LOYAL AND ENTHUSIASTIC DEMONSTRA- TIONS.

On Thursday morning Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, was married to Princess Helen of Waldeck, in the historic Chapel of St. George, at Windsor Castle. The weather was delightfully fine, notwithstanding the prognostications of these who in the old borough, declared that a rainy day was certain. From a very elrly hour the town was astir, and workmen were busily engaged in completing the work of decorating, which consisted chiefly of flags and bunting and floral devices. Here and there were neat monograms with the letters " L.H.," and often, especially in the high street, were to be noticed the words "God bless them both." Castle Hill and its approach presented a very animated scene by ten o'clock. The Berkshire volunteers hart by this time arrived, in strong force, and headed by the hands, marched through the town to the quarters provided for them. The Yeomen of the Guard had also mustered, and t were awaiting orders, whilst a large contingent of me- tropolitan police, under Chief Inspector Gernon, had taken charge of the route along which the procession to St George's Chapel was to pass. The guard of honoar was in position at a quarter-past eleven o'clock, and in addition to the volunteers, was composed of companies of the Guards and the 78th Highlanders, now called the Seafarth High- landers, who had been brought specially from Fort George, the regiment being one,in which Prince Leopold has taken special interest, and of which he holds the rank of honorary colonel. By this time the bells in every steeple of the town ,vere ringing ,merry peals, s.nd the in- terest in the event was at its height. The Ambassadors, Foreign Ministers, Cabinet Ministers, and others invited to the ceremony arrived by special train from London and proceeded in carriages provided for the purpose direct from the Windsor terminus of the Great Western Railway to the eouth entrance ot St. George's Chapel, and were at once shown to the seats reserved for them in the choir. The members of her Majesty's House- hold in Waiting, who did not take part in the carriage pro- cession, assembled at St. George's Chapel at half-past eleven o'clock. The Archbishop of Canterbury, the Bishop of London (Dean of her Majesty's Chapel Royal), the Bishop of Winchester (Prefate of the Order of the Garter, the Bishop of Oxford (Bishop of the Diocese and Chancellor of the Order of the Garter), the Bishop of Worcester (Clerk of the Closes), the Hon. and Very Rev. the Dean of Windsor (Lord High Almoner, Registrar of the Order of the Garter, and Domestic Chaplain to her Majesty), with the canons and minor canons of Windsor, assembled at the Deanery, and took their places within the rails of the altar at a quarter to twelve o'clock. At that time her Rua! Highness the Princess of Wales, with her Majesty's royal guests, who had previously assembled in the Armoury, left the State entrance of Wind- sor Castle in the Queen's carriages,-with their respective suites, for the west entrance of St. George's Chapel, con- ducted by the Lord Chamberlain and the Master of the Horse, and attended by a field officer's escort erf the 2nd Life Guards. On arrival at the west entrance, their Royal Highnessee were received by the Lord Steward and the Vice Chamberlain, and were conducted up the Chapel. Her Majesty's State Trumpeters were stationed at the west en- trance to the Chapel, and announced, by a flourish of trum- pets, as each procession moved from the entrance to the Chapel. Inside St. George's Chapel, which was opened shortly after eleven o'clock, the scene from the organ loft was brilliant. Fitful gleams of sunshine fading through the painted win- dows lighted up and brought into full relief the curiously carved oaken panels of the choir, and the banners, helmets, mantles, and swords of the knights. There was considerable movement in the nave, where the privileged possessors of tickets occupied cnairs or stoed in rows on each side of the columns. The line was kept IT well-drilled beefeaters in their quaint costume of scarlet and gold, and active amongst all was General Ponsonby and the Garter King-at-Arms. Spectators poured in at the north and south doors until half-past eleven, when tha organ pealed forth a voluntary. Amongst the first arrivals were the Marquis of Salisbury, Sir Stafford Northcete, Sir Richard A. Cross, the Duke of Argyle, Earl Granville, Mr. Gladstone, and Lord Carling- ford, all wearing the Ministerial uniform of blue and gold, and wearing shoulder knots of white satin. Earl Spencer, Sir Wm. Harcourt, and Mr. Chamberlain quickly followed, wearing the same uniform, whilst Mr. John Bright and the Lord Chamberlain were arrayed in Court dress of black silk velvet. Cabinet Ministers and members of the diplomatic corps were accommodated with seats in the knights' stalls. The Turkish Ambassador,' conspicuous by his fez, the German, Italian, Austrian, and the Russian and French Ambassadors sat to the left of the Communion rails. The Belgian and Portugese Ministers were also present, as was ..the representative of the Ritch Legation. Inside the communion rails were the officiating clergy, in.; eluding the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Bishops of London, Winchester, Oxford, and Worcester, all wearing their lawn sleeves, assisted by the Dean and Canons, and the minor Canons of Wiedeor. The communion table was laden with antique gold and silver plate, and in the centre of the alter cloth was worked the cross of St. George. The dais fronting the communion rails was laid with a carpet of royal blue velvet, bordered with the badge of the Garter em- broidered in gold. The cognisance of the most noble order of the Garter decorated the chair of crimson and gold pro- vided for her Majesty, and the footstools of the illustrious guests were covered with blue eilk damask.

THE DEPARTURE FOR CLAREMONT. The Duke and Duchess of Albany, atter taking leave of Her Majesty and the Royal Family, left the castle at a quarter-past four o'clock for Claremont, in an open carriage drawn by four greys, preceded by outriders, and attended by an escort of the 2nd Life Guards, under the cornmancl. of Captain Finch. The Royal party took their departure amidst I a shower of rice and slippers from the numerous guests. They were attended by the Hon. Mrs. Moreton and the Hon. A. Yorke. The Duke and Duchess drove slowly down the Castle Hill amidst the cheers of the crowd, and proceeded through High-street and Park-street, both repeatedly acknowledging the enthusiastic reception they met with on all sides. As the procession was passing the entrance to the Castle at the end of the Long Walk, the Prime and Princess of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh, the Duke of Connaught, and other members of the Royal Family had assembled at the gate, having hurredly come down from the Grand Quad- rangle, to take another farewell of the Royal pair, and waved their handkerchiefs as they passed, the bride and bridegroom returning their salutation by kissing their hands. On entering the Long Walk the cortege made for Old Windsor, at which place they passed under an arch of ever- greens erected by the employes of the Royal Tapestry Works. A second arch was erected at Beaumont College by the ' students, where a boquet was presented to the Duchess. On leaving Old Windsor the bride and bridegroom proceeded by way of Egham to Stains Bridge. Here the escort was relieved by an escort of the 11th Hussars. At Chertsey, which was reached at five o'clock, the escort was withdrawn, and after a change of horses their Royal Hig,nesses went on, preceded by a single outrider in scarlet, to Claremont, once the residence of King Leopold of Belgium. In the quiet retirement of this ancient mansion the Duke and Duchess will pass their honeymoon, and then it is their intention to leave for the south in the Royal yacht Osborne for a trip in the Mediterranean. They will afterwards return to Clare- mont, which will be their future residence. Most of the wed- ding guests returned to London by special train on the Great Western Railway. After the departure of the puke and Duchess of Albany the vast crowd still assembled in the main street of the Royal borough. Her Majesty the Queen, accompanied by the Queen of the Netherlands, drove through the town to inspect the grand decorations. The other members of the Royal Family drove through the streets during the evening. A grand banquet took place in the evening in St. George's Rail, Windsor Castle, in honour of the Royal marriage, and a ball in honour of the royal nuptials took place at the Town Hall. The Castle at night was illuminated by Compton's electric light, and the Royal borough was brilliantly illuminated. The bride and bridegroom arrived at Esher at five minutes past six, and met with an enthusiastic reception from the in- habitants and people from the surrounding vil?ages. The place was tastefully decorated, and the carriage passed along a floral arcade, 150 yards long, under several triumphal arches. On reaching Bear Green Rod, the Duke was pre- sented with an address of welcome, and, in reply, said: "On behalf both of the Duchess and myself I beg to return you my true and heartfelt thanks for the terms in which you have welcomed us to our home. We both feel the greatest satisfaction in the thought that the first years of our married life will be spent in the parish of Esher, for it is here that we shall hope for the future to centre our local cares and interests. We willingly accept the splendid reception you have accorded us to-day as a proof of the friendly regard which my neighbours entertain for me, and which I am confident will now be extended to the Duchess also. We congratute ourselves on pos- sessing Claremont as a residence, and should Providence see fit to prolong our lives, we hopefully anticipate spending the greater portion of our lives here." Lady Wilfred Brett then presented the Duchess with a bouquet, and, Her Royal High- ness having expressed her thanks, the royal couple pro- ceeded to Claremont, amidst deafening cheers.

div.head: LOYAL DEMONSTRATIONS.
div.p: LOYAL DEMONSTRATIONS.

The day was observed as one of festivity in many parts of the country. In London flags were displayed on most of the public buildings and elsewhere, and at one o'clnck the Park guns fired a Royal salute. In Manchester numerous flags were displayed from public buildings and warehouses. The stars and stripes were conspicuous over the American Consulate. At noon, and also at intervals later in the day, the bells at the Town Hall and the Cathedral were rung, and on all hands there was much evidence of rejoicing and con- gratulation. From Liverpool, Newcastle, Glasgow, and other places we bear that there was a great display of flags, and the church bells rang. At Aberdeen there was a large dis- play of flags from all the chief buildings, and the city bells were rung. The Corporation gave a banquet in the Town Hall, and the incorp .rated trades gave a dinner. Her Majesty has dirceted that the tenantry on the Bilmoral I estates shall be entertained to a dinner and ball on Friday, May sth. The Archdeacon of Warrington, in his visitation address at St. Saviour's Church, Falkner-square, Liverpool, on Thursday, said—" The day on which I thus address you for the first time !s one which is made memorable by the marriage of one of our princes. In your name, as well as my own, I pray that God's blessing may not only rest on the happy pair, but that this union may bring fresh cause of thankfulness and new sources of interest to our gracious Queen, whom may God long preserve." THE BRIDE AND BRIDESMAIDS' DRESSES.

The Lady's Picforal gives details of the dresses worn by the bride and bridesmaids. The exquisite bridal robe of the Princess Helen was composed of a petticoat of rich white satin, opening round the bottom in several places over orange blossoms and myrtle. It was trimmed with two rob- ings of costly point d'Alencon lace, and the long train was embroidered in silver with raised bouquets of fleur-de-lys, and edged with ccquilles of white satin and point d'Alencon. The low bodice and short sleeves were trimmed to match. ner veil wee of the same delicate fabric, and she wore a wreath of mingled orange flowers and myrtle. The petticoats were of satin trimmed with two rows of pearl flouncing, and pearls being sewn on in triplets, and the edge formed by a light pine or scroll pattern. THE PRESENTS.
The Daily News gives an account of the wedding pre- sents which were laid out on Tuesday in the White Draw- ing Room :

Immediately on the right on entering the room stands one of the Queen's presents—the potrait of the Princess Helen herself, admirably painted by Carl Sohn, junr., a rising artist of the Dusseldorf School. In the middle of the long table extending down ,the room is the superb golden bowl presented by Sir Nathaniel de Rothchild, and on the round table in front of the great malachite vase, the large silver centre-piece forming part of the gift of a Scotch nobleman and gentlemen, friends of the bridegroom. Another stately , gift is the pair of chased silver candelabra, weighing 4450 z., presented by the members of the Christchurch Society of Oxford. The Bachelors' Club presents a handsome dress, lug-case, and the Earl of Aberdeen a pair of silver honey- pails of the Scottish pattern. Mr. Christopher Sykes offers a magnificent anricoe silver Lox, and Duchess of Wellington a grand clock, by Lecluse. A prominent object is the im- mense silver bowl from the Wiltshire Society, and very curious is the Russian liqueur case, with cups instead of classes, given to his brother by the Duke of Edinburgh. Near the Scotch centrepiece is a fine plaque from Sir Albert Sassoon, and a pair of handsome dishes from the Duchess of Connaught's household. Mrs. Wemyss presents a beautiful gold cup, Sir Theodere Martin an exquisitely-carved Augs- burg cup, and Lady Martin a Bible in an antique silver case of great beauty. Lord Rowton's offering is quaint and curious, being the signatures to the draft of the Treaty of Berlin, handsomely framed and glazed; and Mr. Gladstone presents a copy of " Gleanings of past years," with a dedica- tion as follows:—" Humbly presented by the author to H.R.H. Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, on his marriage with respectful hut hearty congratulations and good wishes London, April, 1882." Other presents are described as follows : A beautlfully-framed mirror from Sir W. and Lady Brett, a curious silver box from Lord and Lady Lovelace, an an- tique silver flagon from Colonel and Mrs. Napier Sturt, a superb silver inkstand and candlesticks from the Marquis of Tavistr ck, a curious pirce of old silver work from Captain and Mrs. Arthur Paget, an elegant flap,on from the servants at Claremont, a gold tea equipt."e from Lady Molesworth, ay antique silver bowl from Mr. and Mrs. Jeune, a splendid sil- ver dish from the Marquis and Marchioness of Salisbury, a golden bowl from the Earl and Countess of Bradford, a pair of silver vinaigrettes from Lord and Lady Reay, a fine

LEAVING THE CHAPEL At a quarter-past one those from without beard the strains of Mendelssohn's "Wedding March," which marked the conclusion of the ceremonial, and within a few minutes the procession of carriages returned to the Castle in order the reverse of that in which they entered. First came, with !bar supporters, the bride and bridegroom, the bride blush- ing and smiling affably as the immense concourse cheered tumultuously, and the ladies waved their handkerchiefs almost hysterically in the excess of their womanly sympathy. They were quickly followed by the Queen and the rest Of the Royal Family, ad by half-past one the grey walls and battlements of Windsor Castle hid from view the splendid and glittering cavalcade. The remainder did not follow for a few moments, and then filed through the vestry and signed the registered document. The Queen followed them in her carriage, the Prince and Princess of Wales being next, and the others in the reverse order they had come in. The wedding breakfast to the Royal Family was served an hoar later in the Queen's that dining-room, and at to the gues i ts n Waterloo Chamber. The Queen's and the bride and bridegromit, s were the only healths drunk, after which the party left the table to collect all the slippers in the Cietle, rice being also diligently searched for. On the departure him the Castle a trail of Slippers, some being of fair proportions, rained upon the lucky pair. Those that fell into the carriage the Prince and Princess armed themselves with, and vigorously pelted their assailants. The rice throws, in its density, completely covered for a rucment the hat and bonnet of the fair couple, while a ringing "God bless you," as they drove away sped the couple on their tour to Claremont to manage house for them/el v ea,

Warehousing Minute." The minute of the 21st January states that "the Board of Customs have had under consider- ation the various orders and minutes relating to the ware- housing, esc. of goods in customs premises, and with a view to the consolidation of existing orders and to their agree- ment with the assimilated code of caste= and Inland Revenue practice authorised by the Lords Of the Treasury, the Board direct that all the existing orders be rescinded" and a new set of regulations observed. The "existing orders" referred to in this minute are still in force, however, and the new regulations will only be enforced on the day of actual assimilation, namely the Ist of June. Thus far it was comparatively easy to work out the scheme and to com- mence at once with what has proved to be the gigantic task of transferring the old accounts to the new registers issued to the clerks simultaneously with the minute above referred to. Several months ago the leading bonding merchants of London were requested by the Lords of the Treasury to state what office accommodation they could afford for the clerks who would ultimately be placed in charge'of each warehouse. This evident intention on the part of "My Lords" to pro- ceed seriously with the business of assimilation, alarmed a section of the mercantile community, principally those who maintained that centralization of customs work was far superior to a decentralization which it was loudly asserted would necessitate a large increase of staff in the mercantile offices. One firm went so far as to issue circulars to the others pointing out this danger, and calling upon them to strenuously oppose any innovation which would necessitate an increase of staff. It was also stated that much valuable time would be lost in merchants' clerks having to perform their business at several stations, instead of, as at present, at the Central Office. This argument may apply to those who bond goods at more than one station. But such are com- paratively few, for most bcoders (in London) adhere to one warehouse, especially those who possess -their own. To obviate the necessity of constantly walking to the Central Office to pay duty, or to give 'fond for the removal of goods elsewhere, it is part of the new scheme to allow merchants to pay lump sums in anticipation of deliveries, and also to give bond for large amounts to be acted on continuously for removals Sic. It is obvious that this can only be an ad- vantage to large bonders. For small traders it practically means their extinction unless the old system of journeying to and fro be adhered to by them. Another advantage will be the great decrease in the clerical work performed by merchants. In the future one document will suffic3 for all deliveries out of bond, whether for home consumption, ex- portation, removal coastwise or inland, or for shipment as stores on board out-going vessels. At present several and different forms are in use for each process. All mistakes will be rectified at the warehouses themselves, without the necessity of referring to the central office. In addition there will be granted several privileges rela'ing to opera- tions with goods while in bond. It is hoped that these may compensate bonders for any inconvenience, imaginary or real, they may suffer. So far we have devoted ourselves to a consideration of the present system of clearing, contras- ting it with the new scheme, and pointing out the desire which Mr. Gladstone evidently has to facilitate the busi- ness of the merchants. We will now examine the inten- tions of the Treasury regarding the officials of the indoor- department "My Lords" offer terms of retirement to officials wh'o are old or otherwise unfit for service, under the provisions of ' the "Superannuation Act." The officials petitioned for special terms superior to the provisions of the "Act," and more on a par with those granted to the clerks of the War Office and Admiralty four or five years ago. This petition was refused. To enable the retiring members, however, to provide for the future several months leave of absence on full pay has been allowed. Whilst encouraging retirement" My Lords ",withhold to themselves the right of choosing those who volunteer to retire. Principals, and upper division clerks who prefer to enter the new out-door department, will receive appointments not less in value than those they are now enjoying, while the peculiar order of beings known as "redundant clerks" will be re• tamed on indoor employment of a "lower division" nature until such time as they, and others wire desire a transfer of office, can be placed in other' departments. The members of the "lower division " will be selected for out-door employ- ment as examining officers of Customs with an immediate increase of salary on commencing the new duties. On the whole, the Treasury terms are fair, especially to the younger men. Thus the long period of anxiety which prevailed has given way to a feeling, if not of contentment at least of resig- nation. Certainly the terms of retirement are not nearly so good as were offered to the War Office officials. The Customs clerks were therefore quite justified in praying for similar terms. A precedent had been created, and it was naturally hoped that the precedent would be recognised and followed. "My Lords," however, were not responsible for the doings of their predecessors in office, and moreover con- sidered that the provisions of the Superannuation Act covered all legal claims. To those who feel compelled to enter the new out-door department the change of hours from 10 a.m. to 8 a.m., the exposure to all weathers, anti with some the breaking up of homes in order to live nearer the work will be a real hardship. But unfortunately in all such changes a certain amount of injustice to individuals is un- avoidable—it is another case of a few going to the wall for the sake of the many. Yet with Mr. Gladstone's depart- mental skill it is to be hoped that all will receive full con- sideration at his hands, that as few as possible may suffer, and that in the end the long-expected assimilation will effect all that is hoped from it, in creating a saving to the country, and in increasing the facilities for bonding and ultimately clearing the enormous quantity of dutiable goods which is continually pouring into the country.

Otrr readers have been aware for some time of the great revolution now being worked out in Her Majesty's Customs silent revolution—which its promoters hope will reach its crisis by the Ist June next. It is surprising how little the general public interest themselves in the changes which affect the two great revenue departments of the country, the Customs and Excise. The fact, however, that Warrington is an inland town, and its inhabitants of necessity far removed from contact in any shape or form with the landing and bonding of foreign dutiable goods, is sufficient to explain such lack of interest in the system of collecting the enormous sums which are continually poured into Her Majesty's treasury. It is the system used in the collection of the customs dues which is so soon to be displaced by another altogether different, and, in the minds of a large section of the mercantile community, as well as in the opinion of many high and intelligent officials concerned therein, of doubtful good. For many years past the proposal to substitute the excise system of bonding and clearing for that of the cestoms, and further to amalgamate the boards of the two departments, has met with great favour from successive Chancellors of the Exchequer. But Her Majesty's Chancellors have pre- sumably either had their hands too fully engaged with other projects, or have not had the courage to grapple, with fair expectation of success, so gigantic a scheme. It has been reserved for Mr. Gladstone, with his great skill in the management of fiscal affairs, and with his fertility of resource when unexpected difficulties arise, to set the scheme agoing. This scheme has professedly two great objects in view, firstly, a large ultimate saving to the country by decreasing the expenses incident to the collection of large revenue sums; and, secondly, an augmentation in facilities for land- ing, bonding, removing, or finally clearing goods. Before explaining further the changes themselves, it is perhaps necessary to give a fair description of the system still in use, a system, by the way, which is the gradual growth of centuries, with all its advantages of check against fraud, and with its many disadvantages of officialism which have kept pace with the other silent processes of official evolution. The chief characteristic which underlies the present method of collecting the customs dues, is that of centralization. Every customs port has its custom house, in which every- thing of a clerical nature is performed, and strict supervision exercised over the out-door department. Absolutely nothing of an official nature can be attempted in the out-door department, connected with the actual bonding of, and subsequent dealings with, dutiable goods, whether of direct importation from abroad or of British manufacture, placed for convenience in customs warehouses, without the previous sanction of the in-door officials. On the completion of the legal operations with these goods, whether limited to the warehouse ittelf or in- volving their removal to another station in the same place, or to another port in the same country or abroad, certificates ,of such operations are immediately transmitted to the custom house of the tewn where the goods originally lay. This system of returns to individual houses is extended much further, for every custom house holds itself subordi- nate to the head office in London for statistical, Board of Trade, and other purposes. Consequently there is no possi- bility of any individual, or any set of individuals, save in the central office, taking the initiative in any official matter whatsoever. The whore may be appropriately compared to a huge machine, in which the neglect of lubrication to certain parts, or the breakage of a connecting rod, very speedily affects the whole. More appropriately still may the system be likened to the highly sensitive human frame. No member can perform its own function; no member can refuse its office; nothine in the human economy can occur apart from the brain. Nothing lying outside the usual routine of customs work can possibly happen without the head office in London requiring, sooner or later, a fall and Isufficient reason. Before our readers have reached this I point, it will have been seen that the forthcoming change affects one grea,t department only of the customs, namely, the warehousing department. Other departments, of minor importance and yet dependent to a certain extent upon it, will fall in the general crash, and their officials will be affected accordingly. The warehousing department, as its name implies keeps an account of all dutiable goods from the moment Of landing to the time (occasionally extending to twenty and twenty-five years) when they are finally cleared for home consumption or for exportation. We will seppose for the norice the arrival of a brandy ship from , France. A wine ship from Spain, or a coffee ship from Ceylon would serve the same purpose. The ship has been previously reported to the Customs authorities as well as to the merchants, who are also in receipt of their advicem from the consigners of the goods. The vessel is boarded by the proper complement of officers, and the captain's papers relating to the goods are examined. These papers must tally in every particular with those which the CRSIOM house officer has received previously from the office of the regis- trar who issues duplicates from the merchant's papers pre- sented to him with particulars of landing stations, description and quantity of goods. Should the papers disagree, the , landing of the goods is stopped until the errors are, at the I merchant's request, rectified by the registrar. The registrar retains the merchant's papers (which are called warehousing entries) until the goods are fairly landed, or in the ware- house, and then they are transferred for entry into the general registers to the warehousing department proper. The register office, it will thus be understood, is a sort of connecting link between the indoor and out-door depart- ments, and is in fact the hardest-worked office of the whole Customs service, From the papers entrusted to him the clerk in the warehousing department, above mentioned, DA.RESNURY PETTY SESSIONS. enters the particulars of goods, together with those of the ship, merchant's name, and date, and files them for future TDESDA.Y.—Before Messrs. div.head: RUFFIANISM AT.., WARRINGTON.
div.p: RUFFIANISM AT.., WARRINGTON.
A SERIOUS STREET ROW.

At the Warrington police court, on Monday, befeve the Mayor and Major Cartwright, Patrick Millett, labourer, Ashton-street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on Sunday night; and further with violently assaulting and resisting P.C. Lawrence in the execution of his duty, and also with assaulting Wm. Gray whilst assisting the police. Patrick Hearty, labourer, 12, Naylor-street, was charged with violently assaulting P.C. Lawrence; with injuring the constables's helmet ; and with assaulting Wm. Gray. Thomas Holleran, forgeman, Silver- street, was charged with attempting to rescue the prisoner Millett, and also with assaulting P.C. Hollingworth and Wm. Gray. The prisoners pleaded not guilty. P.C. Lawrence said when in Bridge-street at a quarter-past ten on the previous night, he noticed Millett, with several others, near the end of Dolman's-lane. He was dancing and singing. Witness went to him, and told him to go home, which he appeared to do. In a short time, however, witness heard the noise of shouting and singing further down the street, and nroceeding there he found the prisoner Millett near the Lion Hotel. He was drunk. Lawrence requested him to leave the street. "I will go to —if I will g 3 for you or anybody else "was the reply. He walked a short distance and had a conference with his companions, when he made a rush back, " a perfect run," saying he had been to gaol many a time, but he would have "something worth this time." After this conduct the officer took him into custody. But a crowd closed round the witness and his prisoner. Witness was struck and kicked right and left, and seeing he could not get alone.', he backed his prisoner in a corner and held him there. He then blew his whistle. Whilst standing there, Hearty gave him four or five blows on the head with some kind of a weapon, and blood ran from his temple down his neck. Witness now seized Hearty, but both prisoners escaped after a struggle. P.S. Sphaks and P.C. Hollingworth having heard the whistle, now -came up, and the prisoners were pursued and apprehended. P.S. Spinks deposed to hearing the sound of the whistle of the last witness in Sankey-street, and while proceeding to Bridge-street he was joined by P.C. Hollingworth and Mr. Gray. When he arrived at Rose and Crown-street, he saw P.C. Lawrence bleeding very much from the right side of the head, and in an exhausted condition. Being informed which direction the escaped prisoners had taken, they went to Bridge Foot. The sergeant directed Hollingworth, who was in plain clothes to go in front, as he would have a better chance of catching ;he prisoners. Following closely after, the witness found Hollingworth and Mr. Gray hold of Mi - lett, and both were being struck by the prisoners. Witness had to use his stick pretty freely to get through the grea crowd. Mr. Gray was bLeding very Much from the head. Millett and Holloran were taken into custody, but Hearty escaped. All the way to the police station the prisoners were fighting and struggling, and the crowd acted in a most shameful manner. Millett shoaled, "Is there no man in the one from his pocket, but the sergeant prevented him. P.C. Hollingworth gave evidence as to taking Millett in custody. The prisoners "fought like blacks," and kicked and struck himself and Mr. Gray repeatedly. Wm. Gray (reporter) said he accompanied P.S. Spinks and P.C. Hollingworth. Millett, when apprehended by Honing- worth, was very violent, and he appeared to be on the point of escaping, when he (witness) got hold of him on one side. He received a blow on the side of the head from Holleran, who had some weapon in his hand, and he was itruck several times by other persons, whom he could not identify. He lost an immense quantity of blood, and had his wound dressed at the infirmary., John Millett, brother of Millett, stated he saw Hearty strike Lawrence and Gray with a largd strap, with a strong brass buckle (produced). John Frederick Wilkinson, a:man about 30 years of age, also gave evidence. The Mayor: Did the constable apply :to you for assis- tance? No, sir. Did you assist him? Yes. I picked. his things up. didn't interfere between the parties. When you saw the officer abused in that way, did not you think it was your duty to assist him ?—lf I had put my hand on anyone, they would have killed me at once. Major Cartwright: I would have run the risk if I had been you. Witness: There was close upon a hundred people round. Mr. Hunt: There is a "dead set" made upon people who assist the police. The prisoners had practically no defence, but Holloran accused the police of having illused him in the cells. P.S. Spinks said Holleran was very noisy, and made use of some very obscene language shouted at the top of his voice. He refused to go in any cell but the one in which Millett was placed, and the sergeant was obliged to throw him on the ground, and drag him on his back into the cell. Prisoner Holloran: You would not give me time to get up. The Mayor: That was because you were so violent. Mr. Hunt said Millett had been previously convicted of assaulting the police, and was a returned reformatory lad. He was a " real outlaw" and did nothing but "roll " about the streets. He was a great trouble to his father, who wished to be rid of him. Hoarty had not been before the court pre- viously, but Holloran had been fined ror drunkenness and disorderly conduct. In reply to Major Cartwright, P.S. Spinks said Hearty associated with the worst characters in the town, who con- gregated about Scotland-road, Horsemarket-street, and Bridge-street, and were always ready for a row. The Mayor said the best course would be to comm'

illett for trial. Mr. Hunt remarked that Dr. Richmond said the wounds of P.C. Lawrence and Mr. Gray were very serious, and that they were dtep clean cuts. Major Cartwright: No doubt-. Had anybody handed Hoarty a knife he would have committed murder. The Bench committed Millett to gaol for nine months with hard labour for the assault, and one mouth for being drunk and disorderly. Hearty and Holleran were each sentenced to six months hard labour.

The Mayor, addressing Mr. Gray, said: I think it is very creditable that you acted in the manner you did. If other people in Warrington would assist in ;he same way, there would be no chance for these ruffians to do the work they do to the police—striking right and left. We are exceedingly obliged to you for the part you took. Mr. Hunt asked for an allowance to be given to the wit- nesses, and the Mayor instructed him to bring Mr. Gray's case before the Watch Committee. Major Cartwright said he was sorry the witness Wilkinson had not pluck enough to assist Lawrence, and he hoped he would be manly enough to do so on a future occasion. P.S. Spinks said Wilkinson had rendered good assistance in Mersey-street.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

IMPROVEMENTS.—The constant efforts made to keep Winsford abreast of other towns by the Local Board of Wins- ford deserve the best thanks of the ratepayers when no false economy is the impelling force. The widening of Dingle- lane and its two good approaches, which have become more street like, will soon be a servic,?able connection between High-street and Weaver-street. The best thanks of the town are due to Messrs. Armstrong and Verden for their gifts of land on either side for that purpose. Houses are being raised with considerable ease, such as Royal Oak, The Ark, and such like, which, with better streets, make the town look much better.

TRINITY COLLEGE, LONDON.—The examination for the certificates of this college in senior and junior divisions of elementary music knowledge will be held at the Academy, Winsford, on June 16th. As last year, it is expected there will be several local prizes as well as those offered by the London authorities. Intending candidates must send in their names an fees to the hon. sec., Mr. J. Buckley, M.T.C.L., and F.R.G., early in May to avoid double fees. The science and art examination will commence at the end of next week, and be continued for the next three weeks, in advanced freehand, geometry, perspective, -physiology, mathematics, physiography, magnetism, electric'ty, heat, sound, light, chemistry, mechanici, mining, agriculture, (tc.

WESLEYAN SERMONS.—The annual sermons on behalf of the Sunday school connected with the Wesleyan chapel on Winsford Hill were preached in that chapel on Sunday last by the Rev. James Ritchie, of Sandbach, who, though the weather was very unpropitious, had yet fair congregations and good collections, which amounted to £l5. SALVATION ARMY.—The removal of Captain Thurman, of this Army, connected with the Winsford corps, called for a special worship meeting, tea meeting, and prayer meeting on the evenings of Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, on which occasions there were many present, and especially on the latter day, when after an exciting prayer meeting the corps escorted him to the railway station in considerable force, singing their favourite marching air. It need hardly be said that Captain Thurman has endeared himself to many by his self-denying labours and consistent life during his sojourn at Winsford.

THE RAMSGATE MYSTERY.—The inquest upon the body of Chat les Wagner, aged 17, who was found at the foot of the East Cliffe, Ramsgate, was concluded on Thursday. The coroner, in summing up, pointed to tile circutnstances tending to incriminate Walters, the man in custody, and said he thought there could not be any difficulty in return- ing a verdict of wilful murder against him. After half an hour's deliberation, the jury returned into court with a verdict of wilful murder against James Walters.

PUBLIC LE.ZiTtYlrg.—On Thursday evening, Mr. W. Pickard, of Wigan, gave a very interesting lecture on "Mines and theft lamps," in the Congregational school. Mr. Pickard k'nows the miners' position, and speaks from ex- perience. The miners present must, if they only think of what the lecturer stated, benefit very much. Lectures o; this class throughout the mining districts would do much good. T. D. Grinkle, Esq , presided. Votes of thanks to the lecturer and chairman concluded the most interesting pro- ceedings.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

SHOCKING AccrimiNT.--On Tuesday the borough coroner held an inquest on the body of William Clarkson, provision dealer, who met with a shocking death on Saturday. After brushing out his cart he placed the broom on the floor in order to assiat his descent. When jumping out of the cart, however, the broom slipped and he fell, the broom-handle penetrating the lower part of his body for several inches. He died 20 hours afterwards, after much suffering. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

QUARTER SESSIONS.—The quarter sessions cf the peace for the borough of Wigan were held on Wednesday, before Mr. J. F. Fitzadam, the recorder. The calendar was a light one, and the Recorder, in charging the grand jury, compli- mented the town on the fact that there were so few prisoners for trial, and no cases of violence to be heard ; and also that there had not been any crimes of the latter class since be was appointed to the position he now occupied. That spoke very well for such a busy manufacturing town as Wigan. The cases consisted of ordinary felonies, one prisoner, Fred- erick Millfield alias Murphy, being charged with committing two daring robberies at a public-house and a dining-room. He was found guilty, and the Recorder, in sentencing kim to twelve calendar months' hard labour, said he had only just left gaol in Manchester, where he had promised the chaplain to lead abetter life. He appeared to be respectably connected, and he was sorry to see a man of apparently good education in such a position.
