div.p: FRODSIIAII,

The Ven. Archdeacon Darby commenced his annual visitation and induction of churchwardens, and sidesmen at St. Peter's Church, Chester, on Monday. On Wednesday the Yen. Archdeacon attended at the Iron Church, Frod- sham, when the churchwardens and sidesmen were sworn in.

SCARLET FEVER.—Mr. E. A. Wright remarked during the hearing of some school board cases at the Eddisbury Petty Sessions that he regretted to say that the Frodsham schools were closed for a month in Consequence of the prevalence of scarlet fever in the district. He understood that they would remain closed for a month certain, but said it was impossible to say at present whether they would be re-opened at the ex- piration of that time or not. FRODSHAM CRICKET CLUB—This club bids fair to be- come a permanent institution in the parish, and appears to be increasing in importance and popularity each year, as, although, it is so recently since it was formed, it can now boast of a very creditable ground in a pleasant situation close to the historical "Beacon Hill," and includes amongst its members the elite of the neighbourhood. A neat pavilion has also been erected at considerable expense. The match list for the season contains the names of important clubs and this fact will no doubt stimulate the members to main- tain the standard of success which has been attained in the past. The following are the patrons and officers for the year, viz.:—Patrons Major the Hon. W. F. Tollemache, M.P., Henry J. Tollemache, Esq., M.P.; president, Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar; vice-presidents, Charles Reynolds, Esc?, J.P. James Reynolds, Esq., J.P., Alfred Thomas, Esq., J.P., E. A. Wright, Esq., J.P.; captain, Henry Reynolds, Esq., J.P.; sub-captain, Rev. A. P. Reynolds; hon. secretary and treasurer, Mr. Samuel Davies; committee, Messrs. D. Ashton, F. Hilditch, W. D. Jolliffe, C. E. Linaker,4l. G Linaker, G. Rigby, and R. E. Walford ; auditors, Messrs. Thomas Riley and Henry Tiley. DEATH OF AN AFRICAN PRINCIL—Of the minor poten- tates who hold sway in Western Africa, one of the best known, perhaps, to English newspaper readers, is Ja-Ja, ruler of Opobo. Little more than twelve months ago Ja-Ja allowed his second son, then a fine boy about twelve years of age, by name Warabo, to be brought to this cenntry to be educated. The boy was entrusted to the care of Mr. Walter Johnstone, of the firm of Couper, Johnstone, and Co., Limited, of Glasgow, who are large traders at Opobo; and after careful consideration he was placed in the private academy of the Rev. R. P. Borwick, Manor House, Frod- sham, in the belief that he would there not only receive a substantial education but also enjoy all the comforts of English family life. Warabo possessed a strong physical constitution. He was moreover an apt pupil, and gave evi- dence of the possession of rare talents and a really noble disposition. He had not been long at school before he won the hearts both of the masters and of his fellew-pupils. A hope was indulged that he might in the course of a few years return to Opobo, able to show his people something of the ways of civilised life, and also teach them that there was something in Christianity better than fetish worship. We are sorry to say that this hope has been dispelled, for a little over 'a week ago Warabo, though he had enjoyed ex- cellemt health during all the previous year, was seized with acute inflammation of the lungs, which terminated fatally on Friday morning last week. His painful illness was borne with a resignation befitting a person of maturer years. We are informed that, young though he was, his acceptance of 1 Christian teaching was marked and sincere, and that some days prior to his death he was baptized, in compliance with his own wish, by the Vicar of Frodshatn—retaining the name of Warabo, for he would take no other. His affection for his father and his own people was strongly manifested, yet he betrayed no weariness of English life, but on the contrary was probably the happiest boy in the school. The funeral took place at noon on Monday, and evoked strong manifestations of sympathy on the part of the inhabitants of Frodsham. The shops of the town were nearly all closed, and the blinds of private houses were drawn as the proces- sion passed on its way to Overton Church, where Warabo's remains were buried. A preliminary service was held at Manor House. It was conducted by the Rev. D. Schofield (Primitive Methodist) and the Rev. J. M. Bamford (Wes- leyan), and attended by the Rev. J. B. Johnstone, of Dum- fries (father of Mr. Walter Johnstone, who is at present at Opobo), and certain relatives; also by Mr. Crighton, repre- senting the firm of Messrs. Hutton and Co., African mer- chants, Liverpool: the Rev. E. Williams (Calvanistic Methodist), the Rev. R. P. Borwick, Mr. Pickering, and Mr. Sant, of Frodsham, and all the assistant masters and pupils of Manor House Academy. The coffin bore the simple inscription, "Warabo, died 21st April, 1882, aged 13 years," and was covered with beautiful floral wreaths. There was a large concourse of the inhabitants in the churchyard. The coffin was borne by six of the elder pupils,who also lowered it into the grave. At the grave side the Rev. Mr. Williams read the 4th chapter of Ist Thtmlonians, and the pupils of the school sang the hymn," Safe in the arms of Jesus." A

brief address was then given by the Rev. Mr. Johnstone. He spoke of the affecting circumstances of Warabo's death, and expressed the earnest wish that the words which were almost his last that ViTarabo uttered—"l love Jesus because He is my Saviour "—might also be the language of his father in far-off Opobo. All present were deeply moved by the simple but touching ceremony.
HALM.
THE RECENT EXTRAORDINARY BURGLARY.

At the Chester spring assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Chitty, William Buckley, 18, pattern case maker maker; John Nugent, 18, warehouseman; and Alfred Proud- foot, 33, merchant, were indicted for having, at Lynam, on the 14th inst., burglariously broken and entered the dwell- ing-house of Patrick Proudfoot, father to the last-named prisoner, and stolen an oil painting, ten silver teaspoons, 15 plated spoons, 11 plated folks, one plated sugar basin, and other articles.
Mr. Marshall prosecuted. Mr. HiggEns defended Proud- foot. The other prisoners were undefended.

Mary Clare, domestic, in the employ of Mr. Proudfoot, said that on the night in question the pictures were left hanging in the drawing-room when the inmates went to bed. The spoons were in a basket in the cupboard, and the sugar basin was on the cheffonnier in the dining-room. Next morning they were all missed. An overcol‘t which had been hanging in the hall had also been taken; also a rug which had been on the dining-room floor. Witness identified the articles produced as the property of her waster. Patrick Proudfoot, a gentleman who has retired from business and now resides at Statham, Lymm, iilentified the coat and pair of boots produced, but could not answer to all the articles. His son had not been living at his home for eight or ten years. He took tea with them, however, on the Monday before the occurrence. Joseph Inglefield, engineer, in the employ of the Bridge- water Canal Company, said he saw Proudfoot early on the morning after the burglary had been committed about; 200 yards from his father's house. The other prisoners were with him. Buckley was carrying a bundle. Witness saw Nugent put something bright under his coat. He gave in- formation to Sergeant Harrington, of Lymm. Sergeant Harrington said he went in pursuit of the pri- soners with the last witness and another constable. They came up to the prisoners, who were on board a steam flat. They arrested the prisoners, and found the .property on Buckley and Nugent. Buckley also had with him a dark lantern, a pack of cards, and he was wearing the stolen boots. Proudfoot asked what he was wanted for, and said he knew nothing about the robbery. Witness visited the house of Mr. Proudfoot the same day and found the kitchen window broken, the fastener being undone by some instru- ment like a chisel. Buckley made a statement to witness ,to the effect that Proudfoot met Nugent and himself and asked them to get some things for him. Mr. Higgens submitted that there was nothing to show that the prisoner Proudfoot took any part in the burglary. None of the stolen articles were found upon him, and there was no evidence tending to prove that his meeting with the other ptisoners on the day after the occurrence was not accidental, or that he knew they were in possession of the other property. The Judge, in summing up, said, as regarded the prisoner Proudfoot, a question for the jury to consider was, what obj .ct had he in view in being in company with the other prisoners near his father's house on the morning after the burglary, and also at a later period on board the flat.

div.p: SUBSCRIPTION CONCERT AT ST. HELENS.

Mr. George Barton's last subscription concert of the season was held on Monday night, in the Assembly Room of the St. Helens Town Hall. This series of concert, which we are tempted to hope will be repeated next season, ended in all respects satisfactorily. In point of numbers there was nothing to complain of, except, perhaps, in some portionspf the hall a little crushing which could not without difficulty be obviated. The hall was full, and included members of r the leading families of the town and neighbourhood. Man cheater, which has a wide reputation as the possessor of some of the best musical talent in England, supplied St. Helens people with pleasant enjoyment to be derived from Mr. Edward de Jong's band. This band, which is well kno Am as an exceptionally fine one, was the most con- spicuous feature of the evening's entertainment, and, judging from the applause which frequently marked the approval of the audience of the band's performances, the anticipations had not been disappointed. The programme opened with a rendering of the overture "Poet and Peasant," which was a favourable augury of what was to follow. This was fol- lowed by a song " Waiting," by Mis Ella Herriman, a pupil of Madame Sarnton-Dolby, and in acknowledgement of the flattering applause, she bowed a graceful acknowledgement. This, together with " When the tide comes in," by the same lady, were sung with much taste and in a voice of great power and elasticity, as conspicuously shown in some of the passages; but the songs were not popular ones, and did not produce that sympathetic feeling which an artiste like Miss Herriman is, without doubt, in other songs, quite capable of stirring in the minds of her auditors. A waltz, " Jennesse d'oree," was a pleasant piece of music by the band. While this found much favour, the harmony gavotte which fol- lowed with triangle accompaniments produced a much more favourable impression. Mr. George Barton followed with a new song, "All in all," which he sung well, as also another one in the second part " Ceme into the garden, Maud." The Russir Dance by the band, with piccolo solo and triangle accompaniments, may be described as the gem of the even- ing. This stirring piece met with tremendous applause at the finish, and in this instance, and this only, the rule which had evidently been arranged should be observed, that there should be no encores, was broken, and the band repeated the last refrain. In tl'e selection from "Mignon "the band was successful, the triangle and cymbals being introduced with effect, and the clarionet solo was especially pleasing. The splendid overture, "Le Barbier de Seville," was given in spirited style. The minuet for stringed instruments was a dance in direct contrast to the dashing Russian dance, but was none the less pleasing on that account, and the Turkish patrol which subsequently followed was simply a gem in point of variety and picturesqueness. Mr. De Jong proved himself as efficient a flutist as he evidently is a conductor, and his manipulations on that instrument were simply marvels of execution. A most delightful concert was brought to a close by the march " Sangerlust." The following is the programme : Overture "Poet and Peasant."

MURDER AT NORWICII.—On Tuesday morning a young woman, wife of William George Abigail, formerly billiard marker at the Star Hotel, Norwich, and lately waiter at a cafe, was found dead in her bed with a bullet wound in her head and another in her left side, one penetrating the brain and the other the heart. Abigail and his wife, who had been married only a month, lodged at New Catton, in the house of Abigail's half-brother named Shepherd, whose little boy heard shots at six in the morning. A revolver was found in the bed near the knees of the dead woman, who was about 22 years of age. Suspicion fell on her husband, who is 19 years of age, and who was apprehended by Chief-Constable Hutchinson and Detective Mason, as he was walking into the .market place at noon. Shepherd, who had come up in a cab in the nick of time, pointed him out to the officers. When the prisoner was charged with wilful murder, he said, "Is she dead ?" The left sleeve of prisoner's blue shirt was stained with blood. The murdered woman was chambermaid at the Star when the prisoner was employed there. Four years ago, the prisoner tried to commit suicide by taking vermin powder.

CO-OPERATION PERFECTED.—In towns where the registra- tion of infectious disease is compulsory, and where the public co-operate with the medical officers of health, scarlet fever, small-pox and measles will soon be things of the past. The simplest of all preventives (recommended by sanitary authori- ties) is for heads of families to insiss that each resident in their house washes with Wright's Coal Tar Soap. It can be bought everywhere, but like all valuable remedies it is most fraudu- lently imitated.—Advt. WHAT AMOUNT OF BUFFERING COULD BE AVOIDED IF WE ONLY KNEW How.—Many people have a dull heavy pain lathe head; with tired and languid feelings that sleep does not remove; with a fulness about the chest after eating, often at- tended with palpitation. A pain in the side and back, with frequent sick headache; with nausea after eating, attended with flatulence and a disagre, state taste mornings; loss of appetite, with vertigo or dizziness, Ac. How many people suffer with all these disagreeable feelings and little imagine the real cause of their malady, or the proper mode of obtaining relief. These are some of the symptoms of indigestion and liver complaint, but they will be dispelled at once by the uss of " Siegel's Cura- tive Syrup," a vegetable preparation, sold everywhere.—ADVT, HOLLOWAY'S PlLLS.—There is nothing in the whole" Materia Medics" like these Medicaments for the certainty of their action in lumbago, sciatica, tic doloreux, and all flying or settled pains in the nerves and muscle,. div.p: -- BRITISH. AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY. WIDNES BRANCH.

The annual meetiug was held on Tuesday evening, in Lacey-street Wesleyan school-room. The Rev. J. H. Cum- mings presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes; George Bond, vicar of Farnworth ; J. Tessyman, Wesleyan ; T. Peters, Congrega- tionalist; T. Hughes, Welsh Wesleyan; and Jos. Holden,

curate, Farnworth. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, spoke of his own experience in India in connection with the society, The various evangelical denominations formed a co.nmittee for translating the scriptures; and it was their custom for each denomination to have a separate field of labour. Thus, the London Missionary Society had established itself in Travan- cure ; the Church Missionary Society had its chief seat at Orissa; and their own missionary organisation had its centre at Mysore. There was a German society, of which Leipsic represented the High Church, and the Basle Mis- sionary Society the evangelical bodies. From his own house, in India, he could see, in the adjoining street, the press where thousands of copies of the scriptures were printed, and could even bear the sound of the machinery. The speaker concluded by reading the report. The committee announced, with much regret, that Mrs. McClellan, the treasurer, and Mrs. Colley, the secretary, had left Widnes, and resigned office. The loss of their valued help would be much felt by the remaining members of the committee, who had, however, put their hands to the work of collecting the society's subscriptions in Widnes. Their labours in this respect had been so successful that they had been able to send a donation of £lO to the treasurer of the parent society The treasurer's account showed the total receipts to be £i3 12s. 2d., and there was a balance in hand of £3 Os. 2d. The Rev. J. E. SYMONS, M.A., one of the district secreta- ries, remarked, in the course of his address, that the sale of the scriptures during the previous year had showna decrease both in France and England. This fact, as far as it related to our own country, was attributed to the issue of the revised version; and as to France, owing to the publication of a new version of the Scriptures. The latter was not a revised version, but a complete translation in French, and from what he had seen, he had a very favourable opinion of it. In Austria the work was making good progress, notwith- standing the recent untoward action of the Government In reepect to the trycietir's petelcattons. In conclusion, the speaker graphically described the fire at the Ring Theatre in Vienna, and the marvellous manner in which the society's depOt, which immediately adjoined that place of amusement, had been preserved from destruction. He likewi e paid a high compliment to the ladies of Widnes for the active part they had taken in organising a branch of the society. The VICAR OF WIDNES said that in an age in which the weary growing years were shaking their hope and con- fidence in many things in this world, those years only strengthened their opinion as to the supreme importance of the Book of God. The work of the British and Foreign Bible Society was to bring home this book to the teeming millions whose reformation called forth English Christian sympathy. He went on to compare the organisation to a, precious vessel laded with rich argosies; and said that the society in nobility of aim and in grandeur of object might be fitly compared to that old fightex for God's truth, who, standing on the shore of the Grecian peninsula, seemed to hear pealing through the night watches the cry Come over and help us." (Applause.) The Rev. JOSEPH HOLDEN dwelt upon the noble compre- hensiveness of the platform on which the society was founded. The Rev. T. PEEERS, after alluding to the efforts of the ladies on behalf of the auxiliary, and more especially to those of Mrs Carey, said the motto of the society might be said to be "The Bible for the world." After a reference to the society's operations in China and Austria, he condemned, in erong terms, the supineness of some of the so-called Christians of the present day as to spiritual matters. Let them look at the thousands around them to-day. If these people had any love for that Book which David said was as a lamp unto his feet, would there have been such a paltry attendance at a meeting of that character? Where were the teachers in church and chapel; where the young scholars; where the hearers by whom the ministers presens were surrounded Sabbath after Sabbath? Mr. Peter' concluded an earnest and telling speech, by an appeal for unity. Votes of thanks were passed to the Chairman; and to the ladies; and after a few words from the Rev. George Bond, M.A., the proceedings were brought to a close by the singing of the Doxology, and the pronouncing of the Benediction.

ATTACK ON A ST. HELT.-,NS SOLICITOR'S CLERK. At the Prescot Sessions, on Tuesday, Matthew Booth Lowe, son of a farmer, residing at Rainhill, was charged that he, on the 18th April, at Whiston, did assault and beat Walter Braithwaite,—Mr. Swift appeared for the prosecutor, And Mr, Mackenzie appeared foet --; • AMsoner —r Swift, _tee, e•-- he statement, slid that if he proved the ta.L. in his open., imagined it was a case in which the Tagistrates would feel bound to deal severely. The complainant was a solicitor's clerk in his employ, and he was instructed as part of his daily round to serve a writ on the prisoner. The prisoner ought to have been served in January, but he had been out of the way, and the writ had not 'peen served. lie (Mr. Swift) received information. ;ast week that the prisoner was at home at t!'., pond House, Rainhill. He in- ch-- doted complainant to endeavour to serve the writ, and on Thursday he made several attempts to do so, but whenever the prisoner saw the complainant he ran away out of his reach. On Tuesday evening, however, between five and six o'clock, the complainant met the prisoner on the road near to the Green Dragon Inn. The parties had been intimate acquaintances, and old friends in fact for some time. The prisoner was at that time in a trap, and Braithwaite asked him if he would have a drink. Prisoner said he would, and Braithwaite walked alongside the trap towards the public- house. However, before they got into the public•house Lowe changed his mind, and said he was teetotal, following up the remark with another if he (complainant) had heard anything about a girl in a breach of promise case. The complainant Braithwaite said something in reply (hut he need not mention the lady's name), and then told Lowe that he ' had got a letter to ;how him. Lowe immediately replied to this by saying, " Have you, you —, but you are not going to serve me with any thieg." The complainant then got on the step of the trap to give prisoner the writ, but theprisoner thereupon struck the complainant over the arms, legs, and body with a whip, the remains of which he produced. The complainant held on to the trap, and Lowe lashed the horse. Complainant was obliged to stick to, but Lowe persisted in lashing the horse and complainant alternately. To finish up the complainant fell off the trap after receiving some help by Lowe. Ile was considerably bruised and knocked about both on the head and arms. He (Mr. Swift) believed the defence was going to be somewhat of a novelty, and he imagined their worships would hear some novel propositions in law: that complain- ant was committing a trespass for which Lowe had a right to assault him. He need scarcely remind their worships that in asiv defence of that sort the first principle in crimi- nal jeriecliction was that he must not do more than was absolutely necee7ury for protection, and that the person serving the writ must be first asked to leave; and then if he would not leave be could be turned opt, In this pee, Lowe never asked the comnlainant to.leaYei anti tf 1544 left the „. , . trap the probabilities wet; itai me wculd have been run over. Then again he understood there was going to be— but he really would not mention anything more, as his imagination would not carry him far enough. He thought their worships would come to the conclusion that the assault was an aggravated assault, and that the action of Lowe had amounted to contempt of court in thus evading the service of a writ from the superior court. He (Mr. Swift) had no feeling in that case, as complainant was about to leave his employ, but his leaving was nothing against the complain- ant, and had nothing to do with the case. He simply ap- peared in that case because he felt that people who served writs ought to be nrotected. Walter Braithwaite, clerk to Mr. Swift, St. Helens, and residing in Ecclestoc-street, Prescot, said he had known Lowe for two years, and had been friendly with him. Wit- ness ga 'evidence corroborative of Mr. Swift's statement to the point where complainant pulled out the letter to give to Lowe stating where it came from, and the remarks which followed. Witness stated that Lowe struck him on the head 20 or 40 times. Wirtness did nat manage to get into the trap. Lowe got out of the trap on the other side, and com- ing round to the complainant hit him under the chin, and knocked him off the trap. Lowe then set off running; wit- ness made a grab at him, but missed him, and he was left in charge of the trap for nearly ten miuutes, when a boy came up having in his hand the whip with which Lowe had illused him. He asked the boy for the whip, and the boy gave it to him. The boy then took charge of the trap. His (complainant's) hat was spoiled by being thrown under the wheel of the trap, the skin was scratched off his arm, and the part bled a great deal, and he had no idea where the writ had gone to. He did not treat the attempt as a proper ser- vice, Henry Ashall, collier, and Joseph Strattle, head gardener at the Whiston Wo!khouse, gave corroborative evilence. Mr. Mackenzie, for the defence, said that if a mars tres- passed on the land of another, the owner of that land was justified, after he had n-quested the man leave, to use a cer- tain amount of violence to eject him if he persisted in the trespass. If a man walking the highway was met by another who refused him passage, there was an interference with the liberty of the subject, and in like manner did Braithwate interfere with Lowe. The complainant took upon himself to step on the step of the trap— which was a treepass—and tried to get in There was another trespass. Lie was warned that if he got into the trap the whip would be used to him, but the complainant in- sisted upon getting into the trap a second time, and Lowe then used some gentle violence with the paltry whip. Mr. Evans: I think that is the remnants of one. Mr. Mackenzie was • prepared to show that the whip pro- duced (which was a slender one half an inch in diameter at its thickest part and broken) was the only thing used in the alleged assault. How that could inflict a severe blow on a would-be vows server he failed to see. What their wor- ships had to consider was.—Was the complainant a tres- passer, and was the assault an aggravated assault? Was there a greater violence used than was absolutely necessary? If 3 policeman attempted to arrest a man without producing 3 warrant and the police officer was assaulted, that police officer had his rerne!ly, and if complainant trespassed Lowe had a right to eject him. It was not absolutely necessary for Braithwate to enter into the trap at all. Was it necessary for the effectual service of a writ that a man should put it into Ole corporal possession of the parts on whom it had to be

served? All that was necessary now was that if the Writ- server made reasonable efforts to complete the s-qvice a sub- stituted service would be granted on a petition being filed to that effect. All that was necessary, if Lowe would not re- ceive it was to throw it into the trap. That would be P:a effectual service. But the complainant endeavoured to, get into the trap as if that were absolutely necessary to ':nrust it
down the man's throat. The Chairman: We think the assault is proved, and that It was an unjustifiable one. We shall make the fine 20s.

and costs. Mr. Swift-: This business has cost me a new hat, but I suppose this cannot be included in the costs. ---40--- ARCHDEACON'S ATIICATION AT WARRINGTON. The Venerable, the Archdeacon of Warrington, the Rev. J. Bardsley M.A.), paid his annual visitation at the Parish Church ,yesterday. Very few persons were present in addition to the churchwardens and sidesmen of the various churches in the archdeaconry. The AUCIIDEICON, in his charge, commenced by a touc- hing allusion to the lengthened labours of the Archdeacon of Liverpool, and stated that in the new Archdeaconry of Warrington there were 474, 964 souls, with 97 benefices and and 104 churches. When Archdeacon Jones began his ministry Liverpool did not possess one-fifth of its present population, whilst two events which then stirred the public mind were the defeat of Napoleon at Waterloo and the in- troduction of steam navigation on the waters of our noble river. "If," said the Archdeacon, "commerce can chronicle its advances and war proclaim its triumphs, the Church of Christ can also recall its bloodless victories and the gospel of peace recount her enduring conquests. This day officially we bid farewell to him whom we affectionately designate our Waterloo veteran. Bidding him re- spectfully farewell we pray that his example and experience may for some years be still spared to us, and that in addition to spiritual peace there may be richly vouchsafed to him all that healtheand ease which shall seem best to the giver of all good gifts." The Archdeacon then alluded to church legislation. He ex- pressed his appreval of Mr. Stanhope's Church Patronage Bill, so far as it abolishes the sale of next presentations, in- creases the discretion of the Bishop, and gives to the parishioners a power of appeal in reference to• the bodily in- firmity, mental incapacity, or moral misconduct of the patron's nominee. In the present state of confusion arising from the imprisonment of clergy in connection with ritual, the Discharge of the Contumacious Clerks' Bill, and The Public Worship Regulation Act Amendment Bill deserve very careful attention. If the former bill, which was intro- duced by Earl Beauchamp last session, and which pessed the House of Lords with the approval of both political parties, had not been abandoned in the Commons through what he must call the mischievous action of the member for Scarborough, the prisoner at Lancaster would have long since been at liberty, and the Church would have been spared the worst results of a grave scandal. The end of all legislation on this question should be not so much to punish the parson as to protect the parish and to preserve the Pro- testant Reformation character of our Established Church. If penalty be unavoidable, then let it not involve imprison- ment but speedy suspension, and after renewed offences total deprivation. As, however, the worst has taken place, it be- comes a question of whether it is not better to acquiesce in the position, and to wait patiently for the report of Her Majesty's Royal Commission on Ecclesiastical Courts. He condemned the Churchwardens' Admission Bill as-calculated to make the churchwardens cease to regard themselves as officers of the Ordinary and to bring to an end such gather- ings as those. The opinions -expressed by the Bishops and both Convocations adverse to the bill reflected, he believed the opinions of Churchmen generally. Turning to the immediate duties of churchwardens, the Archdeacon said that in addition to the preservation of the fabric and its furniture, they should see to the proper warming and ventila- tion of churches, dwelling on the evils arising in crowded congregations from a vitiated atmosphere. He also said that tables of fees and degrees, books for entering the names of strange preachers, iron chests for the preservation of registers, and sufficient insurance of the fabric should be carefully seen to. The Archdeacon then pointed out the law in reference to Moneys collected at other times than the celebration of the Holy Communion, saying :—" It is quite within the power of the incumbent to a-k the contributions of the congregation at other times for some lawful object, and to deal with them without any interference on the part of the churchwardrns at his own discretion. This has been decided by the Court of Queen's Bench. It is very much to be wished that the custom now established in many parishes were of universal observance, by which, either at E tster, in connection with the church- wardens' accounts, or at Christmas, a yearly detailed state- ment should be printed and circulated among the parish' ioners and members of the congregation of all moneys con- tributed, and their disbursement for parochial, diocesan, or missionary purposes. Such statements will be found most useful in creating confidence, and thereby elioiting larger responses when appeals are made, and are most desirable for the purpose of preventing misunderstandings which otherwise will probably' arise," He proceeded to speak on e he use eidesmen as one of the many ways in which the t 0..._ Church fitltenedi On attendance at church, he attendance et public worship have id "The revelations re b v=ins :::, staetled many. It is very tr.::' that the Church rctoclaet:lavn fauourably with other religious bodies. _ •,„4 character from these statistics is, however, of a very limo— The old controversies about Church and State, the Este,— 'll ment and Nonconformity, are quickly dying out; whilst the great conflict approaches nearer day by day when the friends of revealed religion, whatever their creed, will be on the one hand, and the social and intellectual forces of unbelief on the other band. At this crisis our Church has a great mission, in which all its faithful laymen should bear their part." He pointed out how the laity might help in building churches and mission chapels, and churchwardens in obeying the 90th Canon, which enjoins them "diligently to see the parishioners duly resort to their church," and en- joins "that they shall earnestly call upon such as shall be found slack or negligent in resorting to the church." He pointed out the importance of the churchwardens and sides- men being themselves regular in attendance at church, and said, as to presentments, "If by gray chance the ministra- tions of the church and the conduct of the minister be such as to cause grave scandal, and so to account for the non-at- tendance of the parishioners, then in their presentment of presentible matters let them not daily, but act advisedly and truly to the discharge of their own conscience as be- cometh honest and godly men." The Churchwardens and sidesmen of the churches in the archdeaconry then signed the usual declaration.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brund; it (chairman), and

C. Reynolds. POORS' RATES.—The following were sanctioned by the magistrates :—For Sutton, 11d, in the £, to realise £305 83. 21.; Halton, 101. in the pound, to realise £283 15s. ; Aston Grange, 101. in the £, to realise £43 lie. ; Aston-by- Sutton, is id, to realise £241 14s. 2!.; Stockham, is. in the £, to realise £39 3s. 3d.; Clifton, 9d. in the £, to realise £l4O 63. 10d. AN ALLEGED DRUNKEN FREAK.—Mary Booth, a married woman, of Stonehills-lane, was charged with having stolen a cow's heart, a shirt, and a basket, value 43. 81., the pro- perty ef Eli ibeth Worthington, her cousin, who lives in pa-,3ax e tu Asson-street.—On Saturday night, toe ecutri was in the Blue Bell, with a basket on her arm, containing the articles mentioned above, when the prisoner came te her side, and took the basket, saying no one should have it that night. She drank the contents of her glass, and then fol- lowed the prisoner to her house in Stonehills. She asked for the basket, but prisoner said she had not got it. Sergt. McMichael and P.C. Finney visited the place on Sunda morning, and found the stolen shirt under a mattress up- stairs, and the cow's heart in a tub in he kitchen.—Booth, in reply to the Bench, said she found the heart outside thr Blue Bell, and she denied knowing anything about how the shirt came under the mattrass.—The Chairman said it Was evident that both prisoner and pros.2cutrix had been worse for drink on the night of the robbery.—Booth would be sent to gaol 21 days, with hard labour. BREAKING INTO A FLAT.—Walter Barker, Wm. Hogan, and Thos. Blakemore, young men, were charged with having broken into a flat, on the 18th instant, and stolen a coat, a singlet, pair of braces, a towel, a comb, and a knife, the pro- perty of Thomas Weedall, and a shirt and pair of trousers, the property of Peter Poole. The latter is the captain, and Weedall the hand on a flat called the Sarah, which they left safe on the 16th instant, at the Bottom Locks, Runcorn, whilst they wentto Northwich for the week end. During their absence the vessel was broken into, and the articles stolen. At abaut a quarter to twelve, on the night of the 21st last., P.C. Noden was on duty in plain clothes at the docks, when he met the prisoner Barker .coming across the Alfred Dock gates. Seeing that he had something bulky under his arm, he stopped him, and asked him what it was which made him look so stout. Barker denied having secreted anything, but, on searching him, at a watchman's hut adjoining, he found he was wearing the stolen coat and trousers under those he had on, and all the other missing things, with the exception of a towel, were in a handker- chief in his possession. He took the man to the police I office, and charged him with stealing, the things and break- ing into the flat, on which he replied that ha had given a man known by the nickname " Prizz!er " is. 6,1. for the coat, and a glass of beer for the braces. He, however, admitted having stolen the trousers. Oa Saturday night, Sergeant McMichael apprehended Hagan in High-street, and on taking him to the office, Barker said he was the person from whom be bought the coat and braces. Hogan denied having sold him the things, and aelted the sergeant" why he had not apprehended Blakemore, who wus there as well as he." The latter was then taken into custody. On being formally charged. Hogan denied having broken into the flat, arid Makernore said be was at Garston at the tine when the act was stid to have been committed.—Prisoners were each sent to the Quarter Sessions for trial. Tnunsnay.—Before Mr. Alfred Thomas. AnyrelEu ROBBERY BY BOATMEN.—WaIter Barker and Thomas Lane, alias Jr,6 Watson, boatmen, strangers to Run- corn, were charged with having stolen one coat, a pair of trousers, and a pair of boots, the property of Wm. Waring, and also with havin received the things, knowing them to have been stolen.—The prosecutor said he was the master and owner of the flat Oak. On the 20th inst., his vessel was lying in the Bridgewater canal, near to Hazieburst's Soapery. He locked up the cabin about nine o'clock the same night, and at that time had safe in it the boots, trousers, and coat now produced, which were his propel ty. There wow mares on the different articles by which he knew them. He re- turned to the fiat about four o'clock, on the afternoon of the

following day, and thee found that the lock had been broken, and '.:he cabin entered. On going inside he missed the dvderent articles, and gave information to the police.—? C. Noden said that from information he received from the last witness, on the 21st inst., he apprehended the prisoner Barker about a quarter to twelve at the Runcorn docks. He saw that he had something bulky under his coat, and asked him what it was. He said "Nothing but my shirt and singlet." He then took him into a hut near, and on searching him, he found that he was meaning three coats. Amongst these was the one produced. He had also some other property in his possession. He apprehended him and charged him with breaking into the flat. He said "I didn't break into the flat; Joe Watson did it, and he gave me the coat." He went to Lane's vessel, which was called the Serious, but he found Lane had absconded.—Sergeant Morris said that on the 26th inst. he apprehended the prisoner Lane at Liverpool, wearing the trousers and boots produced. —ln answer to the charge, prisoner said he did not steal the things, but they were given to him by Barker, who broke into the cabin. He (prisoner) remained outside, and when . Barker came out of the cabin he gave him the trousers and boots.—ln reply to the usual caution by Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, Barker said that on the Friday night he was coming from Runcorn Locks when he saw Lane, and they went on to the flat together. He (Lane) went forward, and with a winch handle broke the cabin lock. Lane stole the things and handed several of them to him, and afterwardsput the scuttle on the cabin,and the lock back as though it had not been touched, and pat the winch ' handle back in the spot from which it had been taken.— Lane told the magistrate that he did not break into the ! cabin, but Barker gave him the things out of it.—Prisoners were each committed to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial.

THE EXAMINER SATURI)AY, APRIL 29, 1882. THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY. In respect to attendance the second weeks' campaign in Warrington, in connection with the Blue Ribbon Army, has been even more successful than the first. Hundreds were unable to gain admission at the Public Hall on Sunday evening, and an over Ilosv meeting was held in Friars' Green Chapel, but even that place was filled to overflowing. At the meeting in the Public Hall the Rev. T. Rippon, in mak- ing the usual annmencernents, remarked that everything seemed to be of an encouraging nature, and everybody seemed disposed to pat them on the back and say "Go on." He thanked God for the Press of Warrington, which was standing by their side. An earnest address was delivered by the Rev. John Yonge, who expressed his sympathy with the movement, and his liking for the unmistakeable and beautiful alliance which was displayed between the Gospel and temperance. In concluding an appeal to those present to sign the pledge, the rev, gentleman stated the movement that was being carried on in Warrington was a great and magnificent one, to raise the fallen and save the lost, and it would be an eternal disgrace upon them as Christian people if they did not rally round the mission and for God's sake and fur man's sake sign the pledge. The Rev. J. A. Beet also addle ssed the assembly, and was fol- lowed by Mr. H. Roberts and Mr. Murphy. Additional attraction has been given to the meetings this week by the presence of Mr. and Mrs. Clark Willson, of America, who c tale to Warrington from Dundee, at which town Mr. Francis Murphy, the originator of the Army, is engaged. Mrs. Willson is the sister of the late Mr. P. B. Bliss, and together with her husband has charmed the audiences with her splendid rendering of sacred songs and melodies. On Monday evening Mr. Murphy was assisted by the Rev. J. B. Anderson, of Liverpool, who gave a characteristic ad- dress. The meeting for women, held on Tuesday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. Murphy, was well attended, and stirring addresses were delivered by Mrs. Parker, of Penketh (President of the British Women's International Temper- ance Mission), Mrs. Rippon, Mrs. R. Garnett. Mrs. Willson and the Rev. J. B.Anderson. In the evening the Rev. S. Wil- kinson, vicar of St. Paul's, who has manifested considerable interest in the movement, delivered an appropriate speech, and the rev, gentleman was succeeded by Miss Pendlebury, whose first public appearance was an unqualified success. Her address, full of womanly feeling, was delivered with great earnestness, and her eloquent peroration elicited the hearty cheers of the crowded audience who had listened to her remarks with evident pleasure. Mr. Murphy compli ! mental Miss Pendlebury upon her success, and remarked that he did not know why they should require assistance frone foreign countries when they had ladies like Miss Pendlebury in Warrington. The Rev. Edward Smith, of Manchester, rendered able assistance on Wednesday even- ing, when the largest number of pledges taken during the week lwas obtained. The committee hired a Wall in the market on Wednesday afternoon for the purpose of taking pledees, and they succeeded in obtaining 137 adherents, and in addition 13 persons donned the ribbon. Nearly all the persons who have interested themselves in the campaign, assembled in the Public Hall yesterday afternoon, when a conference was held for the purpose of eliciting an expression of opinion as to how the work, so auspiciously commenced—shall be continued after Mr. Murphy's departure. Mr. Murphy occupied the chair; after the Revs. 'l'. Rippon, S. Wilkinson, E. C. E. Carleton, J. Morton, and others had given their views on the subject, the feeling of the meeting was embodied in the following; resolution proposed by the Rev. E. Moore: "..that the ex- isting committees be empowered to add to their number representatives from all denominations in the town, and to form themselves into a central committee to carry on the work of the Blue Ribbon Army." This was seconded by the Rev. J. Yonge, and carried. A conversation ensued as to the desirabi ity of ho!ding meetings next, but this it was considered was a subject for the committee to decide upon. As already stated, the attendance at the evening meetings has been so great that overflow meetings have been held each evening in Friars Green Chapel. To- day an open-air demonstration will take place. 'rho mem- bers will assemble opposite St. Paul's Church at half-past two, and after forming into procession will proceed headed by Wycliffe brass b .nd down Bewsey-road, along Tanner's lane, Winwick-street, Horsemarket-street, Bridge-street, Mersey-street, {darn-street, Buttermarket-street, Sankey- street, and Suez-street to the Public Hall, which it is ex- pected will be reached about. 3 30. A meeting will then be held and in the evening Mr. and Mrs. Willson will sing a selection of pieces, and admission will be by ticket only. Up to Thursday evening the total number of pledges was 7,124 and 732 ribbons.

div.head: STRANGE DROWNING CASE AT ST.
div.p: STRANGE DROWNING CASE AT ST.

HELENS. On Friday night, it was reported that a man had com- mitted suicide by throwing himself into the St. Helens canal, near the end of Bold-street. There was, however, no posi- tive evidence that the man, whose name was John Glynn, did commit self-destruction, but the evidence given at the inquest is reported below. Deceased was 28 years of ace, and was a pensioner, having served in East India in 1876; and in Southern Africa, in 1880. He was present at the seige of Candahar, and at the storming of Det lieojet, on the 16th August; likewise at the battle of Candahar on the 18th September, 1880. On Monday afternoon, an inquest was held at the Phoenix Inn, Bold-street, by Mr. Barker, deputy coroner, OA the body of -John Glynn. Michael Kelly, 12, Bold-street, said he knew Glynn, and had known him for nine months. They lodged together at the above address. Glynn was a labourer at Bibby's Copper Works, and so far as he knew, was a steady man, and 28 years of age. Witness had worked at the same copper works, but not latterly. De- ceased was a man of cheerful habits, and had not said any- thing about doing away with himself. He was not a drunken man. On Friday night, deceased asked him to have a pint of beer with him at the " Hare and Hounds." Witness accepted the invitation, and they went together to the public house in question. He stayed there until half-past seven, when dec,eased told witness to drink up and they would go as far as the Old Vaults. They got up to go out. Witness was first, and as deceased was coming out a man named Hughes, a manager at the works, melee to deceased and they went back into the publichouse. He waited there about 2-0 minutes, and then went away. Deceased was not a drunken man, and nothing unusual was to be seen ih his appearance it, the publichouse. Deceased did not seem unwell, nor com- plain of being sick. There was no quarrelling in the public. house. They stood the whole of the time they were there. The Coroner : Do you think he was a likely man to drown himself? Witness: No, sir, I do not believe he would do the likes. A Juryman: Was he at work that day? Witness: Not that I know, sir. I do not believe he was working that day, but I believe he did go to work and had to go home again, having to see Mr. Bibby before going on with his work. 1. Juryman: Was he in the habit of going on the spree when be got his pension? Witness: No; he did not take much drink. He was tell- ing me when I as walking aiong with him that he had IBs. Bd., and he went down to Bibby's to pay 10s. of that that morning. The Coroner: Was any money found upon him? P.C. Callister : Yes, sir. Witness: He got the loan of some ;lone!" at the office in the yard where he worked, and he paid for two pints of ale out of that. And I believe he got his pension on Thursday. He had 30a to pay out of that to the army. The Coroner: You say be was a quiet man; he was not a very excitable man, was he? , Witness: He was as quiet a man as ever I knew. A Juryman: I knew the man and he was very quiet. John Roberts, a foremen at Mr. Bibby's copper works, said the deceased was a steady man. He saw him at ten minutes past nine on Friday night in the Hare and Hounds Vaults, at the corner of Bridgewater-street. At that time deceased had a little drink in him, but was quite able to take care of hitnselt. Deceased seemed strange at times. Sometimes when spoken to he would give no answer, but that did not arise from deafness. The Coroner: Did he give you the impression that he was a man likely to do anything tc himself P—Oh. no. The Coroner: But did you think, judging from his general manner, dulness,—and absence of mind apparently —that he was a likely man to do it. Witness: I many a time thought that he was not alto- gethe.*:" right, o:netitnes he would haputterring and talking to himsel(. The Coraer: tie was not a sociable man. Witnes : No, he was not. The Coroner: His brain might have been affected by sun stroke or something of that kind. Police Sergeant Callister said that about half-past nine on Friday night he was on duty on, the canal bank, Green- bank, Eccleston. He saw a man on the narrow strip of lands between the canal and the rftis which protect the public from the water, Deceased had no business there. Deceased had his hand on the rails, and was walking upwards in the direction of Ravenhead, and away from him (witness). It was rather dark there, the shadow of the lamp being thrown at that point. Witness looked at his watch and went five paces or so towards deceased when he heard a splash in the water. A woman on the opposite side of the road screamed out "there's a man in the canal." Witness ran to the Phcenix Inn, seized a form, went back, and threw it.into the canal for the man to get hold of. The form went right to him, but deceased did not get hold of it, though he called out to him to do so. Deceased appeared to be swimming at that time, and did not take any notice. Witness ran again into the public-house and got a clothes prop, and jumped into the water with it. He placed the clothes prop tinder the man, and drew him close to the side. He was alive, but unconscious. Witness placed him on the form and used every means to restore him, but without avail. A great quantity of water cams out of him. He then tin* deceased inside the house and sent for a doctor; but deceased expired before the doctor arrived, and about three-quarters of an hour after being taken out of the water. Deceased was in the water three or four minutes before witness got him out. He did not actually see the man get into the water, as he was just then looking at his watch. The Coroner: Well, and how did you think he got in? Witness: At the time I thought he went in hieeself, because when I saw him he was in the middle el' the canal, and appeared to be swimming. I iOught he had gone in purposely. 'Di() CerOner: opinion Witness: I have been told that the aide of the canal slopes down, and that would naturally carry him towards the middle. The Coroner: Did yOn find it very steep at the side ? Witneee t I did. The Coroner: How deep is it 11l the:middle ? 'Witness: Seven or eight feet. The Coroner: Can you swim? Witness: No, sir. The Coroner: Then it was rather a risky thing for you. 'Witness: Well, I got in up to the hips. The Coroner: Was there any vomit about there? Witness: I did not see any. I have been told that he was vomiting. A lad came and told at this place that he had seen the deceased vomit there, but the landlord could not discover the lad's name. It might be that while vomit- tine be tumbled over the rails on to the little embankment on the other side. The Coroner: Would that lead him home? Witness: He had gone past the end of the street then. I searched him, and found is. sd. upon him and a pocket handkerchief. The water was very dirty. Richard Hughes, residing inside the yard of Mr. Bibby's copper works, said he had known the deceased 12 months, and he was a very quiet and willing man. Witness last saw him alive at hall-past six in the Hare and Hounds public. house. Deceased had a pint of ale with him. There was no quarrelling with anyone. Witness left deceased in the public-house. Witness had not much talk with deceased, who was very quiet, and did not talk much. Witness did mit think the deceased a likely man to do anything to himself. The Coroner said it Ivae for the jury to say whether the death of deceased was accidental or intentional. If they said it was intentional they must say what was the state of the man's mind at the time. Deceased had been a soldier, had served in India, and had had several engagements else- where ; and it might be that his residence in India had—as in many cases such was the case—affected his brain. It being very hot there he might have had a sunstroke which rendered him liable to a little aberration of intellect, tempor- arily. It might be that some sudden impulse arising from that cause had impelled him to throw himself into the canal. They had it further that he was a quiet man, and one of the witnesses stated his belief that he was not quite right, and that he had known him to mutter to himself. There did not seem any motive for drowning himself; he was a single mar, and was not troubled with any family affairs . though his mind might have been affected by his residence' in India. On the other hand, he might have fallen in as the officer had described, and a bey, it was said, stated he had seen the man sick, though they bad no evidence on that point. If that had been the direct way home one could understand it, and he must have known that he was wrong; It showed that be went there with intent. The jury, how- ever, could form a better opinion of that than he could, for they knew the locality, while he was entirely ignorant of it. Another Juryman (Mr. Livewell) said there was plenty of walking room on the proper side of the rails withoet going over. The Jury, after a short consultation, returned a verdict of "Accidental death by drowning."

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. There were no cases for disposal. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickrnere), and Major Cartwright. FRIGHTENED OF Howe —Wm. White, 12 years of age, of Longford-street, was charged with being a vagrant, having been found asleep in Golden Grove-street.—The mother of the boy said she thought he mast have stayed in the street, being frightened to go home late.—P.S. Spinks said when the boy was found he appeared not to have been washed for a week.—The boy was ordered to be kept in the lock-up until six o'clock. OBSTRUCTING BRIDGE-STREET.—John Flannigan, carter for Mr. Lunt, was charged with having, on the 17th inst., obstructed the passage in Bridge-street by allowing his horse and lurry to stand there a long and unreasonable time.—P.C. Crickett proved the case, and he was fined se. ond costs, BREanif Oft THE LICENSING Anr.--John O'Neil, of Church-street, was charged with aiding and abetting John Foden, on the 9th April, by selling table beer on unlicensed premises. This case was heard on Monday last, when the defendant did not appear. Foden was then fined 40s. and costs, and after hearing the circumstances of the case, O'Neil was fined 10s. and costs. (Mr. Subs sat in this case in the place of the Mayor). "EDUCATION" IN WARRINGTON.—The attendance officer, Mr. G. Riley, had before the court his usual batch of parents who had neglected to send their children regularly to school. The irregular attendance of the children having been proved, the following persons were each fined 55.:—John Higgins, labourer, Latchford ; John Toole, labourer, Latch- ford ; Eunice Cox, Pierpoint-street ; Thomas Bradbury, forgeman, Ship-yard ; Elizabeth Whittaker, greengrocer, Orford-street • John Addison, fustian cutter, Platt-street ; Griffith Williams, forgeman, Pierpoint-street ; Patrick Butler, forgeman, Dial-street ; Peter Begley, hawker, Hay- dock-street; Edward Grounds, forgeman, Pinner's-brow ; Ann Braman, Dial-street. The case of Charles Parry, engine driver, Mersey-street, was adjourned. TUESDAY.—Before Major Cartwright. DRUNEENNESS.—Catherine Brany was fined 58. including costs for being drunk; and for being drunk and disorderly in- Horsemarket-street, a respectably dressed young man named Alfred Wilkinson was fined ss. and. costs or in default seven days' imprisonment.—Fraucia Millett was charged with being drunk and disorq,erly in Bennett-street the previous night. The Pr....soner was drunk in his father's house and be struck 4.is father on the head %.7 ith the poker with such effeet rilat the latter had to be taken to the in- firmary, ihe prisoner continued fighting in the house, and Ws put out, and P.C. McLaren had to lock him up. Millett expressed his willingness to sign the pledge, but he Was told he should have done that before. In reply to Major Cartwright the prisoner said he had been to the Public Hall several times and" heard Mr. Murphy ; " but the magistrate remarked that • Mr. Murphy "bed not made much impreseien upon him apparently." He was fined 10s. including costs. WEDNESDAY.—There were no charges for disposal. TRunsiaava:--Before Alderman Webster. There were only two cases of drunkenness for hearing. One was dismissed, and in the second case Thomas Morgan was tioed 103. and costs or in default .14 days imprison- ment. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. Ziba Armitage. Puovotoreo LANGUAGE—Martha Goodier was summoned by Teresa Turner, of Stockton Heath, for using language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace.—Mr. P.Davies appeared for the complainant.--The defendant pleaded guilty, and gave a promise that she would not further annoy i the complainant. She was, therefote, dismissed. THEFT OF I SHEEP'S HEAD.—M ichael Mahar, of Foundry- lane, and John Wm. Malas, a stranger, were charged with stealing a sheep's head, the property of Frederick Simpson, butcher, Irlam-street.—Whilst standing at the gate of the police station, on the previous afternoon, P.C. Hollingworth saw Mahar take a sheep's head from the shop door, and then Malas spoke to him. The prisoners were taken in custody. They were under the influence of liquor, and pre- tended that they took the sheep's head for a "lark," but it was one they would have carried out to the end, remarked Mr. Hunt, if the constable had not caught them.—Mr. Simpson did not wish to press the case.—The Bench re- corded a conviction, and ordered prisoners to pay ISs costs each. ' ASSAULT.—EIIen Kearns, a young woman, summoned Margaret Lane for assaulting her on the 23rd inst.—lt ap- pears the defendant rented the back kitchen of the complain- ant's house, and some disagreement arising the defendant struck the complainant on the head with a poker.—Defend- ant stated the complainant locked the kitchen door, and would not allow her in the house. She had since left.— Ordered to pay 4s. 6d. costs. A CRASHING CLOG.—A young woman named Margaret Hector was charged with unlawfully damaging the Legh Arms, occupied by John Marsh.—The defendaut went into the house on the 21st inst.- and because the complainant would not serve her with any liquor she sent her clog through a plate glass winnow.—l'efendant, against whom was a long •• sheet," was lined ss. and costs. DEFAULTING FUSTIAN CllTTERs.—Elizabeth Marsh was summoned by Mr. Councillor Platt, master fustian cater, for not complying with an order to pay 16s.—She was ordered to pay the money at the rate of Is. per week.-- Mr. Platt claimed 12s. from Elizabeth Baker, for not fulfil- ling her contract.—Au order was made upon the defendant to pay the money.—An order was made upon Ellen Dol- lard, an apprentice, for 2s. 9d. and costs, for absconding from her work ; and upon Catherine O'Brien, Ann Babbitt, and Eliza O'Brien, for 69. 90. and costs, for not fulfilling their indentures of apprenticeship.--Mrs. Aspey sum- ' mened Wm. Jones to show cause why he should not be committed to gaol for not fulfilling an order of the Bench re- quiring, him to return to his work.—Case adjourned for a week.;--Mabel Gandy was committed to gaol for 14 days' • for a similar offence.--Catherine Mayor. an apprentice, I was summoned by Thomas Hunt for 6s. compensation for wilfully damaging a piece of fustian.—An order was made , for the payment of the money.

div.head: LATEST
div.p: LATEST
David Patterson, a carter, has been arrested at Derby . _
on a charge of causing the death of his wife by a violent
assault.

The Spennymoor branch of the Bishop Auckland co- operative stores was destroyed by fire on Thursday night, the damage being estimated at £20,000. A fire broke out early yesterday morning at Mr. Wasop's, Albert Mill, Pudsey. The mill was dettroyed, and the damage is estimated at £2,000.
A telegram despatched from New York on Thursday
_night says Mr. Ralph Waldo Emerson, the well-known philosophical writer, died at Concord, Massachusetts, at nine
o'clock that:evening.
On Thur;clay nig—lat a large force of police were at the Oldham Skating Rink, and comparative quiet prevailed. A stone was, however, thrown through one of the windows from the Hobson-street side.

To more victims (farmers) of the next•of-Itin frauds are reported from Chadderton, near Oldham. They are named Hall and Wild, and they were led to believe that they were heirs to considerable property. They gave Rogers money

to prosecute their- claim. A Toulon telegram says: The French ironclad Foudvoy- ante, after being launched, was driven by a strong westerly wind, and, breaking from ber moorings, ran aground. Measures have been taken to float her.
-At Exeter, yesterday, a clerk named West was charged with defrauding intending emigrants by charging them a 2s. fee on pretence of obtaining them free passage to Cape
Colony, and £2O bonus when they arrived there. Two hundred persons had paid him money. Prisoner was
remanded.

The Central news learns that Mr. Heneage's motion for the abolition of the Irish Viceroyal Court will probably be econded by Mr Dickson, M.P. for Tyrone. Th% motion is designed as an attack on the system of Irish Government, and not upon those personally concerned in it. The general body of Whigs, acting with Mr. Heneage, are especially desirous that Mr. Forster should not be sacrificed. A riot has occurred in Barcelona between the Castilian and Catalan soldiers of the garrison in consequence of a dis- pute among them relative to the treaty of commerce with France. The officers interfered and restored order. • The
shops in Burgos have been closed as a protest against the seizure of the goods of tradespeople who refused to pay the new taxes.

On Thursday night the dead body of a respectably-dressed man, about 30 years of age, was pulled out of the Manches- ter and Rochdale Canal, near the Skew Bridge, Slattocks, Middleton. The body has the appearance of having been in the water for some time.. Up to yesterday morning it had not been identified, but it is supposed to be that of a tramp. He was drested in a black cloth jacket and vest and brown trousers.

A dariag robbery has been commit4d at the Commercial Hotel, Bolton, belonging to Councillor Priestley. During a banquet at which some 50 brethren of the St. George's Masonic Lodge were present, a man who, it was supposed, was a commercial traveller, abstracted from an ante-room half a dozen overcoats and decamped. One of the coats, belonging to Alderman Harwood, contained a masonic apron, and another, belonging to Councillor Greenhalgh, some valuable papers. The man had been staying at the hotel all day.

At Sale Police Court, yesterday morning, James Mort was charged with bigamy. In 1868 the prisoner was married at St. John's Church, Manchester, and it is alleged that he aftewards married another woman at Bowdon. In each case after living with his wife a short time he left her desti- tute. It is statcd that when apprehended by Sergeant Cooper in Liverpool on Thursiay he was about to be mar- ried a third time.

Yesterday afternoon the Burnley magistrates fined Geo. Beaumont, Ralph Booth, and George Bradley, betting men, a and costs each, under the Vagrant Law Amendment Act, for betting in a street or open space, on Wednesday. Three police officers proved seeing the defendants receiving money, and heard some of them make bets and pay money. In Booth's ,possession were found two telegrams and a letter relating to betting transactions and horse- racing.
RUMOURED RESIGNATION OF THE LORD LIEUTENANT OF IRELAND.
It is reported that Earl Cowper has resigned the Lord Lieutenancy of Ireland, and that his resignation has been accepted. Lord Spencer is g,nerally designated his suc- cessor.

div.head: DEATH PROM EXCESSIVE DRINKING.
div.p: DEATH PROM EXCESSIVE DRINKING.

An inquest was held at Burnley yesterday morning on the body of James Thompson, operative, aged GO years. Since last Christmas he has worked an average of two days a week, and has spent a considerable portion of the other time in drinking. He got drunk on Tuesday, fell down in the road, and died two hours afterwards. The jury returned a verdict of died fro:n natural causes accelerated by exces- sive drinking. FLOODING OF A CHESHIRE COLLIERY.

The water from the upper workings has percolated into the lower range and flooded the Neston Colliery. The col- liery is close to the Dee shore, and as a portion of the works extend under the estuary, an opinion prevails that the mis- chief is serious. Fortunately the occurrence took place at night, when the colliery was clear. Nine ponies are in the pit,and it is feared are dead. A large number of men will be throwsi out of work.

div.head: YOUTHFUL HOUSEBREAKERS.
div.p: YOUTHFUL HOUSEBREAKERS.

At the Stipendiary Court, Fenton, Stok-on-Trent, yester- day morning, Joseph Eardl, 15, who has been several times previously Convicted of felony, was committed for tiial at Staffordshire Quarter Sessions on a charge of house- breaking. Prisoner broke intD the house of Harriet Martin, at Burslem, and stole a silver watch and chain, which he pawned, and then absconded to Manchester and Liverpool, being arrested at the latter. place. Prisoner, although so rung, has had an extraordinary career of crime. MR. GLADSTONE.

Yesterday,.Mr. Gladstone completed the second year ,of his second Premiership. He has now held office longer than any Premier of the century—Pitt being partly of the last century—with the exception of Lord Liverpool and Lord Pal tnerston. Lord Melbeurne had the la:ue ribbon of politics for six years and 226 days, Lord Beaconsfield for six ye„rs and 352 days. Mr. Gladstone has had in two terms a Premiership of seven years and 73 days. Lord Palmerston reigned for nine years and 146 days, Lord Liverpool for nearly fifteen years.

div.head: AN • IMPUDENT BEGGAR.
div.p: AN • IMPUDENT BEGGAR.

At Accrington, yesterday morning, Thomas Davis, a negro, was charged with assaulting Margaret Henderson, housekeeper, Hyndburn House. The prisoner called begging ,n the previous day, and struck the dog, which barked at him. He then struck Henderson on the arm with a thick walking stick and ran away. A groom on horse back fol- lowed him. The prisoner had behaved in a disorderly man- ner at Bentcliffe previously, and was committed to prison for six weeks with hard labaur, and his pedlar's certificate cancelled.

div.head: WIMBLEDON MURDER.
div.p: THE WIMBLEDON MURDER.

EXECUTION OF LAMSON. Great interest was centred in the execution of Dr. Lamson yesterday morning, in Wandsworth Gaol, for the murder o his brother-in-law, Percy John, at Wimbledon, in December last, by administering to him poison. The circumstances of the capital offence are fresh in the public mind, and need not be recounted. The convict's last morning on earth opened heavy and dull, with fitful showers and gusty breezes. From an early hour small groups of idlers gathered outside the gaol, but up to half- past eight nothing like a crowd had assembled as the unfavourable morning prevented any large number of people from collecting. About a dozen police were on duty outside but there was very little call for their services. a flight of 14 steps into the north-east prison yard. He walked with some degree of steadiness, but two warders assisted him on his passage to the scaffold. On emerging from the doorway into the open air Lamson looked about him. The rain was falling heavily, but he ture.ed his face skywards and then gazed at the small knot of pressmen. He descended the stairway and proceeded within the inner gateway where Marwood awaited him. The pinioning straps were then put on and took a minute or so to adjust, the executioner being assisted in this work by two Warders. Lamson bore th 3 ordeal uncommonly well, looking round to see what was being done. The straps having been put on, the melancholy procession again started, and walked towards the scaffold, which was about thirty yards off, but fortunately in an angle of the yard,aad concealed from the view of the convict. On the procession moving, the chaplain,who was dressed in full canonic ils,be, gan reading the burial service, "I am the resurrection emd the life," speaking in a low and somewhat hurried voice. Lamson made no replies, aid in- deed seemed at times to pay mote att'antion to the attendant group of people than to The solemn services in progress. On gaining the scaffold, which was in a shed under cover, he stopped and temk leave of the chaplain, shaking hands with him and saying good-bye in a firm voice. Marwocd thed led him immediately under the drop and put on the white cap. As ate executioner did this the unhappy man was observed to close his eyes, and his body swayed to and fro as if his nerves had at length failed him. In a minute more the fatai bolt was drawn, and the convict was shot into eternity. He died without a struggle. Hardly a movement of a muscle took place, the neck apparently being broken. The chaplain continued reading after the body fell, and concluded by reading the Lord's Prayer. It might be added that there was some difficulty about getting the cap on, during which Marwood whispered to the prisoner to keep steady, but it was, as already stated, beyond his power. Outeipe the prison the idlers increased as the time for the execution drew nigh, until perhaps a couple of hundred had gathered in the vicinity of the main gate. At a quarter to nine, as the prison lJell commenced tolling, a little commo- tion was visible amongst those assembled, but nothing approaching excitement was seen. The black flag was hoisted at one minute past nine o'clock, and the crowd im- mediately dispersed. One young woman was so overcome when the black flag was hoisted that she fainted, but this was the only incident of note which occurred outside the prison.

div.head: CONFESSION OF THE CRIMINAL
div.p: CONFESSION OF THE CRIMINAL

Mr. A. W. Mills, the convict's solicitor, visited his client early on Thursday afternoon, and later in the day Lamson's wife paid him a last visit. The interview, as can easily be ' understood, was of a most painful character, but both bus- , band and wife bore it much better than might have been ex- pected. Mrs. Lamson, indeed, now that the worst is known, appeared to have gained in calmness and self-possession. She was unaccompanied save by her lady friends with whom she has been residing for some weeks past in North London. The father of the prisoner, the Rev. Mr. Lamson, has not v;sited his son since last Sunday, when he then toek leave of him. The parent felt unable to bear any further interview, and has now departed for the Continent to rejoin his wife and daughter to sustain them in the dreadful affliction which has been brought upon them. The following letter, in which the prisoner virtually admits himself guilty of the murder, and explaining the state of mind into which he had fallen through the constant use of morphia and other seda- tives, was written after the interview with his wife, on Thursday afternoon. The letter was addressed to a gentle- man who has shown great interest in the fate of the prisoner : Wandsworth Prison, 27th April, 1882.—My dear Mr. , I feel it my duty to you and all my friends, and especially to my own family and relations, to say a few words in these my last hours upon earth in reference to the offence for which lam condemned to forfeit my life so shortly. I have told you much, and endeavoured to make clear to you my own impressions and ideas as to my mental and moral condi- tion for a long time previous to the act for which I am sentenced to death. The news of my brother-in-law's death roused me from a species of cloud. Then came my long period of imprisonment at Clerkenwell, and while there necessarily the total deprivation of the drug I had so long been accustomed to. With great mental and physical suffering was the weaning accomplished, leaving, however, strongly perceptible results. Then the fearful ordeal of the trial, the awful shock of the sentence, and then the sojourn in the condemned room here, face to face with death, cleared away all cloud from my mind; and now, gazing back into the mists of the past, I believe I can truly and solemnly say, as only can be said under my present condition, that in my right and normal state of mind the compassing and committing such a crime as that for which I must now die would have been utterly and absolutely impossible, and altogether foreign to my own nature and instincts. Subject to mental disturb- ances from slight causes from earliest years, with a brain easily affected, the use or abuse of morphia and sedatives and narcotics made a physical, mental, and moral victim of me. I earnestly pray Almighty God to pardon my yielding to such hakits, and trust they may be an awful warning to others similarly tempted, seeing to what indescribably fear- ful consequences they have led in my case. I earnestly thank you and all my friends for efforts and prayers to obtain mercy for me, and, though ineffectual, you may have the great satisfaction of knowing from me that they were based upon tenable and honest grounds and foundations. Believe me, dear Mr. --, with sincerest gratitude and true friendship and regards, yours, "GEO. H. LAMSON."

div.head: INSANITY QUE STION.
div.p: THE INSANITY QUE STION.

The Lancet says:—ln the case Of Lamson we utterly fail to perceive a particle of evidence whic'a demonstrates his insanity. The plea set up in his behalf has been wholly one of presumption or conjecture that he may have been insane. It is not to be denied that a systematic abuse of poisoned sleep-producers may so deteriorate the brain as to render the mind weak, and place the judgment at the mercy of the lower greeds and impulses. But this is nothing more than admitting that a man may so impair his intellectual powers by drugs or debauchery as to become mentally feeble. Surely we are not as a State or community about to commit the absurdity of allowing self-made stupidity and excitability to be accepted as an excuse for crime ?

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS. Earl MORLEY stated there was no intention that volunteer officers should not have brigade commands.—The House afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. CENTRAL METROPOLITAN RAILWA.Y.—Oa the motion for the second reading of the Central Metropolitan Railway Bill, Mr. W. H. SMITH opposed, as the Bill was promoted by speculators with the desire of obtaining powers which they wanted to sell to other parties.—Mr. Witt-rsitEme also op- posed the bill.—Mr. SIIERIDA.N supported the Bill, and denied it was of the nature represented.—Dr. PLAYFAIR pointed out the defects in the Bill, and declined to vote. for its second reading.—The motion was negatived without a division. THE STATE OF IRELAND —Mr. SEXTON gave notice that en an early day he will call attention to the conduct of Mr. Clifford Lloyd, stipendiary magistrate in Ireland.—Mr. FORSTER, replying to Mr. Ifealy, said the ladies in prison in Ireland under the Protection to Life and Property Act were treated according to prison rules, and the Executive had no power ao alter them. The ladies could release themselves by giving bail.—Mr. HEALY considered the answer unsatis- factory, and gave notice to call attention to the subject.— Mr. FOUSTER said he declined to remove Major Train from the magistracy of Clanmorris. The gentleman was ap• pointed by the late Government. He also declined to order the release of Miss Kirk, arrested by the order of Mr. Clif- ford Lloyd for intimidation. Mr. Clifford Lloyd, he added, was not supplied with blank warrants. LOCAL OPTION.—Mr. GLADSTONE said he could not, as the Government could not introduce the County Boards Bill this session, make any proposals as to Local Option. THE IMPRISONED MEMBERS.—Replying to Mr. Cowen, Mr. CirreaDsToNE declined to answer the question as to the release of Messrs. Parnell, Dillon, and O'Kelly. Mr. Forster would state the views of the Government in the debate next Tuesday. ONE POUND NOTES.—Mr FOWLER called attention to the advantage of the issue of one pound notes, and moved "That in the opinion of the House the prohibition of bank notes of one pound each in England and Wales was un- reasonable, and ought to be removed, and that all needful steps should be forthwith taken to authorise the issue of such notes."—Sir J. LUBBOCK, as an amendment, moved "That it was unreasonable to remove the restriction from circulation of one pound notes without careful inquiry into the effect such chrnge would have on the general currency of the county."—Mr. GLADSTONE OrDRICI not vote for the pro- posals because the effect of carrying the iesolution would require the whole question of the currency to be gone into, which would be impossible in the present position of aft airs. Mr. GOSCHEN thought the Act of 1844 had given the country a good sound currency, and that the resolution of Mr. Fowler was a dangerous proposal in a seductive form. He objected to supplement our present metallic currency with an additional issue of one pound notes.— [LEFT SITTING.] •

That Dar's, Brown Waggon Horse LORI) BEACON ItIFIELD, the property of Mr. Lo)rwrox, Eccleston Grange, will serve Mares during the season at his own stable, Holt-lane Quarry, Wh,ston, at the following charges :—£l each Mare and 2s. od. the Groom, if paid at time 'of serving ; if left for collection £1 10s. each Mare.

ARES WILL BE SERVED at the Stables of Mr. iT Joaxmow, at No. 2, Ford-street, Li7ernool, by any of the well-bred Waggon Entices in his possession, including 'TREE BRITON, "BROWN PRINCE," and "BLACK PRINCE" (who are so well .known for the quantity and quality of their stock), at a fee of LI, and 3s. the groom, if paid on or befare June 24th; and ~L 1 10s., and 3s. tip, groom, if fur- ther credit 'be given. On Wednesdays and Saturdays, between April Ist and June 24th, an Eutire will be in attend- ance during the afternoon, and after six o'clock each evening. " WAXWORK " will serve mares at his own stable, 'Wood- lane, Little Wootton, during the season, on the above condi- tions. Owners of marts will have the privilege of using any horse if they desire a change. No business done on Sundays. All mares tried must be paid for.

MANCHESTER TAILORING & CLOTHING DEPOT, 8, 'HORSEMARKET STREET, WARRINGTON. 1882 SPRING AND SUMMER SEASONS. 1882 The Proprietors of the MANCHESTER TAILORING AND CLOTHING DEPor are convinced that the inhabitants of War- rington and the surrounding Districts see that it is to their interests to support them in their endeavour to supply GOOD FASHIONABLE WELL-MADE CLOTHING FOR MEN, YOUTHS, AND BOYS, at prices so much lower than other houses. Their increasing trade each season is positive proof that the goods give satisfaction, and they are determined' to sustain their reputation by sparing no expense in producing the most FASHIONABLE SIILE3 from the M. OST DUR ABLE CLOTHS at the m7st moderatd prices. From the encouragement they have received, their prepara- tions for the coming season. are far more extensive than any previous year, careful attention having been given to the selection of such high art designs and styles in all the best makes of Woollen Cloths as will ,satisfy the various tastes of their numerous customers.
